body:
## Context

#327 delivered ARIA roles, keyboard operability, accessible chart names, focus-visible states, live
regions and reduced-motion handling for the two embedded UIs it names: the admin status page
(`internal/app/statushtml`) and the flow view (`internal/app/flowhtml`).

A **third** embedded page landed the same day — the audit/webhook event explorer at `/events`
(`internal/app/eventshtml`, #300). It was outside #327's scope because #327 was written before it
existed, so it is in the pre-#327 state: no ARIA roles, no keyboard handlers, no live regions, no
reduced-motion handling.

This is not a defect in either issue; it is the seam between two things built in parallel. Filing it
so the gap is recorded rather than discovered later by someone who cannot use the page.

## Scope

Apply #327's established patterns to `internal/app/eventshtml`. Read #327's completing commit first —
the point is to reuse its conventions, not to invent a second set:

- Live regions for the error and truncation/overflow banners (`role="alert"` / `role="status"`).
- Keyboard operability and `role`/`aria-pressed`/`aria-label` on any interactive row or control,
  following `flowhtml`'s `buildTable()` treatment.
- `:focus-visible` rules, since the defaults are invisible against this page's palette.
- Reduced-motion handling only if the page has perceptible animation — #327 found `statushtml` had
  none and said so rather than claiming a fix.

## Constraints

- **Zero external assets.** The CSP is `default-src 'none'` with no origin permitted in any directive
  (#322), enforced by a test that walks every directive. One inline bundle, as the other two pages do.
- **Assert rendered MARKUP, never a bare phrase.** Every human-facing string on these pages exists
  twice — once in the Go template and once in the JavaScript that rebuilds the same table on poll.
  Five assertions in `statushtml_test.go` have passed with the template block deleted. Verify each new
  assertion by deleting the construct it guards.
- Behaviour that lives purely in JS cannot be proven by a markup test. There is no browser or JS test
  harness in this repo and one must NOT be added. Say plainly what is implemented-but-not-behaviourally-
  verified rather than claiming coverage.

## Acceptance

- [ ] Interactive elements are reachable and operable by keyboard, with roles and accessible names.
- [ ] Error and overflow banners announce via live regions.
- [ ] Focus-visible states are present and legible.
- [ ] Every new guard is negative-tested by deleting the construct it guards.
- [ ] Any acceptance criterion NOT met is stated with its reason, not omitted.
title: Complete accessibility and keyboard support for the /events explorer

body:
## Context

This repo writes logs into the same Grafana Cloud Loki tenant as `opnsense-exporter` and
`graph2otel`. That repo has five promoted index labels; this one has **none**, and cannot have
any as currently built. This issue records why, and what it would cost if that is ever worth
changing. **It is reference, not queued work** — the honest current answer is probably that it is
not worth it.

The shared naming contract lives at
<https://github.com/rknightion/opnsense-exporter/blob/main/docs/otlp-attribute-contract.md>.

## Why nothing here can be promoted today

Loki's `otlp_config` has an `index_label` action **only** under `resource_attributes`.
`scope_attributes` and `log_attributes` accept `structured_metadata` and `drop`, and nothing else.
So a log attribute can never become an index label, whatever the tenant config says.

This exporter's `buildResource()` in `internal/telemetry/provider.go` sets `service.name`, an
optional `service.version`, `service.instance.id`, and the `WithTelemetrySDK`/`WithOS`/`WithProcess*`
detectors. **No custom attribute reaches the resource.** Every domain dimension is set on the
record, so all of it arrives as structured metadata — queryable with `|`, never as a stream
selector.

Nothing is broken by this. Structured metadata is exactly where a non-promoted attribute would land
anyway; the only cost is query scan.

## What promotion would take

Not a rename. An OTLP resource binds to a `LoggerProvider`, not to a record, so **N distinct values
of a dimension means N `LoggerProvider`s**. `opnsense-exporter`'s `internal/logship/sink_otlp.go` is
what that looks like in practice: a provider map keyed on a resource key, one shared exporter so
partitioning costs no extra connections, deterministic per-partition flush ordering, a
`maxLogResources` cap, and a degrade path that drops the custom attributes once the cap is hit —
which had to be raised from 64 to 256 there, and where overshooting silently destroys the labels
that already work.

That is materially more than a config change, and it buys query scan only. Loki bills on volume;
promotion does not reduce ingest cost at all.

## Naming, if it ever happens

Per the contract: namespace under an emitter prefix, never bare unnamespaced names, never squat a
semconv namespace with a foreign meaning, and use a genuine semconv name where the meaning actually
matches. Dimensions stay emitter-specific rather than shared — a unified label whose values mean
different things per exporter leaves `service.name` as the only disambiguator, which is what you
already had.

## The slot question, settled

An earlier framing held that the three exporters compete for a tenant-wide pool of ~15 promotion
slots, and that each one namespacing its own dimensions would exhaust it. **That was wrong.** The 15
is `max_label_names_per_series` — the maximum label names on a *single stream*, enforced by the
distributor at ingest. A stream from this exporter never carries an `opnsense_*` label, so the
pools were never shared and each exporter independently gets its own 15.

The genuinely shared resource is the tenant's promoted-attribute *list*, capped well above what
three exporters need. Adding entries to it is additive and cannot affect another exporter's streams,
but it is one list, so edits are coordinated and must be GET-merge-PUT rather than a blind partial
write.

## If this is ever picked up

- [ ] Decide which dimensions are worth a stream selector rather than a `|` filter, from real query
      patterns rather than in the abstract
- [ ] Check the distinct-value count of each — a `LoggerProvider` per combination is the cost
- [ ] Hoist onto the resource under a `<emitter>.*` namespace, following the `sink_otlp.go` pattern
      including the cap and the degrade path
- [ ] Add the dotted attribute names to the tenant `otlp_config` list, GET-merge-PUT
- [ ] Verify with `gcx datasources loki series` — presence there is proof of promotion, since
      structured metadata cannot appear in `series` output

Filed from rknightion/opnsense-exporter#477.
title: docs: record why no log attribute here can be promoted to a Loki index label

body:
## Finding

A configured object-store `prefix` with a **leading** slash silently destroys durable listing progress. Every persisted scan-position row is classified stale and deleted on the cycle that loads it, so partitioned enumeration restarts from the beginning of each day partition on every cycle and never retains a position.

`dayPrefixes` trims only the **trailing** slash from the configured base (`strings.TrimSuffix(base, "/")`), so a configured `/flow` produces the prefix `/flow/2026/07/24/`. `isConfiguredDayPrefix` trims **both** ends (`strings.Trim(configuredBasePrefix, "/")`), so it looks for a row starting `flow/` and rejects the very prefix enumeration just built.

## Evidence — reproduced directly against `main`

An in-package probe over `dayPrefixes` and `isConfiguredDayPrefix` for the same configured base:

```
base="flow"   dayPrefix="flow/2026/07/24/"       isConfiguredDayPrefix=true
base="/flow"  dayPrefix="/flow/2026/07/24/"      isConfiguredDayPrefix=false
base=""       dayPrefix="2026/07/24/"            isConfiguredDayPrefix=true
```

The middle row is the defect: enumeration lists that prefix, then the loader disowns it.

## Why it is worse than wasted requests

`loadScanState` returns unrecognised rows as `StaleKeys`, and `Collect` deletes them. So the position is not merely ignored, it is erased every cycle. That defeats #285's bounded backlog progression: a deployment whose backlog exceeds one page can never advance past the first page, because the `startAfter` that would carry it forward is deleted before the next cycle reads it. Combined with the timestamp-cursor lower bound, objects beyond the first page of a busy day partition can be starved indefinitely while every health signal stays green.

## Existing inconsistency this also resolves

`internal/config`'s `objectStoreFeedKey` already normalises the prefix with `strings.Trim(prefix, "/")`, so config treats `/flow` and `flow` as the **same feed** for #284's duplicate-feed rejection, while the collector treats them as different. Whatever the fix, the two should agree.

## Recommended fix

Normalise the configured prefix once, at the config boundary, by trimming leading and trailing slashes — a leading slash is never meaningful in an S3 key prefix. That makes `/flow` and `flow` identical everywhere and keeps a single definition of the prefix rather than two functions that must agree. The alternative, making `isConfiguredDayPrefix` trim only the trailing slash to match `dayPrefixes`, leaves `/flow` and `flow` as distinct durable namespaces and keeps the config/collector disagreement above.

Note the flat layout added by #293 is unaffected: `isConfiguredScanPrefix` compares against `flatPrefix(base)`, built the same way the prefix it lists is built, so that path is already self-consistent.

## Acceptance

- [x] A configured prefix with a leading slash retains its durable scan position across cycles.
- [ ] ~~`/flow`, `flow`, `flow/` and `/flow/` resolve to one durable prefix identity, and the config-side feed identity agrees with the collector-side scan identity.~~ **Superseded by the correction comment below and deliberately NOT done** — collapsing the spellings changes the `FeedID` digest and orphans an existing `/flow` deployment's cursor and seen set, re-emitting its history. The spellings stay distinct feeds; the config-side check remains stricter on purpose. See the amended acceptance in the comment.
- [x] Existing rows written under the pre-fix spelling either continue to resolve or are migrated; a fix must not silently orphan a running deployment's progress. State which, with a test.
- [x] Table-driven coverage over the four spellings for both layouts.
- [x] No key, bucket or endpoint value enters a metric label or log line.

## Provenance

Found while implementing #293 and verified independently against `main`. Filed under #478 so nothing is untracked; it is inside this tracker's durable-listing and loss-semantics mission.

comments.body:
## Correction to the recommended fix above

The body recommends normalising the configured prefix at the config boundary. **That is wrong, and would cause duplicate emission.** Verified against `main` after filing.

`objectstore.FeedID` is a plain length-prefixed SHA-256 over its parts with **no normalisation of any kind**, and it supplies the `<feed-digest>` segment of the frozen #453 checkpoint namespace `objectstore/v1/<base64url-tailnet>/<provider>/<signal>/<feed-digest>/`. So trimming the prefix at the config boundary changes the digest for a deployment configured with `/flow`, which orphans its cursor and its whole seen set. The next cycle would cold-start from `initial_lookback` (default 6h) against a bucket whose recent objects are no longer remembered, and re-emit every one of them.

That converts a wasted-LIST-calls bug into a data-duplication bug, which is strictly worse.

## Revised recommendation

Fix the predicate, not the input: make `isConfiguredDayPrefix` trim only the **trailing** slash, exactly as `dayPrefixes` does when it builds the prefix. Two functions describing the same string then agree, `/flow` keeps its existing durable namespace, no state moves, and nothing is re-emitted.

The residual inconsistency is acceptable and errs safe: `internal/config`'s `objectStoreFeedKey` trims both ends, so two tailnets configured `/flow` and `flow` are still rejected as the same feed under #284, even though they would in fact use different checkpoint namespaces. Rejecting an ambiguous pair of spellings is the right direction for that check to fail in.

If normalising the prefix is wanted anyway — and there is a reasonable argument that a leading slash is never meaningful in an S3 key prefix — it needs an explicit, atomic, idempotent state migration in the shape #453 already established for legacy rows, and that should be its own issue rather than being smuggled into this fix.

## Amended acceptance

- [ ] A configured prefix with a leading slash retains its durable scan position across cycles.
- [ ] `dayPrefixes` and `isConfiguredDayPrefix` derive the base identically, with a test that would fail if they diverge again.
- [ ] The feed digest for an existing `/flow` deployment is **unchanged**, so no cursor or seen state is orphaned and nothing is re-emitted. Prove this with a test asserting the digest before and after.
- [ ] Table-driven coverage over `flow`, `/flow`, `flow/`, `/flow/` for both layouts.
- [ ] No key, bucket or endpoint value enters a metric label or log line.

The flat layout added by #293 remains unaffected — `isConfiguredScanPrefix` compares against `flatPrefix(base)`, built the same way the prefix it lists is built.

## Closed by `2fb0c45`

`fix(objectstore): stop erasing durable listing progress under a leading-slash prefix` — pushed
direct to `main`.

Fixed the way the [correction comment](#issuecomment-5091062521) revised it, **not** the way the
issue body originally recommended. One definition of the base — `objectstore.scanBase`, trimming
only the trailing slash — is now shared by `dayPrefixes`, `flatPrefix` and `isConfiguredDayPrefix`,
so the string a cycle lists and the string a persisted row is recognized under cannot diverge again.

### Why the body's recommendation was rejected

Normalising the prefix at the config boundary would change the `FeedID` digest for a deployment
configured `/flow`. That digest is the `<feed-digest>` segment of the frozen #453 checkpoint
namespace and applies no normalisation of its own, so the change would orphan that deployment's
cursor **and its entire seen set**: the next cycle cold-starts from `initial_lookback` and re-emits
everything it had already ingested. A wasted-requests bug would have become a data-duplication bug.

`TestFeedID_PrefixSpellingsStayDistinctFeeds` now pins the digest and asserts the four spellings stay
four feeds, so a later "the prefix should really be tidied up" change cannot make that trade by
accident.

The second acceptance box is therefore **struck through rather than ticked** — collapsing the
spellings into one identity was the thing not to do. The body has been annotated accordingly.

### The residual asymmetry is intentional

`internal/config`'s `objectStoreFeedKey` still trims both ends, so two tailnets configured `/flow`
and `flow` are rejected as the same feed even though they would in fact use different checkpoint
namespaces. Rejecting an ambiguous pair of spellings is the right direction for a duplicate-feed
check to fail in. Both sides now carry a comment saying so and pointing at the other, so neither gets
"fixed" into agreement later.

### One addition beyond the fix

A leading slash is now load-bearing rather than merely harmless, so `Warnings()` advises against it
and `docs/configuration.md`, `config.example.yaml` and the chart's `values.yaml` all say the same
thing: ingestion works, but removing it later reads as a brand-new feed, so drop it while there is no
state to lose. This is the safe half of normalisation — advice, not a silent rewrite. Actually
migrating existing state to a normalised prefix would need its own atomic idempotent migration in the
shape #453 established, and remains unfiled and undone.

### Local verification

Run in a throwaway `git worktree` at `HEAD` holding **exactly** this diff, `cmp`-verified against the
staged tree file-by-file:

- root + `tools/configcheck` + `tools/metricscatalog` + `tools/apidrift`: `go build`, `go vet`,
  `go test -race`, `golangci-lint run` — all clean
- `govulncheck` — no vulnerabilities
- `helm lint`; render tests **141 passed, 0 failed**; `configcheck` on the example and the
  chart-rendered config
- `scripts/regen-generated.sh` — all four generated artifacts already in sync, zero drift
- GoReleaser snapshot, Docker build, `actionlint`, `zizmor` — pass

Both new tests were mutation-proven by restoring the two-ended trim: the round-trip test fails for
`/flow` and `/flow/`, and the end-to-end two-cycle test fails reporting the erased position directly
(`calls = [{Prefix:/flow/2026/07/24/ StartAfter:} {Prefix:/flow/2026/07/24/ StartAfter:}]` — the
second cycle restarting at the beginning of the partition, which is the defect verbatim).

### Actions evidence

All applicable workflows green for `2fb0c45`.

### Deviations

- **No `Chart.yaml` version bump.** The chart change is comment-only — no values keys added or
  altered — and the repo convention is to bump only for a values change. Its version history did gain
  the two notes that were missing for `0.14.6` (#293's `layout` key) and `0.14.7` (#288's audit
  block), both of which landed without one.
- **No new metrics.** A prefix value must never reach a label, so the fix is observable only through
  the existing `objectstore.*` series behaving correctly.

title: fix(objectstore): a leading-slash prefix erases durable listing progress every cycle

body:
## Finding

When **every** row in an object fails to decode, the object is treated as successfully ingested: the seen-set records it, the cursor advances past it, no durable gap is created, and `tailscale2otel.objectstore.gap.healthy` stays at `1`. The object is never retried, so the data is permanently lost and every health signal reports the path as fine.

This is the tail case of a deliberate design — decode and validation failures are row-local sentinels so one malformed record cannot block a feed forever (#286, #448). That is right for *one* bad row. It is wrong for *all* rows, because 100% decode failure is the signature of a **framing mismatch** (the object is not newline-delimited bare records) rather than of individual corrupt records, and a framing mismatch means the whole feed is silently discarded object after object.

## Evidence — reproduced directly against `main`

A probe object containing a single top-level JSON array with no newlines — i.e. exactly what a framing mismatch looks like — driven through one full `Collect` cycle:

```
skipped by reason: map[string]float64{"decode_error":1}
objects metric:    1
records metric:    0
gaps gauge:        0
gap healthy:       1
```

`objects=1` counts it as ingested, `records=0` shows nothing was extracted, and `gaps=0` with `gap.healthy=1` means nothing will ever retry it and no alert can fire.

## Why this matters now

Our flow-log object framing has never been validated against a real Tailscale S3 object — the `.capture/` fixtures are poll-API and Splunk-HEC bodies, and the committed `official-network-export.ndjson` fixture is synthetic. Meanwhile the real log-stream publisher, captured live, emits **concatenated JSON values with no separators** on the HEC path. If the S3 objects share that framing, today's newline splitter yields exactly this all-rows-fail case and would have discarded every object while reporting perfect health. That is the failure mode this guard has to make loud.

## Acceptance

- [ ] An object that yields zero accepted records while producing at least one decode failure is treated as a failed object: durable gap, retried under the existing bounded policy, and reflected in `gap.healthy`.
- [ ] A genuinely empty object (zero rows, e.g. the zero-length objects Tailscale is known to write) still completes cleanly and creates no gap — it is not a failure.
- [ ] An object with a mix of good and bad rows keeps today's row-local behavior exactly: good rows commit, bad rows are counted, object completes.
- [ ] The distinction is visible in bounded telemetry, with no object key, bucket or free-text error in any label.
- [ ] Coverage for all four shapes: all-fail, none-fail, mixed, and empty.

## Provenance

Found while gathering wire evidence for #288. Filed retroactively under #478 so nothing is untracked; it is within this tracker's loss-semantics mission and is a prerequisite for ingesting a second signal whose framing we cannot yet prove.

comments.body:
## Closing receipt

Closed by `4f670abb636afeed079195b9a2634b0477476269`.

**Where the decision is made.** In `ingest()`, after the preparation loop and the existing cancellation gate, and **before** the commit loop:

```go
if acceptedRows == 0 && bad+semanticBad > 0 {
```

`acceptedRows` is a new pre-commit counter — `result.acceptedRecords` is deliberately still zero at that point because it counts *committed* records. `bad`/`semanticBad` are the existing row-local `ErrRecordDecode`/`ErrRecordInvalid` counters. Placement is deliberate on both sides: after `ctx.Err()` so a real shutdown is still attributed to cancellation rather than misreported as a framing mismatch, and before the commit loop so a failed object commits nothing.

**Empty is not failure.** Zero rows means zero failures, so the condition is false and the object completes with no gap — required, because Tailscale does write zero-length objects (upstream tailscale/tailscale#16124 shows one in the field). Blank rows `continue` before the row counter increments, so they reach neither side of the condition.

**Validation failures count, deliberately.** This looks over-broad until you consider the envelope case: a record shaped `{"time":…,"event":{…}}` unmarshals *successfully* into an all-zero value and fails **validation**, not decoding. Excluding validation failures would therefore have missed the single most likely framing mismatch. Confirmed by mutation: restricting the guard to `bad > 0` makes the all-validation-failure test report `skipped = map[semantic_invalid:2], want one undecodable_object`.

**No parallel mechanism.** The guard returns `&objectIngestError{stage: stageUndecodableObject}` — the same type the existing `fetch`/`decompress`/`read`/`process` stages return — so `classifyObjectFailure`, gap creation, `gapRetryDelay` backoff, `persistGap` and `emitGapHealth` are all untouched. The diff to the failure path is one line, swapping a hardcoded skip reason for `skipReasonForStage(failure.stage)`. `state.go` needed no change; no new gap type, retry clock, quarantine trigger, state row or config key.

**Correction to the issue's own framing — my brief was wrong.** The brief said "the existing bounded retry naturally escalates it to quarantine". It does not. `gap.Quarantined` is set only from error classification or an unparseable gap key; `Attempts` feeds `gapRetryDelay` and nothing else, and there is no attempt-count threshold anywhere in the package. `TestCollect_GapRetryBackoffIsBoundedButDoesNotAbandon` already pins retry-forever as deliberate. I verified this against the source rather than accepting it second-hand. So the acceptance item "repeated failure reaches quarantine via the existing bounded policy" was **unsatisfiable as written** and has been dropped.

Retry-forever is also the right behaviour here on the merits, not just the path of least change: a framing mismatch is fixed by a code change, so a pending gap is retried and recovers automatically once the fix ships, whereas quarantine is terminal and writes a seen identity beside the gap, leaving every affected object unrecoverable without manual row deletion. The loud signal is `gap.healthy=0` with `gap.oldest.age` climbing without bound. Pinned by `TestCollect_RepeatedUndecodableFailureStaysPendingAndKeepsRetrying` (nine attempts across the full backoff ladder, gap row stays pending, `gap.healthy` sustained 0).

**Bounded telemetry.** New closed reason `undecodable_object` on `tailscale2otel.objectstore.skipped`, added to the closed set with descriptor text explaining that a non-zero value means a broken feed rather than corrupt data. The metric attribute is the constant alone; the log carries a digest of the identity plus three integers; the error string is integers only. Mutation-proven: appending the raw identity to the stage makes the leak test fail with `diagnostics leaked the raw object key: … stage=undecodable_object:customer-private/flow/…`.

**Boundary tests proven load-bearing by mutation** rather than assumed, since they passed on first run: dropping the failure requirement breaks the empty-object and blank-row tests; dropping validation failures breaks the all-validation case; moving the guard after the commit loop breaks `data-quality points = 1, want 0 — a failed object must commit nothing`; reverting the reason to `read_error` breaks the reason assertions.

**Contracts confirmed unchanged.** #448 atomicity — the decision is pre-commit so a failed object emits nothing, with five existing atomicity tests untouched and still passing. #292 limit accounting — every limit breach returns from the scan/decompress phase, structurally before the prepare loop, so it can never reach the guard and keeps its own `expansion.limit_failures`; four existing limit tests untouched. Mixed objects and blank-line handling each have a new test plus untouched existing coverage.

**Known consequence, accepted:** a single-record object whose one record is permanently invalid now produces a lasting gap and `gap.healthy=0` until acknowledged. That follows directly from counting validation failures, which is required for the envelope case above. `flowlog.Validate` is partly clock-dependent so some violations clear on retry; otherwise the documented acknowledgement path applies. Also, row-local `decode_error`/`semantic_invalid` are no longer emitted for a *failed* object, consistent with the existing contract that a failed object gets no row-local dispositions — so the all-fail case now reads as one `undecodable_object` rather than N `decode_error`, which is worth knowing when reading dashboards.

**Follow-up, not done here:** no dashboard panel or alert covers `undecodable_object` yet. That belongs to #399 under the #481 tracker, which owns object-store ingestion health panels and alerts, and is noted there rather than expanding this child.

**Local verification of the exact committed tree,** in an isolated worktree containing only this change on top of `3df1b32`: root build/vet green, `go test -race ./...` exit 0 across 54 packages with no FAIL/panic/DATA RACE, `golangci-lint run` `0 issues`; all three tool modules green; `docs/metrics.md` regenerated (diff exactly the one descriptor line) and `metricscatalog -check` in sync; `helm lint`/`template` plus 126 render checks; `configcheck` OK; secret hygiene PASS; `actionlint` and `zizmor` clean; `govulncheck` no vulnerabilities; GoReleaser snapshot and Docker build succeeded.

**Actions evidence — all eight applicable workflows terminal success for the exact SHA:** CI `30258925344`, Release `30258926102`, CodeQL `30258926060`, Docker Security `30258925873`, Scorecard `30258925805`, actionlint `30258925785`, zizmor `30258925771`, documentation sync `30258925352`. CI and CodeQL were initially `cancelled` by a later push (`ci.yml` uses `concurrency: cancel-in-progress: true` on the ref) and were re-run against this exact SHA; both are green as recorded.

body:
## Finding

`parseKey` silently refuses the long compression extensions on the `.json` stem, so objects named `<prefix>/YYYY/MM/DD/HH:MM:SS.json.zstd` or `.json.gzip` are **never fetched**. They are counted only as `tailscale2otel.objectstore.skipped{reason="unrecognized_key"}`, and ingestion health stays green while the data is dropped.

The suffix table in `internal/collector/objectstore/key.go` carries the long forms (`.zstd`, `.gzip`) only for the `.ndjson` stem. For the `.json` stem it carries `.json.zst`, `.json.gz` and `.json` alone. `strings.CutSuffix("09:05:00.json.zstd", ".json.zst")` does not match, because the string ends `.zstd`; `.json` does not match either, because the string does not end there.

## Evidence — reproduced directly against `main`

A throwaway probe calling `parseKey` on the four spellings:

```
key=pre/2026/07/27/09:05:00.json.zstd        ok=false comp=0 at=0001-01-01 00:00:00 +0000 UTC
key=pre/2026/07/27/09:05:00.json.gzip        ok=false comp=0 at=0001-01-01 00:00:00 +0000 UTC
key=pre/2026/07/27/09:05:00.json.zst         ok=true  comp=1 at=2026-07-27 09:05:00 +0000 UTC
key=pre/2026/07/27/09:05:00.json.gz          ok=true  comp=2 at=2026-07-27 09:05:00 +0000 UTC
```

`ok=false` means the object never becomes a candidate, so no GET is ever issued.

## Why the long form is realistic, not hypothetical

Tailscale's own other S3 export path documents the **long** extension: Aperture usage export writes `ts-aperture-export-<unix-timestamp>.cbor.zstd`. The log-streaming docs never state the extension↔codec pairing at all — the illustrative key is `…/12:34:56.json` while the default compression is `zstd`, so the docs do not establish which spelling the publisher uses. The existing table already accepts `.ndjson.zstd`/`.ndjson.gzip` precisely because copies land with varied extensions; the `.json` stem was simply missed.

`key_test.go` tests the long forms only against `.ndjson`, which is why this survived #447.

## Acceptance

- [ ] `.json.zstd` and `.json.gzip` parse to the correct timestamp and codec.
- [ ] Table-driven coverage over the full cross-product of stem (`.json`, `.ndjson`) and codec spelling (`.zst`, `.zstd`, `.gz`, `.gzip`, none), so a future addition cannot cover one stem and miss the other.
- [ ] Existing accepted spellings are unchanged.
- [ ] No key, bucket or endpoint value enters a metric label or log line.

## Provenance

Found while gathering wire evidence for #288. Filed retroactively under #478 so nothing is untracked; it is squarely within this tracker's key-contract and loss-semantics mission and is a gap in #447's delivery.

comments.body:
## Closing receipt

Closed by `3df1b32634a32d6116679db63f191f4c5ec6bd3f`.

**Fix.** Both stems now carry all five codec spellings. `.json.zstd` → zstd and `.json.gzip` → gzip, matching what `.ndjson` already had.

**Ordering verified, not assumed.** `strings.CutSuffix` matches in slice order and `parseKey` returns on the first hit without falling through, so a shorter extension that is a byte-suffix of a longer one would shadow it. Checked explicitly: `.json.zst` does **not** shadow `.json.zstd` — the last nine bytes of a `.json.zstd` key are `json.zstd`, not `.json.zst`, so the shorter entry cannot match. `.zst`/`.zstd` and `.gz`/`.gzip` diverge on their final byte and the stem keeps the families apart, so today's order is not load-bearing. The invariant is now recorded in a comment so a later addition rechecks it rather than assuming first-match-wins is always safe.

**RED evidence, established by reverting only the two table rows.** Exactly four cells fail and no others:

```
--- FAIL: TestParseKey/official_long_zstd_layout_on_the_json_stem
--- FAIL: TestParseKey/official_long_gzip_layout_on_the_json_stem
--- FAIL: TestParseKey_StemCodecCrossProduct/official.json.zstd
        parseKey("flow/2026/07/24/09:05:00.json.zstd") ok = false, want true
--- FAIL: TestParseKey_StemCodecCrossProduct/official.json.gzip
--- FAIL: TestParseKey_StemCodecCrossProduct/legacy.json.zstd
--- FAIL: TestParseKey_StemCodecCrossProduct/legacy.json.gzip
```

The precision matters: only the `.json` long forms fail, which is exactly the claimed defect and nothing else.

**Coverage.** `TestParseKey_StemCodecCrossProduct` pins 20 cells — two stems x five codec spellings x both basename shapes (the official time-only basename whose date comes from the partition directories, and the legacy self-contained one). It asserts the exact codec rather than just `ok=true`, so a key matching the wrong entry is caught rather than passing on a false `ok`. Adding a stem or spelling to one family and not the other now fails on the precise missing cell. The cross-product was extended to cover both basename shapes during review; as delivered it covered only the legacy shape.

**Local verification of the exact committed tree,** in an isolated worktree containing only this change on top of `26bb03c`: root build/vet green, `go test -race ./...` exit 0 across 54 packages with no FAIL/panic/DATA RACE, `golangci-lint run` `0 issues`; all three tool modules green; `docs/metrics.md` in sync and `TestEnvReferenceDocInSync` passing; `helm lint`/`template` plus 126 render checks; `configcheck` OK; secret hygiene PASS; `actionlint` and `zizmor` clean; `govulncheck` no vulnerabilities; GoReleaser snapshot and Docker build succeeded.

**Actions evidence — all seven applicable workflows terminal success for the exact SHA:** CI `30258562769`, Release `30258563270`, CodeQL `30258563105`, Docker Security `30258563228`, Scorecard `30258563088`, actionlint `30258563070`, zizmor `30258563099`. Helm and documentation sync correctly did not trigger; this commit touches only `internal/collector/objectstore/**`.

**Process note.** The CI run for this SHA was initially `cancelled`, not failed: `ci.yml` uses `concurrency: cancel-in-progress: true` keyed on the ref, so two later pushes to `main` cancelled it while it was still running. It was re-run against this exact SHA and is now green, as recorded above. Re-runs share that concurrency group, so they had to be serialised one SHA at a time.

body:
## Why

Do not add further dashboard panels, features, or coverage until the dashboard generator can express the navigation and feature-aware rendering expected of the flagship. The current generator must become a first-class Grafana v2 dynamic-dashboard system, rather than accumulating more panels in a flatter layout.

`../opnsense-exporter/grafana/` is the single implementation reference for this work. Its generated `dashboard.json` is the quality bar; specifically study `build_dashboard.py`, `builder.py`, `tabs/`, `README.md`, and its tests before designing or changing the tailscale2otel generator. Reuse the design lessons, not OPNsense metric names or domain-specific dashboard content.

## Required capabilities

- Grafana dashboard v2 output with a coherent dynamic layout model.
- Clear top-level domains with sub-tabs and, where useful, nested navigation instead of an ever-growing flat dashboard.
- Declarative, reusable helpers for panels, rows, tabs, grouping, layout packing, datasource/variable conventions, and value mappings.
- Presence/sentinel-driven conditional rendering: hide rows, tabs, and whole feature areas when their backing signal is unavailable, a collector/source is disabled, a capability is unsupported, or a datasource is absent.
- Preserve useful empty/error states where a feature is configured but unhealthy; absence/disabled must not be rendered as a misleading healthy zero.
- Generated dashboard artifacts with deterministic regeneration, structural tests, and a coverage/quality gate appropriate to the catalog and dashboard contract.

## Scope and sequencing

This is an enabling prerequisite for dashboard expansion, not a request to copy the OPNsense dashboard wholesale. Establish the generator architecture and migrate the existing flagship/dashboard surface onto it before adding new panels or feature coverage. Review and reconcile the existing dashboard issues in EPIC-05, especially #391 through #406, so their work consumes this stable foundation instead of bypassing it.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The implementation starts with a documented, code-backed comparison against `../opnsense-exporter/grafana/`; it identifies the transferable v2/dynamic-dashboard capabilities and explicitly rejects domain-specific parts that do not apply.
- [ ] The tailscale2otel dashboard generator exposes tested primitives for top-level tabs, nested/sub-tabs, rows, panel elements, layout, and conditional rendering.
- [ ] The flagship uses the new navigation model and demonstrates feature-aware hiding at tab and row scope from real availability/configuration signals.
- [ ] Disabled, unsupported, absent, and unhealthy states have deliberate, distinct rendering semantics.
- [ ] Generation is deterministic and guarded by tests that validate the v2 structure, navigation hierarchy, conditional-rendering contracts, and generated-artifact drift.
- [ ] Existing dashboard/rule validation remains green; all affected generated artifacts and documentation are regenerated.
- [ ] No new dashboard panel or coverage issue is implemented ahead of this foundation unless this issue explicitly records why it is independent.

## Agent instructions

Read #481 and every relevant child issue in full before work. Treat this issue as P0: resolve it before starting new dashboard panels, features, or coverage. Keep the EPIC checklist and sequencing current, use TDD, and close from a verified direct-to-main commit.

comments.body:
### Substantially done — remaining scope is nested sub-tab navigation only

**The issue's premise was wrong, and correcting it changed the work.** The generator was *already* emitting Grafana v2: `apiVersion: dashboard.grafana.app/v2`, a real `TabsLayout` → `RowsLayout` → `GridLayout` nesting, panels in `spec.elements` referenced by `ElementReference`, and working `ConditionalRenderingVariable` gating from 34 presence variables. There was no v2 migration to do.

The genuine gaps against `../opnsense-exporter/grafana/`, and what happened to each:

| gap | status |
| --- | --- |
| one 2536-line `build.py` | **done** (`8f36ffd`) — split into `builder.py` + `variables.py` + `maps.py` + `tabs/*.py` + a 128-line orchestrator, verified **byte-identical** |
| sentinels declared in one shared function | **done** — moved into the owning tab module, again byte-identical |
| almost no tests, and none that CI ran | **done** (`5841ebd`) — `test_ingest_freshness.py` was invoked by *nothing*; both Python suites now run in `dashboards-drift`, guarded so a directory with no tests cannot pass vacuously |
| no expression parsing | **done** — `tools/promqlcheck` (#407) |
| no nested navigation | **NOT DONE** — see below |

The split is what made the P2 content wave possible at all: four lanes added panels concurrently to four different tab modules, which one file could not have supported.

**Two findings from the refactor.** It surfaced **10 dead sentinels** — registered variables querying Prometheus on every dashboard load while gating nothing; five are now wired to the row each should always have gated, and the rest carry a written reason. And a `--tab` single-tab preview now registers only that tab's sentinels, so a preview of a tab that *consumes* a sentinel it does not *own* would reference an undeclared variable. Harmless for the full build; recorded so it is not rediscovered as a bug.

### Remaining scope

Ten flat top-level tabs. The reference groups 41 leaves under 7 domains via a second `TabsLayout` nested inside each `TabsLayoutTab`, with two-level gating — a tab containing only conditional rows still renders unless the tab itself is conditional. At 404 panels across 10 tabs the flat model is starting to strain, so this is worth doing, but it is now an independent piece of work rather than a blocker: **every dashboard child of #481 that was waiting on this foundation has since shipped against it.**

### One acceptance criterion that cannot be met as written

> *Disabled, unsupported, absent, and unhealthy states have deliberate, distinct rendering semantics.*

**Conditional rendering is tab/row level only — never per-panel** (the reference states this as a hard rule and has zero panel-level conditions). And presence gating cannot distinguish *disabled* from *unsupported* from *never-deployed*, because all three produce no series. The layout can express **two** states honestly: absent (hidden) and configured-but-unhealthy (rendered, with the value carrying the fault via mappings and thresholds).

So the implementation renders those two, and every empty state names the **config key and prerequisite** without asserting which one is unmet — with a test forbidding text containing *is disabled* / *is off* / *not deployed* / *because*. Claiming the fourth state would be a guess rendered as fact. Recorded here rather than quietly marked done.

Done in `e0e20b9`. Closed by that commit — this was the last open child of #481.

The remaining scope recorded on this issue was nested sub-tab navigation only; everything else (the v2 premise correction, the module split, the sentinel registry, the test suites) was already closed out earlier.

## Ten flat tabs become five

```
Overview                                                    (leaf)
Fleet & Network    -> Fleet & Devices, Network & Flows,
                      Node Metrics [gated], Tailnets [gated]
Security & Policy  -> Security & Audit, Policy & Config
Events & Logs                                               (leaf)
Exporter           -> Exporter Diagnostics, Cardinality & Cost
```

**Events & Logs deliberately stays a plain tab** rather than becoming a single-child "Ingestion" domain — a one-item sub-tab bar is navigation furniture that costs a click and communicates nothing.

A domain is a `TabsLayoutTab` whose `layout` is itself a `TabsLayout`, wrapping already-built leaf dicts **unchanged**, so each leaf `conditionalRendering` survives nesting verbatim. That is the technique from `../opnsense-exporter/grafana/` (`Builder.tab_group`, `organize_tabs`); the structural approach was reused, none of its metric names or domain content.

## Two-level gating

Node Metrics and Tailnets keep their existing tab-level gates (`has_nodemetrics`, `has_multitailnet`) — no new sentinel needed, so `_SENTINEL_ORDER` is untouched.

**No domain is gated, and that is deliberate.** This issue correctly notes that a tab containing only conditional rows still renders unless the tab itself is conditional. But all three domains here contain at least one always-present leaf, and gating one would risk a dashboard rendering with **no visible tabs at all** — strictly worse than one empty tab. A test asserts each domain stays ungated, with a negative test proving a wrongly-gated core domain fails.

## Panel ids did not move

Grouping happens *after* panel construction, so the monotonic id counter never sees it. **405 panels before and after, ids unchanged**, and every alert manifest `__panelId__` came out byte-identical — `git status deploy/alerts/grafana-managed` was empty after regen. Nothing needed re-linking.

## A hazard this created, fixed rather than papered over

The #397 query-budget walker collected every `TabsLayoutTab`. After this change that also matches **domain wrappers**, and because a domain layout recursively contains its children `ElementReference`s, it would have double-counted every grouped tab — quietly inflating the very budget it exists to enforce, while still passing. It now descends into domains without counting them, and the measured totals are numerically identical to before nesting (405 panels / 484 queries / 58 sentinels across 10 leaves).

Two existing test modules needed no changes at all (`test_empty_state_contract.py`, `test_panel_descriptions.py`) because their walkers already recursed generically on `TabsLayout` — so they picked up two-level gate inheritance for free.

## The `--tab` preview gotcha is unchanged

Still present, still recorded: a single-tab preview registers only that tab own sentinels, so previewing a tab that *consumes* a sentinel it does not *own* references an undeclared variable. Nesting neither worsens nor fixes it — `--tab` forces the flat path before grouping is considered.

163 dashboard tests green (was 149), 14 new, four of them negative: a flattened fake domain, a dropped leaf, an ungated optional leaf, and a wrongly-gated core domain each fail as they should.

body:
## Incident

<host-1> stopped delivering all metrics on 2026-07-27 after its cumulative OTLP payload crossed Grafana Cloud Mimir's 20,000,000-byte uncompressed request limit. The gateway returned HTTP 413 for every subsequent minute; requests grew from 33,079,888 to 33,487,966 bytes. Restarting restored delivery only temporarily by clearing the metric SDK's cumulative aggregation state.

## Root cause

High-fidelity raw flow counters continually create new attribute sets. Grafana Cloud requires cumulative metric temporality, so otel-go retains every counter series seen during the process lifetime and exports the complete aggregate each interval. tailscale2otel currently hands that whole collection to the exporter as one request.

otel-go v1.44 can split a collection by datapoint count using `OTEL_GO_X_METRIC_EXPORT_BATCH_SIZE`, but tailscale2otel neither enables nor exposes it. The exporter's `WithMaxRequestSize` is not a substitute: it rejects an oversized serialized request locally and does not split it.

This is the concrete incident slice of #360. That broader issue remains the source for compression, timeouts, retry policy, hard serialized-request guards, standard OTel environment precedence, and complete effective-config reporting.

## Scope

Add a deterministic positive `otlp.metric_export_batch_size` setting, default 10,000 datapoints, pass it into the metric SDK before reader construction, and expose/document the effective value. Preserve cumulative temporality and metric fidelity.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A telemetry-level regression proves one cumulative collection is delivered as multiple OTLP requests.
- [ ] No request in that regression exceeds the configured datapoint count.
- [ ] Built-in/YAML/`TS2OTEL_*` config resolves the setting with a 10,000 default and rejects values below 1.
- [ ] The admin status API/page reports the effective non-secret value.
- [ ] Example config, configuration reference, env reference, Helm values, README, and schema are updated/regenerated.
- [ ] Full root and tool-module build/test/lint/generated-artifact gates pass.
- [ ] <host-1> runs the completing image beyond the previous failure window without another HTTP 413.

## Deliberate non-goals

- Changing cumulative temporality.
- Reducing raw-flow fidelity as the product fix.
- Treating datapoint count as an exact serialized-byte limit.
- Completing every exporter control in #360 in this incident patch.
title: Prevent cumulative OTLP metric payloads exceeding backend request limits

body:
Deferred alternative recorded during #469 (`security:SEC-06`). This is the better long-term answer; it is blocked on work the #486 tracker parks.

#469 shipped `rolloutTrigger` plus the Stakater Reloader annotation, both of which replace the pod. The `prometheus-config-reloader` / `configmap-reload` family does something strictly nicer — it watches a mounted volume and signals the running process, so a rotated credential is picked up with **no restart at all**. Grafana's own Alloy chart uses exactly this.

It was evaluated and rejected for now. Two hard prerequisites are missing:

1. **Credentials are env vars, not files.** `deploy/helm/tailscale2otel/templates/deployment.yaml` injects them with `envFrom: secretRef`. Kubernetes never refreshes environment variables in a running container, so there is nothing for a volume watcher to observe. The chart would have to deliver credentials through the existing `*_file` keys as a mounted Secret instead.
2. **There is no in-process reload trigger.** `cmd/tailscale2otel/main.go` handles only `SIGINT`/`SIGTERM`, and the admin mux has no reload route. Adding either *is* configuration hot reload, which #486 explicitly parks with a research/design-first requirement.

So the ordering is: configuration hot reload first, then this.

## Scope (once unblocked)

- Deliver credentials as a mounted Secret via the `*_file` config keys, with the env path kept for compatibility.
- Add the reload trigger that hot reload defines (`SIGHUP` or an admin route) and wire a config-reloader sidecar to it.
- Keep `rolloutTrigger` and the Reloader annotation as the fallback for anyone not running the sidecar.

## Acceptance

- [ ] Rotating an externally managed `existingSecret` is picked up with no pod restart.
- [ ] A bad replacement credential leaves the process in a safe state with a useful health condition, rather than a half-applied config.
- [ ] Still no secret value or reversible digest in any pod annotation.
- [ ] The env-var path keeps working unchanged for operators who do not opt in.

comments.body:
Reviewed 2026-07-25 alongside the other #486 follow-ups. **Staying open and blocked** — no code change.

Re-confirmed against current `main` (`476f236`), both prerequisites are still missing and nothing has changed since this was filed:

1. `deploy/helm/tailscale2otel/templates/deployment.yaml` still injects credentials via `envFrom: secretRef`. Kubernetes never refreshes environment variables in a running container, so a volume-watching sidecar has nothing to observe.
2. `cmd/tailscale2otel/main.go` still handles only `SIGINT`/`SIGTERM`, and the admin mux has no reload route.

Adding that trigger is configuration hot reload, which #486 parks with an explicit requirement that parked items begin from research/design acceptance criteria rather than jumping to implementation. Implementing it here would be exactly the jump that decision forbids.

Nothing is broken meanwhile: the `rolloutTrigger` value and the Stakater Reloader annotation shipped in #469 both give operators a supported way to pick up a rotated `existingSecret` today. This issue is the *nicer* answer (no restart at all), not the only one.

**Unblocking order:** configuration hot reload needs its own research/design issue first — what can safely reload in-process, what cannot, the reload trigger surface, and failure semantics when a replacement config or credential is invalid. Once that lands, this becomes implementable.

Labelling this as blocked rather than closing it, since the design is sound and the dependency is concrete rather than speculative.

## Closed — the prerequisite it waits on will never land

Rob declined configuration hot reload outright on 2026-07-28; **#313 is closed NOT_PLANNED** and the
#486 parking stands permanently rather than pending research. The deployment model is containers,
where a restart is the reload mechanism.

This issue's own ordering statement — "configuration hot reload first, then this" — is what closes
it. Prerequisite 2 (an in-process reload trigger: `SIGHUP` or an admin route) is not merely
unimplemented, it is now a decision taken against. `deploy/CLAUDE.md`'s "do not add a SIGHUP handler
or a reload route" and `docs/configuration.md`'s statement that there is no SIGHUP and no reload
endpoint both remain correct and in force.

Without that trigger, a config-reloader sidecar has nothing to signal. Prerequisite 1 (delivering
credentials as a mounted Secret via the `*_file` keys rather than `envFrom: secretRef`) is
independently achievable, but on its own it buys nothing here: a watcher would observe a changed
file and have no way to make the process act on it. Worth knowing that even a mounted `*_file`
credential is read exactly once — `internal/config/secretfile.go`'s `resolveSecretFiles` says so in
its own doc comment, and a full trace during #313 confirmed **every** credential in this codebase is
captured at component-construction time, with no per-use read anywhere.

**The shipped answer stays what #469 delivered:** `rolloutTrigger` plus the Stakater Reloader
annotation. Both replace the pod, which is the intended mechanism rather than a fallback. No secret
value or reversible digest appears in any pod annotation, and that property is unchanged.

Reopen only if the hot-reload decision is itself reversed.

body:
Known, deliberate gap recorded while fixing #471 (`security:SEC-08`). Filed so it is tracked rather than living only in a commit message.

#471 replaced the predictable `<path>.tmp` staging file with a randomized `os.CreateTemp` name in the destination directory. Every Go-level error path removes exactly the file that call created, via a `defer` disabled once the rename succeeds.

What is still not handled: a `SIGKILL` (or power loss) landing between `CreateTemp` and `os.Rename` leaves a `.checkpoints.json.<random>.tmp` behind forever. Nothing ever removes it.

The old code had the same gap — but because it reused one fixed name, at most one stale file could accumulate. Randomized names mean they accumulate one per hard kill. On a crash-looping deployment with a persistent checkpoint volume, that grows without bound.

This was **not** fixed as part of #471 because the obvious remedy is unsafe: a startup sweep of `.<base>.*.tmp` risks deleting a *concurrent* instance's in-flight staging file. The chart pins `replicaCount: 1` and uses `strategy: Recreate`, but the checkpoint store is a plain file API with no locking, so nothing in the code enforces single-writer.

## Scope

Pick one and document it:

- A startup sweep guarded by an age threshold (only remove staging files older than some interval), accepting the small residual risk.
- An advertised single-writer lock on the checkpoint directory, after which a sweep is unambiguously safe.
- Accept the leak and document it, on the grounds that the files are tiny and a hard kill mid-save is rare.

## Acceptance

- [ ] A simulated hard kill mid-save leaves a recoverable state, and the chosen policy is proven by test.
- [ ] Whatever is chosen, a concurrent second writer can never have its in-flight staging file deleted.
- [ ] The behaviour is documented wherever checkpoint persistence is described.

comments.body:
Closed by `15b1038`. Implemented as the age-guarded startup sweep.

**Threshold: 1 hour** (`stagingFileMaxAge`). A staging file exists for one small JSON write + fsync + rename — microseconds to milliseconds — so an hour is several orders of magnitude of headroom. That margin is the whole safety argument: a concurrent instance's in-flight file can never be old enough to sweep. A future mtime (clock skew) reads as age zero and is kept, which is the safe direction.

**Three independent gates**, all of which must pass before anything is unlinked:

1. **Name** — leading `.` + basename + `.` AND terminal `.tmp` AND a **non-empty** random component. That excludes by construction: the checkpoint file itself, the historical predictable `checkpoints.json.tmp`, `.checkpoints.json.tmp` (empty random part), another file's staging name, the `.corrupt` rename-aside target, and the `.checkpoint-probe-*` writability probe.
2. **Type** — `os.Lstat`, must be a regular file. A symlink is neither followed nor removed. `os.Remove` unlinks without following, so the Lstat→Remove window is not exploitable.
3. **Age** — untouched for the threshold.

Writer and sweeper derive names from one shared `stagingNameBounds` helper, so they cannot drift apart. `writeFileAtomic` changed on exactly one line to consume it — **byte-identical pattern string, no change to the atomic-write path, fsync ordering, or file mode.**

Invoked from `NewFileStore` before the checkpoint is read: the only place a file-backed store is created, and it runs before that store has written anything, so it can never race a save of its own. Non-fatal throughout — a partial `ReadDir` is still swept, a file vanishing mid-sweep is skipped, and failure logs a WARN and continues, matching how the checkpoint path already degrades when its directory is unwritable.

**Mutation-tested**, so these are real regression tests rather than tests that happen to pass:

```
MUTATION 1: no age guard      → KeepsRecentStagingFile FAILS
MUTATION 2: Stat not Lstat    → DoesNotFollowSymlink FAILS
MUTATION 3: suffix-only match → NeverTouchesTheCheckpointOrBystanders FAILS
RESTORED                      → ok
```

Each mutation is caught by exactly the test that owns that property, and by no other.

Worth recording, because it is easy to get backwards: **`os.Chtimes` follows symlinks**, so backdating a link path ages the *target*. The symlink test uses that deliberately — it puts the tree in precisely the state where a `Stat`-based sweep would see "old regular file" and unlink the link, which makes it a genuine `Lstat`-vs-`Stat` discriminator instead of a test that would pass either way.

The pre-existing `TestFileStore_ConcurrentSetsCannotShareTempFiles` (8 concurrent writers plus a reader looping `NewFileStore`, i.e. thousands of sweeps racing live saves) passes unmodified under `-race`.

Documentation, the third acceptance box: added to the `checkpoint` section of `docs/configuration.md`, plus a note in `internal/collector/CLAUDE.md` warning against "simplifying" the atomic write back to a predictable `.tmp` — that single change would silently reintroduce both this and #471.

The threshold is a compile-time constant, not a config key. `stagingFileMaxAge` is the one place to thread if a knob is ever wanted.

title: Checkpoint staging file is not swept after a hard process kill

body:
Tidy-up follow-up from #473 (`security:SEC-10`).

That work added a bounded `error.type` span attribute to the collector scheduler so a span whose free-text status description has been redacted still names its failure class. `internal/semconv` has no constant for it, so `internal/collector/scheduler.go` declares `spanAttrErrorType` locally, and `internal/collector/catalog.go` already used the bare literal elsewhere.

Three copies of the same attribute name is exactly the drift this repo uses `internal/semconv` to prevent.

## Scope

- Add `semconv.AttrErrorType`.
- Replace the local `spanAttrErrorType` in `scheduler.go` and the literals in `catalog.go` and `selfobs.go`.
- No behaviour change: the emitted attribute name and its closed value set (`panic` | `timeout` | `error`) stay identical.

## Acceptance

- [ ] No literal `"error.type"` remains outside `internal/semconv`.
- [ ] `docs/metrics.md` is unchanged by the refactor (proof there is no behaviour change).
- [ ] Full gate green.

comments.body:
Implemented. `semconv.AttrErrorType` added to `internal/semconv/attrs.go` beside the existing `AttrErrorMessage`, following that block's grouping and the package's `Attr<Thing>` naming.

**Call sites converted** — all production uses across the tree, not just the collector:

- `internal/collector/scheduler.go` — local `spanAttrErrorType` const deleted, both emit sites use the constant
- `internal/collector/catalog.go`, `internal/collector/selfobs.go`
- `internal/telemetry/catalog.go`, `internal/telemetry/selfobs.go` (two sites)

**Important finding: the key is shared, but the value set is not.** Collector scrapes emit `panic | timeout | error`; OTLP export emits `export | timeout`. These classify unrelated failures and are deliberately NOT unified. The constant's doc comment now documents both sets explicitly and says not to merge them — the first draft implied one global enum, which would have been wrong and would likely have been "fixed" into a real bug later.

**Two categories of `"error.type"` literal remain, both deliberate:**

1. **Doc-comment prose** (`internal/collector/selfobs.go:23,124`, `internal/telemetry/selfobs.go:53`). Spelling the wire name out in prose is correct; these are not keys.
2. **`internal/telemetry/pii/registry.go:113`**, inside the `nonIdentifier` map. That table is a flat lookup of roughly 60 bare literals. Converting one entry to a constant would make it *less* uniform, not more, and converting all 60 is far outside this issue.

For (2) I added a guard instead of churn — `TestNonIdentifierTracksSemconvErrorType` asserts the table still contains `semconv.AttrErrorType`, so a rename fails loudly rather than silently dropping the key out of the PII allowlist. Verified it actually catches drift rather than passing trivially, by temporarily renaming the constant:

```
--- FAIL: TestNonIdentifierTracksSemconvErrorType (0.00s)
    registry_test.go:113: nonIdentifier is missing "error.kind"; the semconv constant and this table have drifted
```

**Proof this is a pure refactor**, which was the acceptance bar:

- `metricscatalog -check` → `docs/metrics.md is in sync`, and `git status docs/metrics.md` is empty. The tool was rebuilt first, since it is a separate module and a stale binary would prove nothing.
- Every existing test that asserts the attribute passes **unmodified** — no test file in `internal/collector` was edited. The tests that pin the literal wire name were left as literals on purpose; converting them to the constant would make them tautological and delete the net this refactor depends on.

Gate: `go build ./...`, `go vet ./...`, `go test -race` and `golangci-lint run` (0 issues) across `internal/collector/...`, `internal/semconv/...` and `internal/telemetry/...`.

body:
Follow-up from #468 (`security:SEC-05`).

That work introduced `classifyTransportError` in `internal/tsapi/transport.go`, which returns a `transportDiagnostic` carrying a `Retryable` bool alongside the bounded class, status and message. The value is reported to operators as the `error_retryable` log field, so they can tell "this will not improve" from "transient".

It does **not** drive the retry loop. `retryTransport.RoundTrip` still classifies with its original rule:

```go
retryable := err != nil || resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests || resp.StatusCode >= 500
```

So an OAuth token fetch that fails 401 (bad client credentials — never going to succeed) is still retried up to `tailscale.http.retry.max_attempts` with full backoff, on every collector tick.

This was left deliberate rather than fixed inline: making the classifier authoritative changes retry counts and attempt timing that the #84, #200, #206 and #76 regression tests pin, and #468 was a logging-hygiene fix. Doing it as a drive-by would have put an unrelated behaviour change inside a security commit.

## Scope

- Make `transportDiagnostic.Retryable` authoritative for the transport error path, so a terminal auth failure stops immediately.
- Preserve the existing 429 / 5xx / transport-error behaviour and the `Retry-After` clamping from #206.
- Re-verify the pinned tests rather than adjusting them to fit: #84 (bounded token fetch), #200 (whole-exchange timeout), #206 (`Retry-After` capped at `max_delay`), #76 (rate-limiter wait excluded from `Duration`).

## Acceptance

- [ ] A 401/403 from the token endpoint makes exactly one attempt.
- [ ] 429 and 5xx retry behaviour, backoff timing and `Retry-After` handling are unchanged, proven by the existing tests passing unmodified.
- [ ] The collector scheduler still surfaces the terminal failure at its normal cadence without log spam.

comments.body:
Closed by `15b1038`.

Only the **transport-error** branch now consults the classifier; the HTTP-response branch (429, 5xx) is byte-identical to before.

**Conservative by construction:** `network` is the classifier's fallback class, so anything unrecognised stays retryable — unknown means "might be transient", never "terminal". Only structured verdicts became terminal:

- OAuth 401/403/400 and bare RFC 6749 error codes — the endpoint rejected the grant on its merits; a byte-identical replay is rejected identically.
- `redirect_refused` — the policy verdict is a pure function of the response. Effectively unreachable here anyway, since `CheckRedirect` runs in `http.Client`, above `retryTransport`.
- `canceled` — **observably unchanged**. Under the old rule this already cost exactly one attempt: `retryable=true` fell into the backoff `select`, which fires on `spanCtx.Done()` immediately. The only differences are one fewer misleading "retrying" DEBUG record and which cancellation error is returned; both still satisfy `errors.Is(err, context.Canceled)`. Pinned by a test that passes before *and* after.

Still retryable and covered in the table: timeouts (`context.DeadlineExceeded`, which is what `attemptTimeout` produces), `os.ErrDeadlineExceeded`, any `net.Error` with `Timeout()`, OAuth 429/5xx, plain network errors, and `*url.Error` wrapping any of those.

**The four pinned regressions pass with their files not in the diff at all** — `auth_test.go` (#84/#200), `workloadidentity_test.go` (#84/#200) and `ratelimit_retry_test.go` (#76) were never touched; #206's test body in `transport_test.go` is unmodified.

**One #468 test did have to change, and that deserves stating plainly rather than burying.** `TestTokenErrorLoggingNeverLeaksResponseBody` asserted that an OAuth 401 produces a *retry* log record — which is exactly the behaviour this issue removes. It was not weakened:

- Every leak assertion is byte-for-byte unchanged (body marker, `S3CR3T-CLIENT-SECRET` userinfo, `error_class`, `error_status`).
- The 401 case now asserts the **terminal** record's bookkeeping, ungated by log level — so it is checked at DEBUG *and* INFO, strictly more coverage than the old DEBUG-only block.
- The DEBUG retry-path leak proof — the exact path #468 fixed — moved to a new test driving a retryable **503**, so `logRetry` still fires and that path stays covered.

The two could not stay in one case: the INFO half needs a 401 (a 503 emits no record at INFO), and the DEBUG-retry half needs a retryable status.

Also corrected: the `retryTransport` and `transportDiagnostic.Retryable` doc comments both said the classification was *not* the retry decision. That is now false, so both were updated.

One claim from the implementation notes I checked and did **not** act on: a suggestion that `x/oauth2` flattens token-fetch transport errors with `%v` before `redactURL` can act. It does not. `internal/token.go:261` returns the transport error **unwrapped**; the `%v` at `:266` handles only the body-read error, whose inner error carries no URL. `errors.As` reaches the `*url.Error` fine — as the passing #468 userinfo assertion demonstrates. No follow-up needed.
