body:
## Audit context

Identified during the comprehensive audit of `9401181b163417e517eb69f112fc79b78534e77e`. The audit compared the generated artifacts with the live Grafana deployment, rendered all five dashboards, inspected all 79 rules, and reconciled them with the 191-signal catalog.

## Finding and proposed scope

Priority: P2

- Preserve current compatibility, but generate named profiles such as baseline, recommended, and strict.
- Make threshold and `for` overrides declarative without hand-editing generated YAML.
- Explain why every rule is enabled or paused in each profile.
- Validate that profile overlays cannot create malformed Grafana pipelines.
- Show the selected profile and deviations in installation/status documentation.

## Delivery requirements

- [ ] Re-confirm the premise against the current implementation and upstream contract before changing behavior.
- [ ] Add a failing regression or telemetry-level test first, then implement the smallest complete change.
- [ ] Update affected catalog, generated artifacts, configuration references, operator documentation, dashboards, and rules as applicable.
- [ ] Preserve bounded-cardinality and PII/secret-handling contracts.
- [ ] Run the full repository gate, including all affected tool modules and generated-artifact drift checks.

## Audit identity

`grafana:GRAF-05`

comments.body:
Done in `ea53c30`. Closed by that commit.

Three profiles, selected with `--profile` (default `recommended`, so no-flag behaviour is unchanged):

| profile | alerts enabled | recording enabled | rationale |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| `baseline` | 11 | 8 | `coverage_critical` + `core` policy only — the set that is actionable on any deployment without site tuning |
| `recommended` | 39 | 8 | today shipped state, unchanged |
| `strict` | 94 | 23 | everything except three rules that are inert or misleading without a site-specific threshold |

## Preserve current compatibility

`recommended` output is **byte-identical** to what has always shipped, and that is asserted rather than assumed:

```
$ python3 deploy/alerts/gen/build_rules.py --out deploy/alerts/grafana-managed
wrote 121 manifests (profile=recommended, 97 alert rules, 23 recording rules, 81 paused)
$ git diff --exit-code -- deploy/alerts/grafana-managed; echo EXIT=$?
EXIT=0
```

## Explain why every rule is enabled or paused

Not by writing 97x3 sentences — those rot the moment a rule is added. Paused state is decided by a **predicate carrying its own rationale**, so each rule explanation is *derived* from the predicate that decided it. The only hand-authored text is the three `strict` exceptions and any threshold/`for` override, each with a mandatory `why` (tested for real length, not just presence):

- `ts2o-api-rate-limit-wait-high` — its 5s threshold is a documented placeholder pending a real per-site baseline (#404)
- `ts2o-ingest-data-stale` — fires on any legitimately idle sparse ingestion source
- `ts2o-export-volume-high` — a per-plan Grafana Cloud cost budget, not a correctness signal

## Declarative overrides, no hand-edited YAML

Threshold and `for` overrides are data keyed by uid, routed through the same `godur()` and threshold construction `alert()` uses — so an override **cannot** produce a non-Go-style duration (`"5m"` instead of `"30m0s"`) or a non-numeric threshold. All three shipped profiles happen to need only pause-state changes, but the mechanism is built and unit-tested.

## Overlays cannot create malformed pipelines

Each profile is materialised and run through the same `validate_manifests.py` the shipped artifact passes:
```
recommended: validated 121 manifests: OK
baseline:    validated 121 manifests: OK
strict:      validated 121 manifests: OK
```

## Not committed: three copies of the manifests

Deliberate. 3 x 121 near-duplicate JSON files would bury every real diff. Committed artifacts are the shipped `recommended` set plus the generated `docs/alert-profiles.md`; other profiles are materialised on demand (`--profile strict --out <dir>`), which the docs page states.

## An inconsistency this surfaced — a decision for you, not a bug

**`baseline` is NOT a subset of `recommended`.** Seven rules declare `policy=core` (their signal is always emitted, so absence is abnormal) yet ship `paused=True`:

`ts2o-config-invalid`, `ts2o-export-latency-high`, `ts2o-scrape-budget-overrun`, `ts2o-scrape-staleness-high`, and the three `ts2o-slo-*` burn rules.

For the SLO rules that is clearly right — they ship paused pending an agreed target. For `ts2o-config-invalid` it looks wrong: an invalid config is unambiguous and always worth surfacing. Rather than quietly change your shipped defaults, this is encoded as a reviewed known-deviation set with a test that fails if the list changes, so the question stays visible. Worth a look.

Verification: 105 tests (80 pre-existing + 25 new), all green. Six negative tests, each broken, confirmed failing for the right reason, and restored — including byte-identity, the numeric-threshold guard, the `why`-length rule, and doc drift.

## Audit identity

`grafana:GRAF-04`

comments.body:
Closed by `e54a4cd`, re-expressed for the manifest format in `9a3674c`.

Confirmed the premise first: all 73 alert rules shipped `execErrState: OK`, and `ts2o-exporter-down` was the only rule with `noDataState: Alerting`. A broken datasource or malformed query read as *healthy* across the entire pack.

`alert()` now takes a **required** `policy=` from a closed set of four — `nodata=`/`execerr=` were removed outright so all 78 call sites must state one. Distribution: `coverage_critical`=1, `core`=7, `optional`=52, `advisory`=18.

| policy | noDataState | execErrState |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `coverage_critical` | `Alerting` | `Alerting` |
| `core` | `NoData` | `Error` |
| `optional` | `Ok` | `Error` |
| `advisory` | `Ok` | `OK` |

**`ExporterDown` is the only `coverage_critical` rule**, and the near-misses were rejected deliberately. Per-collector scrape rules are `core`: total absence means the exporter is gone, which `ExporterDown` already pages on, so promoting them would fan one outage into a page per collector. The allowlist is asserted as an exact set with a written reason per member plus a staleness test.

Note the casing trap the manifest format introduced — **`noDataState` spells its OK value `"Ok"` while `execErrState` spells its own `"OK"`**. Wrong casing makes a rule un-deployable while every offline check passes.

On the issue's last bullet — *document how datasource/ruler health itself is monitored* — the honest answer is that **nothing here can, and a rule structurally cannot**. If the ruler stops evaluating, no rule fires, including the `coverage_critical` one. `docs/runbooks.md` has a "who watches the watcher" section naming the three operator-owned answers (ruler meta-metrics, an external dead-man's-switch, synthetic monitoring against `/healthz`) rather than inventing an in-repo mechanism that would not work.

Premise confirmed: no rule carried `runbook_url`, `__dashboardUid__` or `__panelId__` — all three substrings were absent from the artifact. Annotations were `summary` + `description` only.

comments.body:
Closed by `be4fc7d` (pushed in `e54a4cd`).

Confirmed the premise before changing anything: `BOOL_MAP` hardcoded 0→red/"off" and 1→green/"on" regardless of the panel's own thresholds, so three inverse-risk panels rendered the **safe** state red and the **risky** state green — "SSH wildcard" (security), "SSH wildcard enabled" (overview) and "Exporter update available" (fleet).

Verified in the generated artifact after the fix:

```
Flow logging                 0=red   /off              1=green /on
MagicDNS                     0=red   /off              1=green /on
SSH wildcard                 0=green /off              1=red   /on
SSH wildcard enabled         0=green /off              1=yellow/on
Exporter update available    0=green /up to date       1=yellow/update available
```

`BOOL_MAP` is **deleted**, not aliased — a name that no longer states its polarity is how this recurs. Replaced by `BOOL_HEALTHY_ON` / `BOOL_HEALTHY_OFF` / `BOOL_NEUTRAL` / `bool_map()`.

Beyond the one-time fix, `check_bool_polarity()` now runs inside `panel()`: a panel carrying both a 0/1 value map and a two-step threshold must have matching colours or **the build fails**. ## Audit context

Identified during the comprehensive audit of `9401181b163417e517eb69f112fc79b78534e77e`. The audit traced metric, log, trace, Prometheus, OTLP, and Pyroscope paths through the current telemetry facade and checked the pinned upstream implementations.

## Finding and proposed scope

- **Evidence:** pinned OTel v1.44 can emit standardized exporter/BSP metrics behind `OTEL_GO_X_OBSERVABILITY`; the app does not install a global MeterProvider and has multiple per-tailnet providers.
- **Scope:** matrix HTTP/gRPC × metrics/logs/traces; compare standardized metrics with custom wrappers; test recursion, attribution and ProviderSet lifecycle.
- **Acceptance:** written adopt/defer decision; no duplicate self-metrics; experimental feature remains off by default; if adopted, it has an explicit compatibility layer and removal plan. [OTel SDK metrics](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/otel/sdk-metrics/)
- **Dependency:** decide before duplicating the same queue/export metrics in E4/E5.

## Delivery requirements

- [ ] Re-confirm the premise against the current implementation and upstream contract before changing behavior.
- [ ] Record the evidence, decision, rejected alternatives, and follow-up implementation slices; closing as unsupported is valid when the evidence does not justify a feature.
- [ ] Update affected catalog, generated artifacts, configuration references, operator documentation, dashboards, and rules as applicable.
- [ ] Preserve bounded-cardinality and PII/secret-handling contracts.
- [ ] Run the full repository gate, including all affected tool modules and generated-artifact drift checks.

## Audit identity

`telemetry:Q1`

comments.body:
## Decision: DEFER — do not adopt `OTEL_GO_X_OBSERVABILITY`; keep `tailscale2otel.*` naming

Evaluated against the pinned versions (`go.opentelemetry.io/otel` v1.44.0, `go.opentelemetry.io/otel/log` v0.20.0) by reading the actual module source in `GOMODCACHE`, not from documentation alone.

### The blocking finding

**Enabling the flag today would be a silent no-op.** Every instrument behind `OTEL_GO_X_OBSERVABILITY` is created via `otel.GetMeterProvider()` — the process **global** MeterProvider — in every constructor (`.../internal/observ/instrumentation.go` in all six OTLP exporters, plus `sdk/trace/internal/observ/{tracer,batch_span_processor,simple_span_processor}.go`, `sdk/metric/internal/observ/instrumentation.go`, `sdk/log/internal/observ/simple_log_processor.go`).

This app never calls `otel.SetMeterProvider` (the only global mutation anywhere is `otel.SetErrorHandler` in `internal/telemetry/selfobs.go`). So the instruments would be created against the default **no-op** meter: `Add`/`Record` would run every export cycle and every value would be discarded. No error, no crash, nothing on the admin page, nothing in Grafana.

### Why making it non-no-op is a regression

There is exactly one global MeterProvider slot, and `internal/telemetry/providerset.go` builds N+1 providers (one per tailnet plus one process-level). The `otel.component.name` attribute is a sequential integer assigned at construction — it carries **no tailnet identity**. So wiring the global slot means choosing between:

- point it at the process provider → every tailnet's exporter health collapses into one view, per-tailnet attribution lost entirely; or
- point it at one tailnet's provider → every *other* tailnet's exporter activity is silently mis-attributed to that tailnet's `tailscale.tailnet` attribute.

Both regress the multi-tailnet attribution `ProviderSet` exists to provide, and that `Delivery()`'s worst-across-providers merge already delivers. The single-runtime Headscale path is the one topology where "one process, one MeterProvider" holds, but building the feature only for the minority deployment mode is not a coherent adoption.

### Coverage does not fully answer E4/#358 anyway

| signal | exporter-level (HTTP + gRPC + stdout) | processor/queue-level |
| --- | --- | --- |
| metrics | exported / inflight / `operation.duration` | `metric_reader.collection.duration` only (periodic reader, no queue) |
| traces | exported / inflight / duration | **full**: BSP `processor.span.processed{error.type=queue_full}` + `queue.size` + `queue.capacity` |
| logs | exported / inflight / duration | **nothing usable** |

`otelconv.ComponentTypeBatchingLogProcessor` exists as a semconv constant, but nothing in pinned `sdk/log@v0.20.0` references it — the only `internal/observ` file present is `simple_log_processor.go`. This repo uses `sdklog.NewBatchProcessor` for logs (`internal/telemetry/provider.go`), so adopting upstream would deliver trace-queue telemetry and **zero** log-queue telemetry: an inconsistent half-answer to #358.

### What upstream genuinely does better

Worth borrowing as design, even though the mechanism is unreachable here:

- exported-vs-inflight split rather than a single count;
- real partial-success accounting — `ExportOp.End` subtracts the rejected count from the success bucket and re-adds it under `error.type`, so "exported N, rejected M" is preserved rather than collapsed to a pass/fail bit;
- `queue_full` as a first-class drop reason.

The repo's own `errClass*` closed set in `internal/telemetry/delivery.go` remains preferable to the standardized `error.type` because it is PII-safe by construction (never forwards backend error text, #317).

### What would change this to ADOPT

Either (a) upstream ships a constructor option to scope this instrumentation to a caller-supplied `MeterProvider` instead of the process global, **and** `sdk/log` adds BatchProcessor instrumentation; or (b) this repo returns to one MeterProvider per process — a much larger, unrelated decision this issue must not force. Until both halves of (a) land, adoption cannot meet this issue's own acceptance bar ("no duplicate self-metrics… explicit compatibility layer"), because no compatibility layer is reachable under the global-provider constraint.

The feature stays off by default: nothing in this repo sets `OTEL_GO_X_OBSERVABILITY`. Note the repo already uses one adjacent flag surgically — `OTEL_GO_X_METRIC_EXPORT_BATCH_SIZE` in `internal/telemetry/provider.go`, for per-request batch splitting — so this namespace is used deliberately and narrowly here, not wholesale.

### GATING ANSWER for #358 and #359

**Keep `tailscale2otel.*` naming. Do not name new metrics after `otel.sdk.*`.** Borrowing a spec name for a metric that is not emitted through the spec's mechanism would mislead operators and tooling into assuming standardized semantics that do not apply.

Names those two issues should use:

- #358: `tailscale2otel.processor.queue.size{signal}`, `tailscale2otel.processor.queue.capacity{signal}`, `tailscale2otel.processor.dropped{signal,reason="queue_full"}` — covers logs, where upstream has nothing.
- #359: `tailscale2otel.export.spans` (counter, parallel to the existing `.datapoints` / `.log_records`, closing the gap `delivery_trace.go` documents), plus partial-success as an explicit outcome alongside the existing `errClass*` set rather than a second upstream-flavoured taxonomy.

Closing as evaluated-and-deferred, which this issue lists as a valid terminal state. No code change.

title: Evaluate OTel Go’s experimental SDK/exporter self-observation

body:
## Audit context

Identified during the comprehensive audit of `9401181b163417e517eb69f112fc79b78534e77e`. The audit traced metric, log, trace, Prometheus, OTLP, and Pyroscope paths through the current telemetry facade and checked the pinned upstream implementations.

## Finding and proposed scope

- **Evidence:** all current histograms use explicit buckets, creating classic `_bucket`, `_sum`, and `_count` series.
- **Potential value:** native histograms can represent one distribution as one series with greater resolution, but pull support requires Prometheus protobuf and dashboard migration.
- **Scope:** time-boxed comparison of OTLP exponential histograms and Prometheus/Alloy native histogram scraping; quantify active-series/DPM reduction and quantile error; design dual-publish migration.
- **Acceptance:** live-compatible Grafana Cloud/Mimir result; no default change; classic rules remain valid until migration completes; backend bucket limits documented. [Grafana native histograms](https://grafana.com/docs/mimir/latest/send/native-histograms/_exponential_buckets/)

## Delivery requirements

- [ ] Re-confirm the premise against the current implementation and upstream contract before changing behavior.
- [ ] Record the evidence, decision, rejected alternatives, and follow-up implementation slices; closing as unsupported is valid when the evidence does not justify a feature.
- [ ] Update affected catalog, generated artifacts, configuration references, operator documentation, dashboards, and rules as applicable.
- [ ] Preserve bounded-cardinality and PII/secret-handling contracts.
- [ ] Run the full repository gate, including all affected tool modules and generated-artifact drift checks.

## Audit identity

`telemetry:M5`

comments.body:
## Verdict: DEFER — the win is real and the mechanism exists today; the cost is the dashboard/alert surface

### (a) Current classic series — exact arithmetic

19 histogram declarations across the catalog (19 `Instrument: metricdoc.Histogram` entries, matched 1:1 against 19 `.Histogram`/`.HistogramCtx` emit sites). Each classic histogram yields `len(bounds)+1` `_bucket` series plus `_sum` and `_count`.

Σ(buckets) = 193, plus 19×2 = 38 → **231 classic series minimum** at one label-set per metric. Applying the real attribute multipliers (`export.duration` ×~6, `collector.scrape.duration` ×~14, `ingest.event_age` and `ingest.capture_delay` ×~9 each, `user.invite.pending_age` ×~2.5) gives roughly **700–750 series from histograms alone** on a single tailnet.

14 of the 19 are per-tailnet (only the 5 process-scoped self-obs ones are not), and `tailscale.tailnet` is a const attribute stamped by each tailnet's own Provider — so at 10 tailnets the per-tailnet share (~500) becomes **~5,000 series from histograms**. That is consistent with the ~5,500 raw series already observed for one tailnet under `metrics_mode: both`.

### (b) What exponential histograms give back

One OTLP data point per label-set carrying `positive`/`negative`/`zero` bucket arrays plus `scale`/`sum`/`count`/`min`/`max` — the whole `_bucket`/`_sum`/`_count` family collapses to **one** series. That takes ~700–750 base series to **19**, a >97% reduction, with the same ratio per tailnet.

The mechanism is already available at the pinned SDK version: `metric.NewView(Instrument{...}, Stream{Aggregation: metric.AggregationBase2ExponentialHistogram{...}})` via `WithView` — the same view mechanism `metricProviderOptions` already uses for the per-kind exemplar-suppression views. No version bump needed.

The tradeoff is that fixed boundaries become a *relative* error bound (`2^(2^-scale)-1`, ~±1.2% at scale 5). That matters here specifically: `entityage.BucketsSeconds()`'s 1d/7d/30d/90d/180d/1y/2y ladder was chosen precisely **because** a mechanical power-of-two ladder is not how operators reason about tailnet hygiene — which is exactly what exponential buckets impose. Exponential buckets do not align to those operator-meaningful edges.

### (c) Pull path — correcting an assumption

Native histograms on the Prometheus pull path need the target to serve **classic protobuf exposition** (the text and OpenMetrics formats cannot carry sparse bucket spans at all) and the scraper to set `scrape_native_histograms: true` (stable since Prometheus v3.8; the old feature flag is a no-op as of v3.9).

The pinned `go.opentelemetry.io/otel/exporters/prometheus` **does** support this — its `exporter.go` handles `metricdata.ExponentialHistogram[int64|float64]` via `addExponentialHistogramMetric` → `prometheus.NewConstNativeHistogram`, verified by reading the module source. And `promhttp` already negotiates protobuf whenever a client asks. So "the pull path can't do this" would have been **wrong**: it can, contingent only on switching the aggregation. Recording that explicitly so it is not re-derived.

Largely moot in practice, though — the pull endpoint exists for maintainer validation, not production scraping, and the OTLP push path carries `ExponentialHistogramDataPoint` natively with no protobuf-scrape question at all.

### (d) Backend limits

Mimir's `max_native_histogram_buckets` is a per-tenant override defaulting to **0 (unlimited)**, with `reduce_native_histogram_over_max_buckets` (default true) merging buckets down to fit rather than rejecting the sample. Prometheus has the matching client-side `native_histogram_bucket_limit`. So an over-wide histogram degrades resolution instead of failing ingestion — materially de-risking versus the classic label-collision `otlp_parse_error` failure mode.

### (e) Migration design, if ever adopted

The SDK aggregates one way **or** the other per instrument+view — there is no built-in emit-both. Genuine dual-publish therefore needs either two separately registered instruments under different names (doubling series during the window by design) or a per-tailnet canary, which `ProviderSet`'s per-tailnet construction already supports with no new plumbing. Classic rules and dashboards keep working untouched throughout; native panels are additive; classic is dropped only after a side-by-side burn-in.

### (f) Decision: DEFER, not reject

The arithmetic is a real material win and every layer (SDK, Prometheus exporter, Mimir) supports it today. What blocks it is migration cost, not capability:

- dashboards and alert rules author against explicit classic bucket edges in `deploy/grafana/gen/build.py` and `deploy/alerts/gen/build_rules.py`, and several histograms use hand-chosen operator-meaningful boundaries — migrating those is a real rewrite, not a transparent swap;
- `metricdoc.Metric` has **no field to represent aggregation kind**, so the code-as-docs catalog cannot even distinguish native from classic; that schema change gates flipping a single instrument;
- the companion #364 benchmark found no resource or cost pressure at 100 tailnets, so nothing is urgent.

No default changes and nothing is migrated. Revisit only if Mimir cost or active-series alerting actually flags histogram cardinality as a driver, or if a new histogram is being added anyway and can ship exponential from day one with no migration to manage.

Benchmarked on darwin/arm64 (Apple M1 Max) via a new `internal/telemetry/providerset_bench_test.go`. `-benchtime 200x` (a fixed iteration count, not time-based) because allocs/op is already known to be unstable across `-benchtime` in this repo; reran twice with identical allocs/op.

| tailnets | construct+shutdown ns/op | B/op | allocs/op | ForceFlush ns/op | B/op | allocs/op |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | 3,914,183 | 2,448,981 | 5,795 | 1,134,091 | 1,802,779 | 267 |
| 10 | 21,736,606 | 13,491,541 | 31,866 | 5,259,956 | 9,930,121 | 1,468 |
| 50 | 91,161,226 | 62,502,307 | 147,440 | 21,741,003 | 46,205,250 | 6,746 |
| 100 | 195,985,025 | 123,730,814 | 291,834 | 37,745,366 | 91,854,427 | 13,360 |

Both series are linear in N (~1.96 ms/tailnet to construct+shut down, ~370 µs/tailnet to flush). No super-linear term, no lock contention, nothing O(N²) anywhere in the range.

Live footprint from real `runtime.ReadMemStats`/`NumGoroutine`:

| tailnets | heap delta | goroutine delta | goroutines/provider |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | 2,216 KiB | 6 | 3.00 |
| 10 | 12,340 KiB | 33 | 3.00 |
| 50 | 57,200 KiB | 153 | 3.00 |
| 100 | 113,128 KiB | 303 | 3.00 |

Exactly **3 goroutines per provider at every N** and ~1.1 MiB heap per provider — constant, so no leak and no accumulation. At the top of the range asked for (100 tailnets): ~113 MiB heap and 303 extra goroutines. Neither is material; 100 tailnets in one process is already an unusual topology, and those numbers are noise against the chart's 256Mi default.

### The one hypothesis that IS confirmed

Export bursts really are synchronized. With 10 tailnets + the process provider (11 providers) at a 50 ms `MetricInterval`, the first tick across all 11 landed within a **17.26 ms spread — 34.5% of one interval**. `NewProviderSet` constructs every provider back-to-back microseconds apart with an identical interval, so every `PeriodicReader` fires in the same fraction of the cycle. That is correlation by construction, not coincidence.

Connection count is the other genuinely wasteful dimension, derived from code rather than measured (the benchmark deliberately touches no network): `newMetricExporter`/`newLogExporter` each construct their own exporter per `Provider` with no shared `grpc.ClientConn` and no shared `http.Client`, so `protocol: grpc` opens **2×(N+1)** independent connections to the same endpoint — 3×(N+1) with tracing on — with zero reuse, and `protocol: http` gets no cross-provider keep-alive either.

### Decision

Closing as **not material** on today's evidence, which this issue explicitly allows. The heap/goroutine/allocation cost does not justify shared-transport work. Neither constraint was at risk: no per-device or per-node MeterProvider exists to reintroduce, and distinct Resources with distinct `service.instance.id` per tailnet are preserved.

Captured as a follow-up rather than implemented, since it is out of this issue's measured scope: if an MSP deployment ever grows past ~100 tailnets on gRPC, **deterministic per-tailnet interval jitter** (a small hash-of-name offset added to `MetricInterval`) breaks up the confirmed burst cheaply, without touching transport sharing or the frozen Resource/instance-ID contract. Transport sharing is the more invasive fix and the numbers do not currently justify it.

title: Benchmark and reduce multi-tailnet exporter fan-out and synchronized bursts

Live incident validation on <host-1> (2026-07-27): this scope now has a concrete failure mode.

The HTTP metric exporter began receiving `413 Request Entity Too Large` once the uncompressed request reached 33,079,888 bytes against Grafana Cloud Mimir's 20,000,000-byte limit. Later requests grew every minute (33,221,520; 33,370,806; 33,487,966). Restarting the process restored export temporarily by clearing SDK aggregation state.

Root cause:

- <host-1> intentionally runs `cardinality.flow.metrics_mode: both`, raw flow identity/port dimensions, reverse DNS, node-metric passthrough, and `cardinality.metric_limit: 100000`.
- Raw flow metrics are monotonic counters. The required cumulative temporality retains every attribute set seen for the process lifetime, so the serialized request grows even when current-interval active cardinality is modest.
- The current cardinality page measures only sets emitted in the latest interval. After restart it showed ~1.7k–2.2k active series while `tailscale2otel.export.datapoints` had already counted ~53k datapoints across the first five exports. It does not expose the cumulative series retained by the SDK.
- `sdkmetric.PeriodicReader` does not queue a failed export. Exporter retry is internal, and HTTP 413 is not transient. The next tick collects the still-growing cumulative aggregate and fails again.
- otel-go v1.44 has `OTEL_GO_X_METRIC_EXPORT_BATCH_SIZE`, which splits `ResourceMetrics` by datapoint count before calling the exporter. tailscale2otel neither sets nor exposes it.
- `otlpmetrichttp.WithMaxRequestSize` is only a client-side rejection threshold; it does not split a request. Exposing that option alone would fail earlier and would not restore delivery.

Scope correction needed for this issue: distinguish (1) a hard serialized-request guard from (2) export batching that keeps each backend request below its ingest limit. Acceptance must include a regression proving one cumulative collection is delivered as multiple OTLP requests and that one oversized batch no longer wedges all metric delivery.

title: Expose deterministic OTLP compression, timeout, retry, and request-size controls

comments.body:
## Parked — blocked on a tailnet change I am not authorised to make. @rknightion, this needs one decision from you.

**Premise re-confirmed.** `.github/workflows/live-contract.yml:46-59` mints its token from `secrets.TS_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID` / `TS_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET` via OAuth client-credentials — long-lived GitHub secrets. WIF itself is implemented and exercised only against synthetic servers: `internal/tsapi/workloadidentity.go` posts `client_id` + `jwt` to `/api/v2/oauth/token-exchange`, and `workloadidentity_test.go` drives it against an `httptest` server. Nothing has ever performed a real exchange. The issue is accurate.

### What blocks it

Proving the exchange needs a **federated identity created in the Tailscale admin console**, bound to the GitHub Actions OIDC issuer and this repository's subject. Creating one is a tailnet mutation, and my standing authorisation covers the Grafana stack only — explicitly not the tailnet. So I have stopped here rather than doing it.

### What I could verify without touching anything, and one finding that changes the design

The failure half of the acceptance criteria can be probed against the live endpoint unauthenticated, because every attempt is rejected. I did that. **Every failure mode returns an identical opaque response:**

```
POST https://api.tailscale.com/api/v2/oauth/token-exchange
  client_id=knonexistent-client & jwt=not.a.jwt
    -> 400  "invalid request"   (REQ-20260728095718c2c1ea7198a62a3a)

  client_id=ktest & jwt=<well-formed JWT, iss=token.actions.githubusercontent.com,
                         aud=wrong-audience, exp=1, sub=repo:rknightion/tailscale2otel:...>
    -> 400  "invalid request"   (REQ-20260728095718c646cfcef28256ee)
```

Unknown client, malformed JWT, wrong audience and expired token are **indistinguishable from the response**. That is correct API design — differentiating them is an oracle for an attacker — but it means this acceptance criterion cannot be met as written:

> - [ ] Wrong audience/issuer/expired token fail predictably.

They fail *identically*. A CI test can assert "a bad token is rejected with `400 invalid request` and no access token is issued", which is worth having, but it cannot assert *which* thing was wrong, and any test claiming to distinguish them would be asserting nothing. Recording this so it is not re-derived: the negative test is a single case, not four.

### Decision needed from you

**Create a dedicated read-only federated identity in the Tailscale admin console for this repo?**

If yes, what it needs — and note the whole point is that **no long-lived secret is stored in GitHub**, so there is nothing to add to repo secrets afterwards:

- **Scopes:** `all:read` only. Same least-privilege posture as the existing live-contract client.
- **Issuer:** `https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com`
- **Subject:** `repo:rknightion/tailscale2otel:ref:refs/heads/main` — or narrower. The lane is `schedule` + `workflow_dispatch` only, so a fork PR can never reach it (the same reasoning already recorded in that workflow's header for why hosted-runner secrets are safe there).
- **Audience:** the code and chart both default to `api.tailscale.com/<client id>` (`tailscale2otel.wifAudience` in `_helpers.tpl:421`). GitHub will mint a token with any audience via `ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_URL`, so whatever the console requires can be matched — I just need to know the client ID it issues.
- **Then tell me the client ID** and I will wire the lane: `id-token: write`, request an OIDC token with that audience, exchange it, make one read-only API call, and add the single negative case above. No new secret.

If **no**, this closes as unsupported and the honest record is: WIF ships tested against synthetic servers only, and `docs/` should say so plainly rather than implying the path is live-verified. I would rather write that down than leave the current silence.

Nothing else on tracker #483 is blocked by this — it is the last open child alongside the P3 Helm work.

## Done and live-verified. @rknightion authorised the tailnet change, so this is no longer blocked.

Commits `8de36d5` (implementation) and `b75d3db` (a correction, below). Proven by run [30351935446](https://github.com/rknightion/tailscale2otel/actions/runs/30351935446) — every step green against the real tailnet.

### First, a correction to my earlier comment on this issue

I wrote that the exchange returns *"an identical opaque `400 invalid request`"* for every failure mode. **That was wrong**, and it was wrong because I derived it by probing with a *fake* client ID before any real identity existed. With a valid federated client, the live run shows:

```
wrong-audience token rejected with HTTP 403, no access_token issued
```

So the real behaviour is:

| condition | response |
| --- | --- |
| unknown `client_id`, or a malformed request | `400 invalid request` |
| valid `client_id`, token it must refuse | **`403`** |

The response separates *"no such client"* from *"this client refuses that token"*. It still does not distinguish a wrong audience from a wrong issuer from an expired token — so the conclusion stands and the acceptance criterion is still **one** assertion, not four. Only the status code was wrong.

### What was created

Two federated identities via `POST /api/v2/tailnet/-/keys` (`keyType: federated`), both issuer `https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com`:

| description | scopes | tags | subject | purpose |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `tailscale2otel CI federated read` | `all:read` | — | `repo:rknightion/tailscale2otel:ref:refs/heads/main` | this lane |
| `tailscale2otel Actions tailnet join` | `auth_keys` | `tag:ci` | `repo:rknightion/tailscale2otel:*` | Actions joining the tailnet as an ephemeral node |

Neither returns a secret — that is the whole point. The API response carries only an `id` and an `audience`, and the audience is exactly `api.tailscale.com/<client id>`, which **confirms the default the code and chart already compute** (`tailscale2otel.wifAudience`, `_helpers.tpl:421`). That default was never live-checked before.

The read identity is pinned to `refs/heads/main` deliberately: this lane is `schedule` + `workflow_dispatch` and schedules always run on the default branch, so anything broader would be slack. A `workflow_dispatch` from another branch will fail the exchange — that is intended, not a bug.

### Acceptance

- [x] **CI proves successful exchange and a read-only API call.** The exchange step succeeded and `TestLiveContract` then ran against the live API and reported clean — not skipped; the lane fails on a skip precisely so a no-op cannot look green.
- [x] **Wrong audience/issuer/expired token fail predictably.** As one assertion, for the reason above. The negative case runs **first**, so a broken exchange cannot be mistaken for a working one, and it asserts on both the status and the absence of an `access_token` — a non-200 alone would still pass if the endpoint ever returned a token beside an error.
- [x] **No long-lived Tailscale secret is stored in GitHub.** `TS_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID` and `TS_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET` are **deleted** from the repo secrets. What remains — `TS_WIF_CLIENT_ID`, `TS_WIF_AUDIENCE`, `TS_JOIN_CLIENT_ID`, `TS_JOIN_AUDIENCE` — are identifiers, not credentials; they grant nothing without a GitHub-signed OIDC token whose `sub` matches. They are stored as secrets only to keep tailnet identifiers out of tracked files.
- [x] **Rotation behaviour is exercised.** Every run mints a fresh OIDC token and exchanges it for a fresh short-lived API token; there is nothing persistent left to rotate. The daily schedule exercises it unattended from here.

### Guards

`internal/ci/liveauth_test.go` fails if a long-lived Tailscale secret name reappears, if the exchange endpoint stops being called, if `id-token: write` is lost, or if the negative case is reduced to minting a token without asserting on the outcome.

That last guard **was itself vacuous when first written** — it substring-matched `"id-token: write"`, which a commented-out line satisfies exactly as well as a live one. Mutation testing caught it; it now parses the permissions block. Fifth instance of that class in this repo, and a security guard is the worst possible place for it.

### One thing left for you

The Tailscale-side OAuth client **`tailscale2otel-repo`** (`all:read`) still exists in the tailnet. Nothing uses it any more and its GitHub-stored secret is gone, so it is now a dangling credential. Revoking it is yours to do — I create-authorised only, and deleting a credential I did not create is not something I will do unasked.

Also created and ready but **not yet used by anything**: the `tag:ci` join identity. Wiring it is a one-step `tailscale/github-action@v4` with `oauth-client-id: ${{ secrets.TS_JOIN_CLIENT_ID }}`, `audience: ${{ secrets.TS_JOIN_AUDIENCE }}`, `tags: tag:ci` and `id-token: write`. Per your call, no issue filed — the foundation is there for whenever you want it.

## Credential cleanup done — the tailnet now holds exactly one tailscale2otel credential

Both follow-ups from the closing comment are resolved, on @rknightion's instruction (2026-07-28).

**Revoked `tailscale2otel-repo`** (`k7tvNVam6N11CNTRL`, OAuth client, `all:read`, created 2026-07-13) — `DELETE /api/v2/tailnet/-/keys/{id}` → HTTP 200. It was the lane's old stored-secret credential, unused since `8de36d5` and with its GitHub secret already deleted.

**Revoked `tailscale2otel Actions tailnet join`** (federated, `auth_keys`, `tag:ci`) → HTTP 200, and deleted `TS_JOIN_CLIENT_ID` / `TS_JOIN_AUDIENCE` from repo secrets.

The reasoning, recorded because the answer was "no" and a future session should not re-create it on a hunch: **nothing in this repository's CI needs tailnet access.** `live-contract` reaches `api.tailscale.com` over the public internet, and every other lane is build/test/lint/publish. Keeping it would have left an idle credential able to mint auth keys for `tag:ci` nodes — a strictly larger blast radius than the read-only identity that was revoked for the lesser offence of merely being unused.

The one plausible future use, if anyone wants it: joining the tailnet so CI can scrape a real `tailscaled` `/metrics` endpoint, which is tailnet-only and is currently the gap in `nodemetrics` live coverage. That is speculative and has no issue. Recreating the identity is a single `POST /api/v2/tailnet/-/keys` with `keyType: federated`, `scopes: ["auth_keys"]`, `tags: ["tag:ci"]`, issuer `https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com`, subject `repo:rknightion/tailscale2otel:*` — then `tailscale/github-action@v4` with `oauth-client-id`, `audience`, `tags: tag:ci` and `id-token: write`.

**Final state:** one credential, `tailscale2otel CI federated read` (federated, `all:read`, subject pinned to `repo:rknightion/tailscale2otel:ref:refs/heads/main`). Repo secrets hold `TS_WIF_CLIENT_ID` and `TS_WIF_AUDIENCE` only — identifiers, not credentials. No long-lived Tailscale secret exists in GitHub.

## Finding and proposed scope

**Priority/theme:** P4 / API research  
**Evidence:** Current client can PUT sink URL/token (`internal/tsapi/logstream.go:14-32`) but status GET decodes health counters only at `:64-97`; collector API at `internal/collector/logstream/logstream.go:55-120` has no destination identity. Explicitly parked in #173.  
**Why:** A drift gauge is useful only if an API exposes a safely comparable destination configuration.  
**Scope/out:** Verify current official/live API and wire shape; determine whether URL/fingerprint can be read without token disclosure. Research spike, not assumed implementation.

**Acceptance:**

- [ ] Official spec and live capture are compared.
- [ ] Read permission and secret exposure are documented.
- [ ] If viable, exact metric/status design and cardinality are proposed.
- [ ] If impossible, issue records the negative result and closes.

## Delivery requirements

## Audit identity

`operator:OUX-58`

comments.body:
## Research complete — NOT VIABLE. Closing with the negative result.

This is the acceptance criteria’s 4th branch ("If impossible, issue records the negative result and closes"), not a failure to deliver.

### 1. Official spec vs. live capture — compared

`spec/tailscale-api.json` documents four Logging paths. Only two are relevant:

| Path | Verbs | Carries destination identity? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `/tailnet/{tailnet}/logging/{logType}/stream/status` | `get` | **No.** `LogstreamEndpointPublishingStatus` is delivery-health counters only |
| `/tailnet/{tailnet}/logging/{logType}/stream` | `get`, `put`, `delete` | **Yes** — `LogstreamEndpointConfiguration` |

The status endpoint — the only one this project reads — has no URL, hostname, destination type, user, or any other hashable identifier. It is pure health telemetry. So there is **no way to detect drift from the endpoint we already consume**, and the question reduces entirely to whether `getLogStreamingConfiguration` can be read safely.

### 2. Read permission and secret exposure — documented

Verified directly against the vendored spec:

| Field | Schema | Returned on GET? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `url` | `{"type":"string"}` | **yes** |
| `user` | `{"type":"string"}` | **yes** |
| `token` | `{"type":"string","writeOnly":true}` | no |
| `s3SecretAccessKey` | `{"type":"string","writeOnly":true}` | no |
| `gcsCredentials` | `{"type":"string"}` | **yes** |

Scope-wise there is no additional cost: `getLogStreamingConfiguration` and the already-consumed `getLogStreamingStatus` both require `log_streaming:read`. The problem is the payload, not the permission.

Two exposures, either sufficient on its own:

- **`gcsCredentials` is not marked `writeOnly`.** Its own description calls it the JSON workload-identity credentials for the GCS account. For a GCS sink, a GET returns live credential material. `token` and `s3SecretAccessKey` are protected; this one is not.
- **The `url` is credential-shaped for several destination types.** Splunk/Cribl/Panther-style HEC sinks routinely carry a token in the path or query string. A live capture from a lab tailnet confirms `url` and `user` come back in plaintext exactly as the spec says (contents not reproduced here — it is a real sink address).

A hash does not rescue this. A stable hash of a URL that embeds a token is a stable secret-derived value, and it would live in **metrics**, which are exported to Grafana Cloud, rendered on dashboards, and readable by far more principals than the credential itself. That widens the blast radius rather than containing it.

### 3. Metric design — not proposed

No viable design exists, so none is offered. Proposing one would imply the read is acceptable.

### 4. This reaffirms a decision the repo had already made

`internal/tsapi/contract/operation_dispositions.json` already classified `getLogStreamingConfiguration` as **`privacy-rejected`**. This spike independently reached the same verdict — but found the recorded *reason* was partly wrong, and corrected it in `29f57c8`:

> the note said the endpoint "returns the log-stream destination url, username and **token** fields"

`token` is `writeOnly` and is **not** returned. The field that actually leaks is `gcsCredentials`, which the note never mentioned. The verdict was right; the stated mechanism was not. That matters because the next reader asking "can we just read the config endpoint?" would have weighed a token they were never going to receive and missed the field that does carry a secret.

### What would have to change upstream

Tailscale would need a **stable, secret-free** sink identifier on a read-scoped endpoint — a server-computed hash whose input provably excludes path and query, or a `destinationType` plus host-only summary with credentials documented as stripped. Absent that, there is nothing to compare against.

### Scope note

`#173` parked this and the tracker (#483) requires parked items to begin from their research/design acceptance criteria rather than jumping to implementation. That is what happened: no gauge was built, no client method was added, and `internal/tsapi` and `internal/collector/logstream` are untouched.

Closing as unsupported.

comments.body:
Closing as **out of direction** — decision by @rknightion, 2026-07-28. Not a rejection of the design; the feature is coherent and buildable. It is a rejection of the surface.

**Premise re-confirmed.** No HTTP-SD endpoint is served. Node-metrics discovery exists but is internal to the `nodemetrics` collector — it discovers targets *for its own scraper*, emitting `tailscale2otel.nodemetrics.discovery.{success,targets}`. The Prometheus pull endpoint (`:2112`) serves `/metrics` only. Everything the issue states is accurate.

### Why it closes rather than ships

**It is in the parked bucket of #173, and its neighbours have been decided the same way.** #173 lists as deliberately out of scope: *"Config hot-reload (SIGHUP/watcher) · shared checkpoint backends (S3/Redis) + multi-replica story · **Prometheus HTTP-SD endpoint serving tailnet devices as scrape targets** · Kubernetes operator."* Two of those four have now been settled: config hot reload is parked as #486 with an explicit instruction not to add a SIGHUP handler, and shared checkpoints + multi-replica were closed on #352 this session with "do not file implementation subtasks." This is the third, and there is no reason to treat it differently.

**#173 also locks "No Prometheus mixin."** The project's dashboards and alerts are Grafana dashboard-v2 JSON and Grafana-managed rule manifests generated in-repo. The consistent position is that Prometheus-ecosystem integration surface is not what this project provides — and an HTTP-SD endpoint is precisely that.

**The Prometheus listener is not a supported consumption path.** It exists so the wire format can be inspected during development; the product direction is OTel-native. Building service discovery *on top of* a listener that is not itself the intended consumption path compounds the mismatch.

### The design problem it would have forced, recorded because it is the interesting part

An HTTP-SD response must carry each target's address, which for a tailnet means `<tailnet-ip-2>/10` addresses and usually hostnames. Both are redacted by default: `pii_filter.tailscale_ips: true` and `pii_filter.hostnames: true`.

That is not an unresolvable contradiction — the filter governs what leaves for a third-party observability backend, whereas SD would be served to the operator's own Prometheus on the operator's own network — but it does mean the endpoint would have to **deliberately emit what the rest of the project strips by default**. Consequences, had it been built:

- it must **fail closed without a token**, unlike `/metrics`, which is open by default when `prometheus.auth.token` is empty. Two endpoints on one listener with opposite auth defaults is a genuinely confusing contract.
- the PII exemption would need to be explicit and documented rather than implied, or the next reader treats it as a leak.

If this is ever revisited, that tension is the first thing to resolve, not the caching or the filters.

Reopen only if someone actually asks for it and the Prometheus-surface direction changes.

## Audit context

Identified during the comprehensive audit of `9401181b163417e517eb69f112fc79b78534e77e`. The audit exercised configuration validation and reviewed the CLI, admin/status/flow UIs, Compose assets, Helm chart, installation paths, and operational documentation.

## Finding and proposed scope

**Priority/theme:** P4 / Design  
**Evidence:** Shared S3/Redis checkpoints and multi-replica were parked in #173; chart enforces singleton at `values.yaml:13-18`, following #203.  
**Why:** Shared storage alone does not prevent duplicate polling/emission or split-brain.  
**Scope/out:** Design issue for leader election, fencing, checkpoint consistency, receiver routing, failover RTO, and exactly/at-least-once semantics. Do not file implementation subtasks until the contract is agreed.

**Acceptance:**

- [ ] Failure-mode table covers crash, partition, slow leader, and rollout.
- [ ] Fencing/ownership protocol is selected.
- [ ] Signal duplication/gap guarantees are explicit.
- [ ] Chart scaling remains locked until the design is implementable.

## Delivery requirements

- [ ] Re-confirm the premise against the current implementation and upstream contract before changing behavior.
- [ ] Add a failing regression or telemetry-level test first, then implement the smallest complete change.
- [ ] Update affected catalog, generated artifacts, configuration references, operator documentation, dashboards, and rules as applicable.
- [ ] Preserve bounded-cardinality and PII/secret-handling contracts.
- [ ] Run the full repository gate, including all affected tool modules and generated-artifact drift checks.

## Audit identity

`operator:OUX-56`

comments.body:
## HA design — deliverable for this issue

Design only. No implementation, no subtasks filed, and `replicaCount` stays locked, per the tracker's rule for parked items.

### Verified starting state

| Fact | Evidence |
| --- | --- |
| Scaling is locked two ways | `values.schema.json` `replicaCount {min:1,max:1}`, plus a template `fail` in `deployment.yaml` for `--skip-schema-validation` |
| Strategy is `Recreate` | `deployment.yaml` — never two pods, even briefly, during a rollout |
| **Series identity is per-TAILNET, not per-pod** | `instanceFor()` (`internal/app/options.go:162`) derives `service.instance.id` from the tailnet name; the pod contributes nothing |
| Checkpoints have no CAS primitive | `CheckpointStore` is `Get/Set/Keys/Delete` (`internal/collector/checkpoint.go:24`) — no conditional write, so no fencing token can be enforced today |

### The problem is not cost, it is corruption

The obvious framing — "two replicas means we pay twice" — is wrong, and it matters for the design. Because `service.instance.id` is derived from the **tailnet**, two replicas observing the same tailnet emit series with **identical identity**. Two writers, one series:

- **Counters**: each replica keeps its own cumulative total. The backend sees a single series whose value jumps between two independent sequences — read as resets, so `rate()` invents traffic that never happened.
- **Gauges**: last-write-wins between two pollers at different points in their interval. The value is real but arbitrary.
- **Logs**: genuinely duplicated records, which the existing cross-source dedup (`internal/dedup`) does **not** cover — that set is per-process and bounded, so it cannot see another pod's emissions.

So shared checkpoint storage alone is not merely insufficient (as the issue says) — it does not address the actual failure at all. Checkpoints coordinate *what to fetch*; nothing coordinates *who emits*.

### Failure-mode table

| Mode | Without ownership | What a correct design must guarantee |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Crash** | Standby must take over. Window collectors resume from the last checkpoint, so a crash between emit and checkpoint-advance replays that window → duplicate log records | At-least-once for logs, explicitly. Bounded replay = one poll interval |
| **Network partition** (replica alive, cannot reach control plane) | Both replicas believe they are healthy; both poll and emit into one series identity | Only a holder of a currently-valid lease may emit. Losing the lease must **stop emission**, not just stop polling |
| **Slow leader** (GC pause, throttled node) | Lease expires while the process is still running and mid-export. It wakes and finishes a write the new leader has already superseded | Fencing: the checkpoint write must be rejected if the lease generation moved. Needs a CAS the store does not currently have |
| **Rollout** | `Recreate` guarantees no overlap today. `RollingUpdate` would put two emitters on one identity for the whole surge window | Either keep `Recreate`, or make the new pod wait for the lease before emitting |
| **Receiver traffic during failover** | HEC/webhook pushes to a Service are load-balanced across replicas regardless of who holds the lease | Receivers must be treated separately from pollers — see below |

### Receivers do not fit the leader model

Pollers pull, so exactly one owner is the right answer. Receivers are pushed to by Tailscale, and a Service load-balances across ready pods. Making a non-leader reject a webhook is wrong: Tailscale retries on non-2xx, so a leaderless moment turns into delivery failure and eventual data loss upstream.

Receivers are also *already* nearly safe to run N-wide — records are deduped by content and the flow/audit processors are stateless per record. The blockers are per-process state: the ingress WAL (per-pod filesystem; a pod that dies with an un-drained WAL strands data until it returns) and the bounded dedup set (per-process, so cross-pod duplicates are invisible).

**Conclusion: a receiver-only replica set and a single-leader poller are different workloads and should not share a Deployment.** Any HA design that scales one Deployment to N is wrong on its face.

### Ownership protocol — three options

| Option | Fencing | Works outside k8s | Automatic failover | Verdict |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **A. Kubernetes Lease** (`coordination.k8s.io`) | Yes, via `resourceVersion` CAS | **No** | Yes | Rejected as the *only* mechanism: it makes the k8s API a hard runtime dependency for a binary that also ships to Compose, systemd and bare metal. Also needs RBAC the chart deliberately does not grant |
| **B. Shared-store lease** (S3 conditional PUT / Redis) | Yes, if the store offers CAS | Yes | Yes | The only option that preserves "single static binary, runs anywhere". Requires adding a conditional-write primitive to `CheckpointStore` |
| **C. Static sharding by tailnet** | Not needed — disjoint ownership by config | Yes | **No** | Cheapest by far, and genuinely useful for the MSP case |

### Recommendation

**Do not build leader election. Offer C (static sharding by tailnet), and keep `replicaCount: 1` per shard.**

Reasons:

1. The multi-tailnet architecture already partitions cleanly — one `tailnetRuntime` per tailnet, its own emitter, client, cache, scheduler and checkpoints. Sharding is a config split, not a distributed-systems problem: N tailnets across M deployments, each a singleton.
2. It removes the failure modes rather than handling them. No lease, no fencing, no split-brain, no CAS requirement, nothing new to get subtly wrong under partition.
3. What it does not give is automatic failover for a single tailnet. For this workload that gap is small: a poller that is down for one interval resumes from its checkpoint and refetches the window. The data loss from a 60-second outage is **zero**, not 60 seconds' worth — which is precisely why the expensive option earns so little here.

Option B stays the documented path if someone genuinely needs sub-interval failover for one tailnet, and its prerequisite is concrete and small enough to state: a conditional `Set` on `CheckpointStore` (compare-and-swap on a generation counter), plus an emission gate that closes when the lease is lost — **not** merely a polling gate, since a mid-flight export must also be suppressed.

### Guarantees the contract must state, whichever option is chosen

- **Logs: at-least-once.** Checkpoints advance after emit, so any crash replays at most one window. Never claimed as exactly-once.
- **Metrics: exactly one emitter per series identity, always.** This is the invariant that must never be violated, because violating it corrupts data rather than duplicating it.
- **Receivers: at-least-once, independent of leadership**, and never rejected for lack of a lease.

### Answering the acceptance criteria

- [x] Failure-mode table covers crash, partition, slow leader, and rollout
- [x] Fencing/ownership protocol is selected — **C, static sharding**, with B as the escape hatch and its exact prerequisite named
- [x] Signal duplication/gap guarantees are explicit — stated above per signal class
- [x] Chart scaling remains locked until the design is implementable — unchanged and re-verified; both the schema bound and the template `fail` are still in place

### Open decision for @rknightion

This design recommends **not** building leader election, which is a narrower answer than the issue implies. If you want option B built anyway, say so and it becomes a real implementation issue with the CAS prerequisite as its first task. **Default if unanswered: adopt C**, document sharding in the chart, and close the door on B until someone asks with a concrete need.

Closing this issue as the design deliverable it asked for. No implementation subtasks filed, per the tracker's instruction not to until the contract is agreed.

## Decision confirmed by @rknightion — no leader election

Rob approved the recommendation on 2026-07-28. Recording it here so it is binding rather than a proposal, and so a future session does not re-litigate it.

**Adopted: option C, static sharding by tailnet. `replicaCount` stays locked at 1 per shard.**

**Rejected: option A (Kubernetes Lease)** — makes the k8s API a hard runtime dependency for a binary that also ships to Compose, systemd and bare metal, and needs RBAC the chart deliberately does not grant.

**Rejected for now: option B (shared-store lease with CAS fencing).** Not ruled out forever, but it is not to be built speculatively. Its prerequisite is recorded and unchanged: a conditional `Set` on `CheckpointStore` (compare-and-swap on a generation counter), plus an emission gate that closes when the lease is lost — not merely a polling gate, because a mid-flight export must also be suppressed. Reopen only with a concrete need for sub-interval failover on a single tailnet.

**Do not file implementation subtasks for shared checkpoint storage, leader election, or fencing.** The invariant that survives regardless of mechanism: *exactly one emitter per series identity, always* — because `service.instance.id` is derived from the tailnet (`internal/app/options.go:162`), two replicas produce colliding series rather than merely duplicate cost.

**Why:** ExternalSecrets, SOPS, and GitOps users cannot supply the full YAML config without generic volume overrides or storing multi-tailnet credentials in Helm values.  
**Scope/out:** `existingConfigMap`/`existingConfigSecret`, configurable key, mutual exclusion, rollout checksum/manual restart annotation. No external controller implementation.

**Acceptance:**

- [ ] Existing resource can replace chart-generated config.
- [ ] Multi-tailnet secret config works without Helm value disclosure.
- [ ] Invalid combinations fail rendering.
- [ ] Upgrade/reload behavior is documented.

## Delivery requirements

- [ ] Re-confirm the premise against the current implementation and upstream contract before changing behavior.
- [ ] Add a failing regression or telemetry-level test first, then implement the smallest complete change.
- [ ] Update affected catalog, generated artifacts, configuration references, operator documentation, dashboards, and rules as applicable.
- [ ] Preserve bounded-cardinality and PII/secret-handling contracts.
- [ ] Run the full repository gate, including all affected tool modules and generated-artifact drift checks.

## Audit identity

`operator:OUX-51`

comments.body:
Closed by `098dbb3`.

## Premise — CONFIRMED

The deployment mounted only chart-generated objects, and `existingSecret` (values.yaml:108) covers the **credential env-var Secret**, not the config file. So a GitOps/ExternalSecrets/SOPS user had two bad options: a generic `extraVolumes` override fighting the chart's own `config` volume, or putting multi-tailnet credentials into Helm values — where `helm get values` exposes them to anyone who can read the release.

## What shipped

`existingConfigMap` / `existingConfigSecret`, plus `existingConfigKey` (default `config.yaml`) naming the key inside. The key is **projected** to `config.yaml`, so the container's `-config /etc/tailscale2otel/config.yaml` argument is unchanged whatever the source key is called.

## Two deliberate design calls

**1. The override is total, not a merge.** Either setting makes the chart render no config object and leaves the entire `config:` tree inert. A partial merge would mean `helm template` shows values the pod never sees — a silent divergence between what you can inspect and what actually runs, which is worse than refusing to combine them.

**2. No `checksum/config` annotation in this mode.** The chart cannot read another object's contents, so any hash it produced would be of its own **inert** `config:` tree: it would change when the pod's real config did *not*, and stay put when the real config changed. A misleading rollout trigger is worse than none. `rolloutTrigger` / Reloader remain the documented path, exactly as for a rotated `existingSecret` (#469).

## Acceptance

- [x] Existing resource can replace chart-generated config — asserted for both ConfigMap and Secret, including that the chart renders none of its own
- [x] Multi-tailnet secret config works without Helm value disclosure — `existingConfigSecret` is precisely that path; credentials never enter Helm values
- [x] Invalid combinations fail rendering — both sources at once, and an empty `existingConfigKey`
- [x] Upgrade/reload behavior is documented — the checksum reasoning and the `rolloutTrigger`/Reloader path are in `docs/installation.md`

## Negative tests

| Mutant | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Render the chart's ConfigMap alongside an external one | "chart still rendered its own ConfigMap" |
| Emit `checksum/config` for an external config | "a checksum was emitted for a config the chart cannot read" |
| Accept both external sources | "accepted two config sources" |

Two assertions guard the *unchanged* default as well — the chart's own ConfigMap and its `checksum/config` must both still be there — so this cannot silently disable the normal path.

## Process note

My gate ordering ran `check_doc_commands.py` **before** `regen-generated.sh`, so it briefly flagged `--set existingConfigSecret` as an unknown chart value — the schema had not yet been regenerated. The commit itself contains the regenerated schema and the gate passes at `098dbb3` with a clean tree; the check simply ran too early in my sequence. Recording it because the transcript shows a red gate next to a push, and that pairing should never be left unexplained.

Chart 0.18.0 → 0.19.0. Full gate green at `098dbb3`, regeneration confirmed a fixed point.

- [ ] Examples terminate HTTPS and route only the intended path/port.
- [ ] Missing receiver credential/TLS dependency fails clearly.

## Audit identity

`operator:OUX-50`

comments.body:
Closed by `9993b50`. Chart 0.20.0 → 0.21.0.

**Premise re-confirmed.** #344's per-listener Services are in place (`templates/service.yaml`, four discrete default-off Services each mapping only its own port). The chart had no Ingress and no Gateway API resource. Webhook still binds `:8089` by default while Tailscale requires HTTPS on 80/443.

**Scope decision: receivers only.** `ingress` and `gateway` blocks exist for `streaming` and `webhook`. There is **no key at all** for `admin` or `prometheus` — those are introspection and scrape surfaces, and putting them one `--set` away from public exposure is not a default worth shipping. Both templates hardcode `[streaming, webhook]` rather than ranging over all four listeners, so it is structurally impossible rather than merely discouraged. Case V forces every admin/prometheus ingress and gateway key on simultaneously and asserts zero of each kind renders.

**Guards, each failing with the values key to fix**

| condition | why |
| --- | --- |
| route requires `service.<listener>.enabled` | a route with no backing Service is a silently broken route |
| route requires the listener credential | publishing an unauthenticated receiver is the failure mode this issue exists to prevent |
| Ingress requires a non-empty `host` | a host-less rule is a catch-all that swallows traffic for unrelated apps on the same controller |
| `tls.enabled` (default) requires `tls.secretName` **or** an annotation | otherwise the Ingress claims TLS with nothing to terminate it |
| HTTPRoute requires ≥1 `parentRefs` entry | Gateway API accepts an empty list syntactically; it attaches to nothing |

`tls.enabled: false` stays possible for a mesh that terminates upstream, and `values.yaml` states plainly that Tailscale will not deliver webhooks to a plaintext endpoint.

**One honest wrinkle, recorded rather than papered over.** The credential check inside `validateIngress`/`validateGateway` is **transitively unreachable today**: the Service precondition already requires `service.<listener>.enabled`, and `service.yaml` runs the same check on the same key and reports first. Verified by a real render — enabling a streaming Ingress with no credential produces `service.yaml:27: service.streaming.enabled requires a credential on that listener (config.streaming.token)`. The call is kept and commented as such, so relaxing that precondition later cannot quietly remove the protection, and case T's assertion matches on the credential key rather than pretending the ingress guard fired. The acceptance criterion is still met: exposing a receiver with no credential fails, naming the exact key.

**Negative-testing.** Eleven mutations by the implementing lane, then three independently by the dispatcher against the committed tree:

| mutation | assertion that fired |
| --- | --- |
| `admin` added to `ingress.yaml`'s listener list | `V: expected 1 Ingress total, got 2` + `V: an admin Ingress rendered` |
| host guard disabled | `T: rendered a host-less (catch-all) Ingress (rc=0)` |
| TLS guard disabled | `T: rendered an Ingress claiming TLS with nothing configured to terminate it (rc=0)` |

The implementing lane also caught a **vacuous assertion in its own test** before shipping: `yq 'has("tls")'` checks the document root, not `.spec`, so the TLS assertion reported `false` unconditionally and passed under a mutation that should have broken it. Fixed to `yq '.spec | has("tls")'` and the mutation then failed correctly. That is the fifth instance of this class in this repo and the first one caught before landing.

**Gate:** `go build` · `go vet` · `go test -race ./...` · `golangci-lint` (0 issues) · `verify-modules.sh` (all 5 modules) · `render-tests.sh` **317 passed, 0 failed** · `helm lint` · `compose-tests.sh` (40/40) · three `python3 -m unittest` suites · `promqlcheck` (579 promql, 0 failures) · `actionlint` · `check_doc_commands.py` · `regen-generated.sh` a fixed point with a clean `git status`. Docs: a new Ingress/Gateway section in `docs/streaming-webhooks.md`.

`operator:OUX-49`

comments.body:
Closed by `e01d6c6`.

## Premise — CONFIRMED

No Service and no monitor template existed. The Prometheus config block is at `values.yaml:971-990` (the issue's 719-741 had drifted), and `deployment.yaml` declared exactly **one** named containerPort (`admin`) — nothing for the Prometheus listener. That named port was #345's stated dependency and was added in #344.

## What shipped

A default-off `PodMonitor`. It scrapes pods **directly** through the named container port, so it needs no Service — which is why it landed before the ServiceMonitor (#458).

## Credentials are referenced, never embedded

`bearerTokenSecret` and `tlsConfig` carry only Secret references. Rendering a token into a PodMonitor would place it in a namespaced custom resource readable by anyone with `get podmonitors` — a strictly wider audience than `get secrets`. That is the same reasoning SEC-07 (#470) applies to the config ConfigMap, applied to a different object.

## Two render-time failures, both for *silent* modes

- PodMonitor without `config.prometheus.enabled` — nothing to scrape.
- `config.prometheus.auth.token` set with **no** `bearerTokenSecret`. This is the important one: the scrape is rejected with 401, the target goes down, and the series simply stop. Nothing errors anywhere. That is precisely the failure class `dashboardrefs_test.go` exists to prevent for panels, so it is a render error here rather than a warning.

The scrape `scheme` follows the listener's own TLS setting — the same rule the probes have followed since #342 — so enabling `prometheus.tls` cannot leave the scrape speaking plaintext to an HTTPS port.

| Mutant | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Remove the 401 guard | 2 failures |
| Embed the token value instead of a reference | 2 failures, incl. "the token VALUE was embedded" |
| Hardcode `scheme: http` | "scheme did not follow listener TLS" |

- [x] PodMonitor works without a Service — asserted that zero Services render in the same case
- [x] Render tests cover absent CRDs and auth combinations

**Why:** Operators repeatedly hand-write Services for enabled Prometheus, webhook, or streaming surfaces.  
**Scope/out:** Separate admin/prometheus/streaming/webhook Services, all default-off, named ports, configurable type/annotations. Never expose an unsafe listener.

**Dependencies:** OUX-13/14 should land first.

**Acceptance:**

- [ ] Default chart still renders no Service.
- [ ] Each Service maps only its matching enabled listener.
- [ ] Unsafe missing-auth combinations fail rendering.

## Delivery requirements

- [ ] Re-confirm the premise against the current implementation and upstream contract before changing behavior.

## Audit identity

`operator:OUX-48`

comments.body:
Closed by `1e5d29a`.

## Premise — CONFIRMED

No Service template existed. `deploy/CLAUDE.md` ("No Kubernetes Service (deliberate)", now at lines 96-108) documents the omission as intentional and explicitly permits this design, with two binding conditions: **default off**, and **never map a receiver port without its credential**. Both are implemented as render-time failures, not documentation.

## Frozen listener seam

Enumerated exhaustively before writing anything, since #345/#458/#346 all build on it:

| Listener | Config path | Port | Default | Credential |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| admin | `config.admin.listen` | 9091 | **enabled** | `admin.auth.token` (optional at runtime) |
| prometheus | `config.prometheus.listen` | 2112 | disabled | `prometheus.auth.token` (optional at runtime) |
| streaming | `config.streaming.listen` | 8088 | disabled | `streaming.token` |
| webhook | `config.webhook.listen` | 8089 | disabled | `webhook.secret` |

"Optional at runtime" is the point: the app tolerates an empty token on those two, so the *chart* has to be the thing that refuses to publish them.

## What shipped

Four discrete Services, one per listener, each mapping only its own port. Never an aggregate — an aggregate maps ports whose listeners have different credentials and different exposure needs, so enabling one surface would silently publish the others.

`type` defaults to `ClusterIP` on all four. A `LoadBalancer` default would put a receiver on the cloud provider's public ingress path from a single `enabled: true`.

The deployment now declares a **named containerPort per enabled listener**, derived from its listen address rather than restated. Services target by name, and #345's PodMonitor will too — that was its stated dependency.

## The guards

| Combination | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Service for a **disabled** listener | render fails, naming `config.<name>.enabled` |
| Service for a listener with **no credential** | render fails, naming the credential key |
| Credential supplied via `*_file` | **allowed** — demanding the inline form would push operators back to command-line credentials, which #341 just removed |

The credential-guard message states the specific hazard rather than a generic warning, because the two are genuinely different: prometheus serves every series unauthenticated with an empty token, and webhook **fails open** — an empty secret skips HMAC verification entirely.

## Two of my assertions initially proved nothing

Both found by mutation testing, both fixed:

1. **A `yq` length query over EMPTY input returns 1**, not 0. "N: exactly one Service" passed happily when *zero* Services rendered. Replaced with a document count over the raw manifest.
2. **The disabled-listener test passed for the wrong reason.** With no credential set, the *credential* guard fired first — so deleting the listener-enabled guard entirely changed nothing and the test stayed green. It now sets a credential and matches the specific message `requires config.prometheus.enabled`. Re-running that mutant afterwards correctly produced `FAIL N: rendered a Service for a disabled listener (rc=0)`.

That is the second and third guard this session to pass while asserting nothing.

## Other mutants

| Mutant | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Remove the credential requirement | 4 failures, one per listener |
| Default a Service `type` to LoadBalancer | 2 failures |
| Turn it into an aggregate (extra port on one Service) | "maps ONLY its own port" fires |

## Acceptance

- [x] Default chart still renders no Service
- [x] Each Service maps only its matching enabled listener — port count asserted, not just presence
- [x] Unsafe missing-auth combinations fail rendering — all four listeners individually
- [x] No aggregate or default LoadBalancer Service exists

Chart bumped 0.15.1 → **0.16.0** (new feature surface). `configcheck` over the chart-rendered config passes. Full gate green at `1e5d29a`.

Unblocks #345, #458 and #346, which all needed the named ports and the per-listener Service seam.

## Audit context

Identified during the comprehensive audit of `9401181b163417e517eb69f112fc79b78534e77e`. The audit exercised configuration validation and reviewed the CLI, admin/status/flow UIs, Compose assets, Helm chart, installation paths, and operational documentation.

## Finding and proposed scope

**Priority/theme:** P2 / Keyless auth  
**Evidence:** Chart disables SA token automount at `values.yaml:25-33` and exposes WIF fields at `:235-245`, but operators must hand-author `extraVolumes`/mounts. Tailscale’s audience is `api.tailscale.com/<client ID>`.  
**Why:** The advertised keyless path is cumbersome and easy to misconfigure.  
**Scope/out:** Default-off projected service-account token volume/mount, audience, expiry/path, and config wiring. No Kubernetes API RBAC.

**Acceptance:**

- [ ] Enabling WIF renders only a projected audience-scoped token.
- [ ] Client ID/audience/path validation is actionable.
- [ ] Token rotation works without restart.
- [ ] No broad Kubernetes API token is mounted.

## Delivery requirements

- [ ] Re-confirm the premise against the current implementation and upstream contract before changing behavior.
- [ ] Add a failing regression or telemetry-level test first, then implement the smallest complete change.
- [ ] Update affected catalog, generated artifacts, configuration references, operator documentation, dashboards, and rules as applicable.
- [ ] Preserve bounded-cardinality and PII/secret-handling contracts.
- [ ] Run the full repository gate, including all affected tool modules and generated-artifact drift checks.

## Audit identity

`operator:OUX-47`

comments.body:
Closed by `30589c4`.

## Premise — CONFIRMED (one line reference had moved)

`serviceAccount.automountServiceAccountToken: false` is at `values.yaml:33` as filed. The WIF fields are **not** at `values.yaml:235-245` — they live under `config.tailscale.auth.workload_identity` (`client_id`, `id_token_file`), around line 302. Substance unchanged: no WIF-specific volume wiring existed, so operators hand-authored `extraVolumes`/`extraVolumeMounts`.

## What shipped

`workloadIdentity.enabled` renders a projected, audience-scoped ServiceAccount token, mounts it read-only, and points the exporter at it.

Two things are **derived rather than restated**, which is the substance of "easy to misconfigure":

- **Audience** = `api.tailscale.com/<client_id>`, computed from the configured client id. An explicit `workloadIdentity.audience` still overrides it.
- **`id_token_file`** = `mountPath` + `fileName`, set as an env var so one expression feeds both the volume and the path the exporter reads.

A wrong audience is the nastiest failure here: it fails neither at render nor at startup, only when the token is first exchanged — and it surfaces as an auth error that looks like a bad OAuth client. Deriving it removes the class.

## "No broad Kubernetes API token" — the important negative

`automountServiceAccountToken` is deliberately **untouched**. Turning it on would mount a general-purpose Kubernetes API token: one the exporter never uses, and a far more valuable credential to leak than the Tailscale one. The render test asserts it is still not `true` while WIF is enabled, and the projected volume is asserted to have **exactly one** source so nothing else can be smuggled alongside it.

## Rotation — already worked, verified not reimplemented

`workloadIdentityTokenSource` re-reads `idTokenFile` on **every** `Token()` call, and the kubelet refreshes a projected token in place at ~80% of its lifetime. So rotation without restart was already true and needed no change. `expirationSeconds` is guarded at ≥600 because Kubernetes silently clamps shorter requests — a lower value would simply misdescribe the real lifetime.

## Guards

| Combination | Why it fails |
| --- | --- |
| WIF enabled, `auth.method` ≠ `workload_identity` | a token mounted and never used |
| No `client_id` | the audience derives from it; unscoped tokens are rejected only at first use |
| `expirationSeconds` < 600 | Kubernetes clamps it silently |
| `extraEnv` naming the token-path variable | would silently repoint the exporter at a path with no token |

That last one is #348's reserved-name policy extending automatically: the chart now sets that variable, so it joins the reserved set only while WIF is enabled.

## Negative tests

| Mutant | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Swap the projected token for `automountServiceAccountToken: true` | 3 failures, incl. "a general-purpose Kubernetes API token is being mounted" |
| Hardcode the token path | the mountPath-agreement check fires on a custom path |
| Drop the `client_id` guard | "rendered an unscoped audience" |

## Acceptance

- [x] Enabling WIF renders only a projected audience-scoped token — source count asserted at exactly 1
- [x] Client ID/audience/path validation is actionable — four guards, each naming the setting and the consequence
- [x] Token rotation works without restart — pre-existing behaviour, verified rather than rebuilt
- [x] No broad Kubernetes API token is mounted — asserted directly, and negative-tested

Chart 0.19.0 → 0.20.0. Full gate green at `30589c4`, regeneration a fixed point.

Note: #355 (exercise WIF in live-contract CI) remains open under P3 and is the natural follow-on — this change is render-level only and does not prove a real token exchange against Tailscale.
