comments.body:
## Closing receipt

Closed by `0794f61a1658776888120d36a806200117aa5792`.

**Premise confirmed, and worse than "not discovered".** `parseKey` tries the self-contained legacy basename first, explicitly to "preserve flat copied-export compatibility", but `enumerate` only ever listed `dayPrefixes(...)`. So a flat object was never **listed** — it did not even reach the skip counters. Pinned by `TestCollect_PartitionedLayoutNeverListsAFlatObject`: zero records *and* zero skip counters under the default layout. The asymmetry holds as expected: the official basename needs four or more path components to recover its date, so it cannot be flat-parseable.

**Config.** `collectors.flowlogs.objectstore.layout` and its per-tailnet sibling `tailnets[].objectstore.flow.layout`, values `partitioned` (default) or `flat`. Empty means partitioned; anything else is a startup error naming both valid values. No `auto` — a flat and a partitioned bucket are distinguishable only by listing them, and guessing wrong changes what the durable scan positions mean. Normalisation happens in exactly one place, applied on both branches of `FlowObjectStore`, and `objectstore.New` independently refuses an unknown value.

**Flat enumeration reuses the existing machinery** rather than adding a second path: one scan prefix instead of the day list, with the same `prefixProgress`, the same bounded page, the same durable `startAfter`, the same filters and ordering. `flatPrefix` mirrors `dayPrefixes`' base normalisation, pinned across six spellings of the configured base.

**#285's late-key clearing still holds, proven by mutation.** Disabling the position-clear for flat mode only produced `flow records = 10, want the ten original objects plus the late key`.

### Deviation from the frozen design — accepted, because the literal version double-emits

The frozen brief said "the same `stale` filter". Implemented literally, flat mode **provably** duplicates records: `object "flow/2026-07-24-08-00-00.ndjson" fetched 3 times, want exactly once`.

Mechanism: the filter is `at.Before(from) && !progress.active`. For a **day** partition the `active` exemption spans one day. For the **flat** prefix it spans the whole export, so while the walk is truncated every object in the bucket becomes a candidate — and because the seen set is pruned at `cursor - 2*Lookback`, an object too old to be in the window is also too old to be *remembered*, so each wrap re-fetches and re-emits it. It also silently defeated `initial_lookback`.

The lower bound is therefore **absolute in flat mode**, with partitioned behaviour byte-identical. Nothing is lost, because that exemption is not the retry mechanism: a failed object keeps its durable gap row and is retried with no listing at all — proven by `TestCollect_FlatLayoutFailedObjectIsRetriedFromItsGapAfterFallingOutOfTheWindow`, where the object is hidden from every later listing and still recovered. Consequence, documented: `layout: flat` does not backfill older than `initial_lookback`/`lookback`, the same rule as partitioned.

**Layout switches prune cleanly, in both directions,** and this required a `state.go` change that is load-bearing rather than cosmetic. Without a layout-aware staleness predicate the flat row is not a `YYYY/MM/DD/` prefix, so it was classed stale and **deleted every cycle**, destroying resumability — proven by reverting the predicate: `flow records = 8, want all 10`. Separately, an empty encoded scan prefix (flat at the bucket root) is now legitimate; the old guard made that configuration fail every cycle as corrupt state: `objectstore: invalid scan checkpoint "scan//MjAyNi0wNy0yNC0xMS01MS0wMC5uZGpzb24"`.

**`maxDayPrefixes` cannot misfire in flat mode** — `positions` can hold at most one entry and the listing window plays no part in choosing it. Pinned by a 30-day window producing exactly one LIST per cycle.

**Honest cost, stated in the startup warning and in all three docs surfaces:** flat mode has no partitions to bound re-listing, so once caught up each cycle re-walks the prefix. Each cycle is still one bounded, resumable LIST, so no cycle scans an unbounded bucket — but a large flat prefix needs several cycles per sweep, and a newly written object is only discovered when the walk reaches its key, so ingestion latency rises to roughly one sweep. Tailscale's own exports are always partitioned; `flat` is for copied or mirrored exports.

**Deliberately not part of the feed identity:** `layout` is excluded from `objectStoreFeedKey`, so two tailnets on one bucket and prefix still collide under #284 even with different layouts.

**Chart version bumped to 0.14.6** per `deploy/CLAUDE.md`, matching the repo convention of a patch bump for a new value (comment-only chart edits are not bumped).

**A pre-existing defect found while doing this is filed as #498:** a configured prefix with a *leading* slash makes the loader disown the very prefix enumeration builds, so every scan row is deleted each cycle. Verified independently, and the fix recommendation on that issue was corrected after finding that normalising the prefix would change the feed digest and orphan the cursor.

**Local verification of the exact committed tree,** in an isolated worktree containing only this change on top of `7ebdb9c`: root build/vet green, `go test -race ./...` exit 0 across 54 packages with no FAIL/panic/DATA RACE, `golangci-lint run` `0 issues`; all three tool modules green; `docs/env-vars.md`, chart `README.md` and `values.schema.json` regenerated with the pinned tools and all three confirmed **idempotent** against a snapshot on a second run; `docs/metrics.md` in sync; `helm lint`/`template` plus 126 render checks; `configcheck` OK on `config.example.yaml` and on the chart-rendered config; secret hygiene PASS; `actionlint` and `zizmor` clean; `govulncheck` no vulnerabilities; GoReleaser snapshot and Docker build succeeded.

**Actions evidence — all nine workflows terminal success for the exact SHA:** CI `30260977916`, Helm `30260978111`, Release `30260978810`, CodeQL `30260978394`, Docker Security `30260978470`, Scorecard `30260978409`, actionlint `30260978352`, zizmor `30260978447`, documentation sync `30260978121`.

## Audit context

Identified during the comprehensive audit of `9401181b163417e517eb69f112fc79b78534e77e`. The audit traced poll, HEC, webhook, object-store, processor, enrichment, checkpoint, and built-in flow-view behavior end to end and checked the current Tailscale logging contracts.

## Finding and proposed scope

Problem: object ingestion caps only one line at 16 MiB and then scans an unbounded number of lines (`objectstore.go:290-335`). One compressed object can expand into unbounded CPU and telemetry work.

Acceptance:

- [x] Configurable decompressed-byte and record-count caps apply per object and cycle.
- [x] Limit breach enters the durable gap/quarantine path, not “seen”.
- [x] Counters distinguish compressed bytes, decompressed bytes, records, and expansion-limit failures.
- [x] Normal large-tailnet objects are benchmarked before choosing defaults.

## Delivery requirements

- [x] Re-confirm the premise against the current implementation and upstream contract before changing behavior.
- [x] Add a failing regression or telemetry-level test first, then implement the smallest complete change.
- [x] Update affected catalog, generated artifacts, configuration references, operator documentation, dashboards, and rules as applicable.
- [x] Preserve bounded-cardinality and PII/secret-handling contracts.
- [x] Run the full repository gate, including all affected tool modules and generated-artifact drift checks.

## Audit identity

`ingestion:D11`

comments.body:
## Pre-implementation decision record

Live premise review at `d701ebe45ffabe34b5ccf1d3923372ff38270759` confirmed that only a 16 MiB per-line scanner cap exists. Total decompressed bytes, rows per object, and bytes/rows per cycle remain unbounded. Atomic staging for #448 is unsafe until these bounds exist.

The repository has no representative exported-object corpus or observed object-size/compression distribution. The existing evidence is the bulk-log API budget: 32 MiB, measured at about 2.4 KiB per flow record / 13,600 records, plus the receiver precedent of a separate 500,000-row amplification cap. That is useful policy evidence but does not satisfy the requested exported-object benchmark.

Recommendation pending owner confirmation:

- `max_object_decompressed_bytes: 33554432`
- `max_object_records: 100000`
- `max_cycle_decompressed_bytes: 268435456`
- `max_cycle_records: 500000`
- require both cycle caps to be at least their object counterparts;
- deterministic object-cap breaches enter quarantine and retain the existing paired seen row as disposition state, not successful-ingestion state;
- cycle shortfalls only defer untouched objects and preserve resumable scan state; they do not create gaps.

Independent work can proceed with explicit test limits. Public defaults and acknowledgement wording will not be committed until this decision is confirmed. #450 will own the final stored/wire/decoded metric names; this issue will expose the measured facts without silently reusing the mixed `ingest.size` meaning.

Maintainer decision (2026-07-26): approved the proposed bounded-expansion contract.

Frozen defaults:
- per object: 32 MiB decompressed bytes and 100,000 non-blank records
- per cycle: 256 MiB decompressed bytes and 500,000 non-blank records
- cycle limits must be at least their corresponding object limits
- a deterministic per-object breach uses the existing durable quarantine disposition, including its paired acknowledgement marker; it is not successful ingestion
- a per-cycle shortfall defers untouched work to the next cycle and is not quarantined

Addition: all four limits must be configurable for genuinely large tenants. Breach errors and operator diagnostics must identify the measured value and configured limit without exposing bucket, key, object identity, credentials, or record content.

Implementation remains strict TDD and must preserve #453 identity/checkpoint contracts and #477 ingestion behavior.

Review found one additional resource-bound decision (2026-07-26).

Evidence: the current implementation limits bytes only after decompression. A valid stream containing arbitrarily many empty gzip members or zstd skippable frames can consume unbounded compressed GET bytes and CPU while producing zero or negligible decoded bytes/records, so none of the four approved expansion limits fires.

Recommendation: add configurable actual-wire limits:
- per object: 64 MiB
- per cycle: 512 MiB
- deterministic object-wire breach follows the approved quarantine disposition
- cycle-wire shortfall defers without a gap
- diagnostics report actual compressed bytes consumed versus the configured cap, without object/bucket/key content

This is awaiting maintainer confirmation because no universal safe wire cap can be derived from a decompressed-byte cap. Independent review fixes (zstd minimum-memory handling, corrupt-frame classification, documentation) continue without waiting.

Implementation contract update from maintainer approval:

- decoded/object: 32 MiB; decoded/cycle: 256 MiB
- records/object: 100,000; records/cycle: 500,000
- actual compressed/wire bytes/object: 64 MiB; actual compressed/wire bytes/cycle: 512 MiB
- all six limits are configurable for large tenants
- startup validation rejects non-positive limits and cycle values below their object values
- object breaches report measured and configured values and quarantine the object; cycle exhaustion defers the untouched/uncommitted object for a later cycle

The wire limits close a bounded-work gap left by decoded and record limits alone: concatenated empty gzip members and zstd skippable frames can consume unbounded GET bytes and CPU while producing almost no decoded data. The 64/512 MiB defaults leave headroom above the 32/256 MiB decoded limits without making the default effectively unlimited. No request path, object key, credential, or body data is included in diagnostics.

comments.body: ## Closing receipt Closed by `7ebdb9c4f4408d096f05468c60e3b11f213af515`. **Premise confirmed, and the arithmetic is worse than the issue stated.** One shared `readAllClose` bound of 1 MiB applied to both credential documents and `ListObjectsV2` XML. A realistic full page in AWS's actual response shape costs **1,221 bytes per object** — `` + up to 1024 key bytes + `` + `` + `` + `` + `` and closing tags. 1,000 keys plus 258 bytes of prolog/root/`KeyCount`/`MaxKeys`/`IsTruncated` measures **1,221,258 bytes = 1.16 MiB** against a 1,048,576-byte cap. Break-even key length is roughly 851 bytes, so **any full page whose keys average more than that was being truncated.** The RED run reproduced the exact reported symptom: `s3: decode list response: XML syntax error on line 862: unexpected EOF` — a client-side cut presented as a server fault. **The failure was worse than a bad error message.** A body cut at an element boundary **parses cleanly** as a complete listing that is quietly missing objects, with nothing reported at all. So the fix cannot rely on the decoder noticing: the decoder is not a witness to truncation. **Design.** Listings now stream-decode via `xml.Decoder` over an `io.LimitedReader`, re-capped through the existing `boundedBody` struct so the close still goes through the original body — the same drain-and-close discipline `readAllClose` and `containercreds.go` use, not a fork of it. The reader is allowed exactly **one byte** past the bound, which makes "the allowance ran out" distinguishable from "the document ended on the last permitted byte". That signal, checked **before and in preference to** any decoder error, decides whether the response is refused — so a truncation-induced decode error can never be reported as a malformed bucket response. Because the decoder stops on the root's closing tag and may never ask for the slack byte, there is a deliberate one-byte probe read after a successful decode. **Mutation-proven load-bearing:** removing it makes `TestList_CompleteDocumentAtTheCapWithMoreToComeIsRefused` fail with `error = , want one matching errListResponseTooLarge` — i.e. without the probe a truncated listing silently parses and returns short. A body that genuinely ends there answers EOF and is unaffected, since only bytes actually delivered count against the allowance. **Two independent caps, deliberately not tracking each other.** - `maxListResponseBytes = 8 MiB`. Sized from the true ceiling, not a guess: 1,000 keys x 1,024 bytes plus per-entry XML is ~1.2 MiB, and XML escaping can expand one key byte to five (`&` → `&`), so a page of escape-heavy maximum-length keys reaches ~5.07 MiB. 8 MiB clears that with headroom and is still a bound. Generosity is affordable only because the decode streams — the wire bytes are never held alongside the result. - `maxMetadataResponseBytes = 1 MiB` — **the pre-existing value, unchanged**; the edit only names the magic number and documents why it stays small. IMDSv2, the STS web-identity exchange and the container endpoint all still read at that bound, with the container path re-capping itself tighter at 64 KiB. Mutation-proven: setting the metadata bound equal to the listing bound fails `metadata bound … is not smaller than the listing bound …; the two must not track each other`. The point is that widening listings can never widen what an environment-supplied metadata endpoint may make the process read. **Error text names the limit and disclaims the server**, so it cannot be mistaken for a malformed response: "…exceeds this client's read limit of 8388608 bytes: the response was discarded rather than parsed, because parsing a truncated listing silently drops objects. This is a bound in this client, not a malformed response from the bucket…". Wrapped with `%w` around an unexported sentinel, matching `internal/stream`'s existing `errBodyTooLarge` pattern. **The 1,000-long-key case succeeds** and its size is asserted rather than assumed: the fixture is built programmatically (nothing large committed), the test asserts it exceeds the metadata bound and fits the listing bound, then asserts 1,000 objects each with a 1,024-byte key, `Truncated == false`, and the last timestamp. Logged size: **1,221,258 bytes — 172,682 bytes (16.5%) past the old cap.** **Preserved behaviour.** HTTP error bodies are still read whole through `readAllClose` at the metadata bound before any re-capping, so fault messages are unchanged and verified live: malformed XML → `s3: decode list response: XML syntax error…`; HTTP error → `s3: list: 403 Forbidden: AccessDenied`. Trailing junk after a complete root element is still ignored, as before. One unavoidable text change: a transport failure mid-body on a 200 now reports as `s3: decode list response:` rather than `s3: list:`, which is arguably more accurate when streaming. **Notes.** A response whose document ends exactly on the last permitted byte but has trailing bytes is refused even though the document itself fitted — it is over the cap regardless, and no real listing gets within 7 MiB of it. The three 8 MiB boundary tests cost about a second each under `-race` only (0.05s without), from the race detector instrumenting an 8 MiB scan. **Local verification of the exact committed tree,** in an isolated worktree containing only this change on top of `4f670ab`: root build/vet green, `go test -race ./...` exit 0 across 54 packages with no FAIL/panic/DATA RACE, `golangci-lint run` `0 issues`; all three tool modules green; `docs/metrics.md` in sync; `helm lint`/`template` plus 126 render checks; `configcheck` OK; secret hygiene PASS; `actionlint` and `zizmor` clean; `govulncheck` no vulnerabilities; GoReleaser snapshot and Docker build succeeded. No config key added and no generated artifact affected. **Actions evidence — all seven applicable workflows terminal success for the exact SHA:** CI `30259063593`, Release `30259064098`, CodeQL `30259063889`, Docker Security `30259063814`, Scorecard `30259063836`, actionlint `30259063869`, zizmor `30259064001`. Helm and documentation sync correctly did not trigger; this commit touches only `internal/s3/**`.

comments.body:
## Closing receipt

Closed by `1e716e11fa2d0aa23e22f4845b7073619cc99cda`.

**What changed.** `Client.requestPath` is now the single place a request path is composed — the normalized endpoint base path, then the bucket when addressing path-style, then the caller's path. `request()` assigns that result straight onto the `*url.URL` that becomes `req.URL`, which is exactly what `sign()` reads via `EscapedPath()`. There is no second copy of the join for signing to disagree with, so the signed path and the sent path cannot diverge by construction. `sign.go` needed no change: it already derived the canonical URI from `req.URL` rather than recomputing it.

**Root-endpoint behavior is byte-identical.** `basePath` is `base.Path` with trailing slashes trimmed, so `""` and `"/"` both normalize to empty. Path-style then yields `"" + "/" + bucket + path`, matching the previous `"/" + bucket + path`; virtual-host yields `"" + path`, matching the previous `path`. The two pre-existing root-endpoint tests (`TestAddressing_PathStyleAndVirtualHost`, `TestGet_EncodedKeyIsSentAsSigned`) were left untouched and pass unchanged, and four table cases pin the root shapes directly.

**RED evidence.** Before implementation, on a `https://gw.example.net/storage/s3` endpoint: list path came out `"/flows/"` and get path `"/flows/flow/2026/07/24/a.ndjson"` with the `/storage/s3` prefix discarded; virtual-host likewise. The escaping case failed on both the decoded path and a separator count (`6 '/' separators, want 8`), proving the encoded wire path was also wrong and not merely the decoded form.

Identified during the comprehensive audit of `9401181b163417e517eb69f112fc79b78534e77e`. The audit traced poll, HEC, webhook, object-store, processor, enrichment, checkpoint, and built-in flow-view behavior end to end and checked the current Tailscale logging contracts.

`ingestion:D6`

comments.body:
## Wire-evidence blocker identified before decoder implementation

Current Tailscale documentation and the vendored API contract confirm S3/S3-compatible configuration-log streaming, independent prefixes, `YYYY/MM/DD/HH:MM:SS.json` keys and none/zstd/gzip compression. The current validation premise is stale.

Neither the official docs nor vendored OpenAPI defines the S3 object payload framing. No ignored capture contains a configuration-log S3 object. Existing polling/HEC fixtures prove audit event fields and polymorphic `old`/`new`; they do not prove whether S3 contains bare NDJSON events, an envelope, concatenated JSON, or which timestamp fields are present.

Required unblock evidence is one sanitized real S3 configuration-log object proving top-level framing, record boundaries, timestamp/capture semantics and compression/extension pairing. The current lab destinations are Splunk-only; no external sink will be mutated to manufacture evidence.

Until that evidence exists, backend/config/checkpoint plumbing may be designed but `NewAuditSignal` will not guess `json.Unmarshal(line, audit.Event)`. Owner/unblock condition: provide or authorize a read-only capture from an existing S3 configuration-log destination. If no such evidence is available after independent work is exhausted, this child will remain explicitly blocked rather than ship an invented wire contract.

## Independent evidence re-audit: the block is real, but narrower than recorded

An adversarial evidence hunt was run specifically to try to **overturn** the previous block rather than confirm it. The core finding survives: Tailscale documents the S3 key layout and the compression choices for configuration-log streaming, and documents nothing at all about the object payload. But the consequence was overstated, and the hunt turned up two shipped defects along the way.

### What is documented, and what is not

- The log-streaming docs (S3 tab) give the key shape verbatim — a prefix of `audit-logs/` "will produce S3 object keys similar to `audit-logs/2024/04/22/12:34:56.json`" — state that both log types can share one bucket separated by prefix, and offer compression `none` / `zstd` / `gzip` with `zstd` the default. The identical wording repeats for configuration logs, network logs, S3, S3-compatible, GCS and Azure: one destination model.
- The same page has **no** object-format section. Confirmed by two independent fetches worded differently, by the vendored spec, by three Tailscale blog posts, by the changelog, by the upstream FR thread (tailscale/tailscale#8523), and by four code searches that found no open-source consumer of these objects anywhere.
- `spec/tailscale-api.json` defines one `LogstreamEndpointConfiguration` serving both log types with identical S3 fields and one `compressionFormat`. That is the strongest available evidence for "one pipeline, two feeds" — but it describes the *destination configuration* and not one byte of object content.
- Tailscale's *other* S3 exporter, Aperture usage export, documents its framing precisely: `…​.cbor.zstd`, "a sequence of CBOR-encoded records". So Tailscale states object framing when it exists; the log-streaming silence is a genuine gap, not a search failure.
- `.capture/` on the workstation (43 files) confirms the earlier finding exactly: both lab feeds are Splunk, and there is no S3 object anywhere in the set. `logging_config.json` is a poll-API body and `stream_capture.ndjson` is an HTTP POST body — they prove the *record* shape, not the *object* framing.

### The inference that most needed killing

"Flow-log S3 ingestion works, so audit will work the same way" is **false**, and for a specific reason. Flow records are self-timestamping — `start`/`end` are present in both the API form and the streamed form — so the flow decoder is accidentally immune to the ambiguity that blocks audit. A **streamed configuration-log record carries no inner timestamp at all**: in the live capture the only times are the HEC envelope's `time` and `fields.recorded`. If an S3 object holds bare events with no envelope, the only time available is the object key, which is batch upload time rather than event time.

That is a data-correctness problem, not a decode problem, and it bites twice: `audit.Processor`'s `DedupKey` falls back to `eventTime|action|target.id` when `eventGroupID` is absent, so a zero `eventTime` collapses distinct events; and cross-source dedup buckets on `eventTime` truncated to one second, so a zero time buckets everything into 1970 and can suppress unrelated changes. `internal/audit` also has no `Validate`, unlike `internal/flowlog` — so an envelope-shaped object would unmarshal into an all-zero `Event` and emit one garbage record while silently deduping the rest.

**So the truly evidence-gated part is the timestamp source, not the whole decoder.** The backend, traversal, checkpoint, gap, decompression and budget contracts need no new code — the engine is already signal-neutral and `engine_contract_test.go` already drives it end to end with an `audit` signal.

### Also found: two shipped defects in the flow path, now filed and being fixed

The same gap has already cost us silently, in code that ships today:

- **#496** — keys ending `.json.zstd` or `.json.gzip` fail to parse, so those objects are never fetched and are counted only as `unrecognized_key`. Reproduced directly.
- **#497** — an object whose every row fails to decode is marked complete, advances the cursor, creates no gap and leaves `gap.healthy` at `1`. Reproduced directly: `objects=1, records=0, gaps=0, gap.healthy=1`. This is exactly what a framing mismatch looks like, and today it is invisible.

Both are filed under #478 and are prerequisites for ingesting a second signal whose framing we cannot prove.

### Capture authorised — but one prerequisite is missing

The maintainer has **authorised** a short capture: point the lab's configuration-log destination at a throwaway S3-compatible bucket, take 2-3 objects at `zstd` and at `none`, sanitise, revert to Splunk. That would fully unblock this issue and would also retroactively validate the flow path, which has never once been tested against a real Tailscale object.

It cannot be executed from this workstation as things stand, for a reason worth recording so nobody retries it blindly:

1. **No object-store credentials exist locally.** `.secrets/creds.local.env` carries Tailscale and Grafana Cloud credentials only — no S3/R2/MinIO access key.
2. **A local MinIO will not work.** Tailscale's publisher runs in Tailscale's own infrastructure, so the destination must be reachable from the public internet. `http://127.0.0.1:9000` or a tailnet-internal address cannot receive the upload.

**Unblock condition:** a publicly reachable S3-compatible bucket plus write credentials for it (a scratch AWS S3 bucket, Cloudflare R2, or a MinIO exposed publicly), and confirmation that the lab's configuration-log destination may be repointed for a few minutes. A Tailscale Funnel-exposed MinIO would in principle satisfy the reachability requirement using only existing infrastructure, but that is untested here and is a maintainer decision.

Owner: repository maintainer. Until that exists, this issue stays blocked on the timestamp question alone — the plumbing above it is implementable, and the two defects it exposed are being fixed now regardless.

## Capture executed — the blocker is cleared, with evidence

Maintainer authorised a lab capture and supplied AWS access, so the prerequisite recorded in the
earlier comment is satisfied. Captured live on **2026-07-27** from the `m7kni.io` lab tailnet.

### How it was set up (reusable recipe)

Temporary, private, tagged S3 bucket in AWS account `515966537543` (`eu-west-2`, public access fully
blocked), plus an IAM role trusted by Tailscale — **role-ARN auth, no long-lived access keys**:

1. `POST /api/v2/tailnet/-/aws-external-id` `{"reusable":true}` →
   `{"externalId":"…","tailscaleAwsAccountId":"891612552178"}`.
2. IAM role trust policy: principal `arn:aws:iam::891612552178:root`, condition
   `StringEquals: {"sts:ExternalId": "<externalId>"}`. Permission policy: `s3:PutObject` on
   `arn:aws:s3:::<bucket>/*` — that is the *only* permission Tailscale needs to publish.
3. `POST /api/v2/tailnet/-/aws-external-id/{id}/validate-aws-trust-policy` `{"roleArn":"…"}` → `200`.
   **Do this before repointing a live stream** — it proves assumability without an outage.
4. `PUT /api/v2/tailnet/-/logging/{configuration|network}/stream`.

Both log streams were repointed and then **restored** to their prior Splunk-HEC sink; the restore was
dry-run first (byte-identical `GET` afterwards) so the rollback path was proven before the outage began.

### API-contract findings (cost real calls to learn)

- **`s3ExternalId` is REQUIRED in the `PUT` body** even though `spec/tailscale-api.json` marks it
  `readOnly` on `LogstreamEndpointConfiguration`. Omitting it fails with
  `HTTP 400 {"message":"invalid awsExternalId parameter"}`. No drift-CI impact — `internal/oas`
  keeps only `get` operations — but the vendored spec is wrong here, the same way it is wrong about
  the audit envelope's `tailnet` vs `tailnetId`.
- `GET …/logging/{type}/stream/status` returns `HTTP 404`
  `{"message":"unexpected error on fetching status from logstream publisher"}` for both log types,
  before and after the change. It is not a usable health signal.
- `GET …/logging/{type}/stream` never returns `token`, so restoring a Splunk sink requires the token
  from your own side. Capture it *before* repointing.

### Real object-key format

```
<s3KeyPrefix>YYYY/MM/DD/YYYY-MM-DD-HH-MM-SS.ndjson
```

Observed: `audit/2026/07/27/2026-07-27-12-11-29.ndjson`, `flow/2026/07/27/2026-07-27-12-13-35.ndjson`.

Two things follow:

- **This is the layout `internal/collector/objectstore/key.go` calls `legacyKeyLayout`** (self-contained
  date-bearing basename), *not* the `officialKeyLayout` (`2006/01/02/15:04:05`, bare-time basename) its
  doc comment presents as what Tailscale writes. `parseKey` tries legacy first, so **real keys parse
  correctly today and no behaviour change is needed** — but the naming and the doc comments are
  backwards relative to the live export and will mislead the next reader.
- `s3KeyPrefix` is used **verbatim** with no separator inserted, so a prefix must carry its own
  trailing slash.

### Zero-byte objects are real

`audit/2026/07/27/2026-07-27-12-13-00.ndjson` was **0 bytes** — Tailscale writes an empty object for an
upload period with nothing to report. Any object-store signal must treat that as a normal empty object,
not as undecodable (relevant to the #497 guard, which is safe here because it requires `bad > 0`).

### Audit payload shape (20 records)

NDJSON, one event per line. Top-level key frequency:

| key | count |
| --- | --- |
| `logged` | 20 |
| `eventTime` | 20 |
| `eventGroupID` | 20 |
| `origin` | 20 |
| `actor` | 20 |
| `target` | 20 |
| `action` | 20 |
| `actionDetails` | 10 |
| `new` | 5 |
| `old` | 2 |

**`eventTime` is present on every record.** That is exactly the premise the block rested on, so
**#288 is unblocked**: the object payload carries its own event timestamp and needs no envelope.

Delta against the polled `GET /logging/configuration` payload (`.capture/logging_config.json`, 70
records): the **poll** path carries `type` and no `logged`; the **object export** carries `logged` and
no `type`. So `audit.Event` needs an additive `Logged` field to supply `CaptureTime`, and nothing may
assume `type` is present.

### Flow payload validated against real objects — a separate open unknown, now closed

Recorded on #478 as never having been checked: our flow-log framing had only ever been validated
against synthetic fixtures. 118 real records decode cleanly into `flowlog.FlowLog` with no unknown
fields. Top-level keys: `logged`, `nodeId`, `start`, `end`, `srcNode`, `dstNodes`, `virtualTraffic`,
`physicalTraffic`, `subnetTraffic`, `exitTraffic`; `srcNode`/`dstNodes` are populated with
`name`/`addresses`/`user`/`os`/`tags`. The `proto`-as-number quirk is present as documented.

Raw captures live in the gitignored `.capture/objectstore-288/`; sanitized fixtures will land under
`internal/collector/objectstore/testdata/`.

## Closed by `2018f07`

`feat(auditlogs): ingest the configuration-log S3 export` — pushed direct to `main`.

The premise this issue rested on is confirmed by evidence, not argument: every record in a real
configuration-log export object carries its own `eventTime`, so the timestamp question that blocked
the work is answered. See the [capture comment](#issuecomment-5091174514) above for the full evidence,
including the setup recipe and the four API traps it cost real calls to find.

### What shipped

| Area | Change |
| --- | --- |
| Decode | `objectstore.NewAuditSignal` adapts the SHARED `audit.Processor`, so an export object reaches exactly the path poll, HEC and webhook use |
| Record type | additive `audit.Event.Logged`; `audit.EventTimestamp` / `CaptureTimestamp` mirroring the flow-log pair |
| Config | `collectors.auditlogs.objectstore` (single mode) and `tailnets[].objectstore.audit` (per entry), same fields/defaults/credentials as flow, **no inheritance** from it |
| Validation | the stale "audit is not exported to object storage" rejection removed; feed-collision checking generalised across signals |
| Wiring | `internal/app` feed spec, one code path per signal; audit registration deliberately not gated on `cp.Supports("auditlogs")` since reading a bucket makes no API call |
| Docs / chart | `config.example.yaml`, `values.yaml` (+ `credentialPaths`), chart `0.14.6→0.14.7`, `docs/configuration.md`, `docs/streaming-webhooks.md`, `README.md`, regenerated `docs/env-vars.md` / chart README / `values.schema.json` |

### Two hazards the work exposed, both guarded

Neither was in the original scope; both are the kind of thing that would have shipped silently.

1. **The pre-v1 checkpoint migration is FLOW-only** — its keys are literally
   `objectstore.flowlogs.*`. An audit collector running it would have adopted flow's cursor, seen set
   and gaps as its own **and deleted them out from under flow**, rewinding or skipping flow ingestion
   depending on which collector started first. `objectstore.New` now gates the migration on the
   signal, so no caller can get it wrong. Regression test: `TestNew_LegacyMigrationIsFlowOnly`.
2. **Feed collisions must be checked across signals, not just across tailnets.** Two engines on one
   feed each fetch every object and then fail to decode the other's records, burning both budgets to
   produce undecodable-object errors. One rule now covers both shapes, and only destinations an
   *enabled* collector actually reads are considered — a leftover block for a polling signal stays
   inert rather than failing startup.

`Collector.Name()` also became signal-aware (`objectstore-audit`), because the name keys the
`tailscale.collector` scrape attribute and the admin status row; one shared name would merge both
collectors' durations, failures and last-error into one indistinguishable series. **Flow keeps the
bare `objectstore`** on purpose — renaming it would break existing dashboard queries for no
functional gain.

### Corrections to committed claims

- `key.go` called the live export's self-dated basename **`legacyKeyLayout`** and the
  never-observed time-only form **`officialKeyLayout`** — exactly backwards. `parseKey` tried the
  right one first, so behaviour was always correct; only the names and comments lied. Now
  `selfDatedKeyLayout` / `timeOnlyKeyLayout`, each documenting what was actually observed.
- `docs/configuration.md` documented `<prefix>/YYYY/MM/DD/HH:MM:SS.json` as what Tailscale writes.
  It writes `<prefix>/YYYY/MM/DD/YYYY-MM-DD-HH-MM-SS.ndjson[.zst|.gz]`. Corrected, with the
  zero-byte-object and verbatim-`s3KeyPrefix` behaviours documented alongside.

### Local verification

Run in a throwaway `git worktree` at `HEAD` holding **exactly** this diff, `cmp`-verified against the
staged tree file-by-file, so the gate ran on the tree that was pushed:

- root + `tools/configcheck` + `tools/metricscatalog` + `tools/apidrift`: `go build`, `go vet`,
  `go test -race`, `golangci-lint run` — all clean (isolated `GOLANGCI_LINT_CACHE`)
- `govulncheck ./...` — no vulnerabilities
- `helm lint`; `deploy/helm/tests/render-tests.sh` — **141 passed, 0 failed** (12 of them new, and
  mutation-proven: removing the three audit paths from `credentialPaths` fails exactly those 12)
- `configcheck` on `config.example.yaml` and the chart-rendered config — both OK
- `scripts/regen-generated.sh` — all four generated artifacts already in sync, zero drift
- GoReleaser snapshot, Docker image build, `actionlint`, `zizmor` — all pass
- secret-hygiene sweep: no lab tailnet name, node address, bucket, external ID or AWS account number
  outside the gitignored `.capture/`

Tests were mutation-checked rather than assumed load-bearing. Four mutations, four caught: dropping
the zero-Event guard, zeroing `EventTimestamp`, zeroing `CaptureTimestamp`, and un-tagging the
`logged` JSON field. One earlier version of the real-export test passed under mutation — it asserted
only "timestamp is non-zero", which the `logged` fallback satisfied — so it was tightened to pin the
exact instant.

### Actions evidence

All workflows green for `2018f07`: CI, CodeQL, Helm, Release, Docker Security, Scorecard, actionlint,
zizmor, Trigger Documentation Sync.

### Deviations from the stated scope

- **`collectors.auditlogs.source: both` is still accepted** for poll+stream, unchanged. Object-store
  is exclusive with the other two per signal, exactly as for flow.
- **No new metrics or catalog descriptors.** The object-store engine's telemetry (#451) is already
  per-signal via its `signal` attribute, so audit ingestion is visible through the existing series
  with no new cardinality.
- **No dashboard or alert-rule changes.** Nothing in `deploy/grafana` or `deploy/alerts` filters on a
  specific object-store signal, and the flow collector name is deliberately unchanged.

### Cleanup

The temporary capture bucket, its objects, and the IAM role were deleted and their absence verified
(`HeadBucket` → 404, `GetRole` → `NoSuchEntity`). Both lab log streams were restored to their prior
Splunk-HEC sink — confirmed byte-identical by `GET`, and confirmed *delivering* by two readings of
`tailscale2otel_ingest_records_total{source="stream"}` 90s apart on the live deployment. The reusable
Tailscale AWS external ID remains provisioned but is inert with no role to assume.

## Audit context

Identified during the comprehensive audit of `9401181b163417e517eb69f112fc79b78534e77e`. The audit traced poll, HEC, webhook, object-store, processor, enrichment, checkpoint, and built-in flow-view behavior end to end and checked the current Tailscale logging contracts.

## Finding and proposed scope

Problem: day enumeration keeps only the newest 14 days (`objectstore.go:66-68`, `internal/collector/objectstore/key.go:73-109`). A configured longer initial lookback silently skips older days and then advances the cursor.

Acceptance:

- [ ] Persist a low-water/backfill cursor separate from live ingestion.
- [ ] Live recent objects continue while historical days drain.
- [ ] Progress, ETA/backlog, pause, and reset are observable.
- [ ] Until implemented, validation rejects or loudly warns on unsupported lookbacks.

## Delivery requirements

- [ ] Re-confirm the premise against the current implementation and upstream contract before changing behavior.
- [ ] Add a failing regression or telemetry-level test first, then implement the smallest complete change.
- [ ] Update affected catalog, generated artifacts, configuration references, operator documentation, dashboards, and rules as applicable.
- [ ] Preserve bounded-cardinality and PII/secret-handling contracts.
- [ ] Run the full repository gate, including all affected tool modules and generated-artifact drift checks.

## Audit identity

`ingestion:D5`

comments.body:
## Backfill seam and operator-control decision

The loss premise is confirmed: `maxDayPrefixes = 14` keeps only the newest fourteen partitions, the ordinary cursor then advances, and no historical low-water mark revisits older ground.

Recommended durable seam inside the existing scoped namespace:

```text
backfill/v1/target
backfill/v1/low_water
backfill/v1/seen/...
backfill/v1/scan/...
backfill/v1/gap/...
```

Live work retains the existing rows and runs first with its own budget. Historical work drains recent-to-old ground with a separate budget, advances `low_water` only after every encountered object is durably represented, and never changes the live cursor. `target` is frozen when initialized so restart does not move the goal.

An exact object count or ETA would require unbounded enumeration. The truthful observable is remaining historical time range plus current-page lower-bound backlog, scan truncation and coverage-seconds drain rate; dashboards may derive an explicitly approximate ETA.

Recommendation for controls:

- startup `backfill_paused` stops only the historical lane and preserves state;
- no unauthenticated/admin mutation route under this issue;
- reset remains documented offline deletion of only the selected scoped `backfill/v1/*` subtree while stopped;
- changing `initial_lookback` never silently reinterprets an existing target.

Please confirm pause/reset policy and that the explicitly approximate time-range ETA satisfies the acceptance intent. Independent state-machine RED tests can proceed.

Product decision (2026-07-26): declined.

Grafana Cloud retains the relevant history for at most 14 days, so this project will not add an object-store backfill path beyond that horizon. Building a second historical cursor/checkpoint lane, pause/reset controls, and approximate ETA for data the target backend cannot retain would add state and migration risk without a supported operator outcome.

The existing bounded 14-day traversal remains the contract. No code change is required. This issue is closed as not planned; it may be reconsidered only if the target retention constraint changes and a new maintainer decision authorizes the product scope.

Identified during the comprehensive audit of `9401181b163417e517eb69f112fc79b78534e77e`. The audit traced poll, HEC, webhook, object-store, processor, enrichment, checkpoint, and built-in flow-view behavior end to end and checked the current Tailscale logging contracts.

## Finding and proposed scope

Acceptance:

- [ ] Storage configuration can be keyed per resolved tailnet.
- [ ] Each runtime gets its own backend, prefix, credentials, checkpoint namespace, and health.
- [ ] Single-tailnet global configuration has a documented migration path.
- [ ] Credentials and records can never cross runtimes.

Dependency: D1 should land first as the safety guard.

## Delivery requirements

- [ ] Re-confirm the premise against the current implementation and upstream contract before changing behavior.
- [ ] Add a failing regression or telemetry-level test first, then implement the smallest complete change.
- [ ] Update affected catalog, generated artifacts, configuration references, operator documentation, dashboards, and rules as applicable.
- [ ] Preserve bounded-cardinality and PII/secret-handling contracts.
- [ ] Run the full repository gate, including all affected tool modules and generated-artifact drift checks.

## Audit identity

`ingestion:D2`

comments.body:
Maintainer decision (2026-07-26): approved the proposed per-tailnet object-store configuration contract.

Frozen policy:
- object-store destinations and credentials live under each tailnet entry
- there is no global inheritance or fallback
- configured tailnet identity remains the checkpoint identity even when `-` resolves to a display name
- duplicate normalized feeds are rejected
- structural destination/authentication errors fail startup rather than disabling only one runtime
- provider, signal, feed, and configured-tailnet checkpoint namespaces remain those delivered by #453

The implementation must preserve secret/`_file` precedence and redaction from #449 and must not add non-S3 providers.

## Closing receipt

Closed by `ddef9181e92240a2e2fa783c9e89f1cb79dcd4e2`. Implements the maintainer-approved contract from the decision comment above, verbatim, with one deliberate narrowing recorded below.

**Shipped shape.** `TailnetConfig` gains `ObjectStore TailnetObjectStore` with a single `Flow ObjectStoreConfig` field, so the YAML is `tailnets[].objectstore.flow.*` reusing the whole existing `ObjectStoreConfig` field set including the three `_file` siblings. `internal/app` reads exactly one new seam, `(*Config).FlowObjectStore(tailnet) (ObjectStoreConfig, bool)`.

**Policy, as implemented.** The global `collectors.flowlogs.objectstore` block remains the only form when `tailnets:` is empty. With a list present nothing is inherited from it — not the endpoint, not the credentials — and a runtime with no destination of its own is refused rather than falling back. Two entries whose normalized `(endpoint, region, bucket, prefix, path_style)` match are a hard error naming both tailnets, since explicit duplicates would recreate the cross-attribution hazard #283 closed. Ingestion source selection stays global per signal. The literal configured tailnet name remains the checkpoint identity, so the frozen #453 namespace `objectstore/v1/<base64url-tailnet>/<provider>/<signal>/<feed-digest>/` is unchanged. Credentials are read only from the resolved destination, keeping #449's `Secret` typing, `_file` XOR precedence and redaction per entry.

**Deliberate narrowing.** Only `objectstore.flow` ships. The approved shape also showed an `audit` sibling, but object-store audit ingestion (#288) is blocked on external wire evidence, and a documented key that ingests nothing is worse than an absent one. `TailnetObjectStore` exists precisely so `Audit` is a purely additive later change.

**Two premise corrections found during implementation, both load-bearing.**

1. `d.multi` is `len(resolved) > 1`, but the contract's multi-tailnet mode is `len(cfg.Tailnets) > 0`. A **one-entry** `tailnets:` list has `d.multi == false`, so dispatching the app on `d.multi` would have made it read the global block while validation demanded the entry — silent no-ingestion. The app now dispatches on config shape, matching validation exactly.
2. `s3.New` can fail for seven structural reasons and `Validate()` covered only four. Endpoint URL parseability and scheme were unchecked, so a bad endpoint reached client construction and was logged rather than fatal. `Validate()` now covers every one, so a structural fault fails startup with a message naming the exact key and tailnet.

**Scope addition.** A `collectors.flowlogs.objectstore` block left behind after migrating to a `tailnets:` list is now an advisory warning rather than being silently inert — silently ignored destination config is how an operator concludes the exporter is broken. Kept a warning, not an error: the frozen contract says "no inheritance", not "mutually exclusive". Per-destination advisories (lookback-shorter-than-interval, plaintext signing) are now emitted per entry, keyed `tailnets[i].objectstore.flow.*`.

**Interpretation the contract did not cover.** A list entry cannot pass through `Default()`, so a destination naming only endpoint/region/bucket would have been rejected by the budget rules. Only the tuning fields (interval/lookback/initial_lookback/max_objects and the `max_object_*`/`max_cycle_*` budgets) fall back to the **built-in** defaults — never to the operator's global block, so this is not the forbidden inheritance. Destination identity, `path_style`, `allow_insecure_http` and every credential are never defaulted. Documented in `docs/configuration.md`.

**Env plumbing — none invented.** `tailnets` is already in `structSliceEnvKeys`, so a `TS2OTEL_TAILNETS__0__…` path is a hard Load error by the pre-existing #79 guard. Consequence, now documented in all three places: per-tailnet static credentials must come from a `*_file` sibling (a mounted Secret) or be left empty for the ambient chain.

**Chart.** No template change was needed. `tailscale2otel.config` renders `.Values.config | toYaml` verbatim, and `_helpers.tpl` already treats any non-empty `config.tailnets` as credential-bearing, so per-tailnet S3 credentials already route into the `<fullname>-config` Secret rather than a world-readable ConfigMap. Verified by rendering, and by the 126 render-contract checks.

**State/migration note.** For a one-entry `tailnets:` list the checkpoint scope tailnet changes from `tailscale.tailnet` to the literal `tailnets[0].name`. Such a config is a validation error until the destination moves under the entry, so the operator edits config regardless; the consequence is one cold start from `initial_lookback`. Pre-#453 flat state still migrates (that logic is untouched) and canonical `objectstore/v1/...` rows are never remapped. For two or more tailnets, and for plain single-tailnet mode, the namespace is byte-identical to before.

**Residual hazard flagged, not deviated from.** `path_style` is part of the duplicate-feed key per the frozen contract, so two entries differing *only* in `path_style` are permitted even though they address the same objects. Their distinct tailnet namespaces keep checkpoints separate, but records would be double-attributed.

**RED evidence.** Three build-failure REDs (`undefined: TailnetObjectStore`, `c.FlowObjectStore undefined`, `undefined: objectStoreDestinationFor`/`objectStoreScope`/`objectStoreTailnetIdentity`), one behavioural RED for per-entry `_file` handling, one for the ignored-global warning. The two security-critical guards were additionally **mutation-checked**: injecting a global-block fallback made `beta inherited the global destination …` and `beta inherited the global credential "GLOBAL-ACCESS-canary"` fail, and disabling the duplicate branch made `Validate accepted two tailnets reading the same object-store feed` fail. Both mutations reverted.

**Local verification of the exact committed tree,** in an isolated worktree containing only this change on top of `cc6e498`: root build/vet green, `go test -race ./...` exit 0 across 54 packages with no FAIL/panic/DATA RACE, `golangci-lint run` `0 issues`; all three tool modules green; `docs/metrics.md` in sync; chart README regenerated with the pinned `helm-docs` v1.14.2 (exactly one line) and `values.schema.json` unchanged, both confirmed **idempotent** on a second regeneration against a snapshot; `helm lint`/`template` plus 126 render checks; `configcheck` OK on `config.example.yaml` and on the chart-rendered config; secret hygiene PASS; `actionlint` and `zizmor` clean; `govulncheck` no vulnerabilities; GoReleaser snapshot and Docker build succeeded.

**Actions evidence — all nine workflows terminal success for the exact SHA:** CI `30257534585`, Helm `30257534595`, Release `30257535232`, CodeQL `30257535106`, Docker Security `30257535098`, Scorecard `30257535006`, actionlint `30257534985`, zizmor `30257535062`, documentation sync `30257534606`.

**Open for your judgement, both with a working default already shipped:** whether a populated global block alongside a `tailnets:` list should be a hard error rather than a warning, and whether an explicit `0` budget on a list entry should be rejected rather than read as unset.

body:
## What happened

The `binaries / goreleaser` job of the v3.0.0 Release run ([30152306402](https://github.com/rknightion/tailscale2otel/actions/runs/30152306402/job/89664680618)) failed:

```
⨯ release failed after 1m13s
  error= failed to proxy module: exit status 1: go: downloading github.com/rknightion/tailscale2otel/v3 v3.0.0
         go: github.com/rknightion/tailscale2otel/v3@v3.0.0: verifying module:
             github.com/rknightion/tailscale2otel/v3@v3.0.0:
             reading https://sum.golang.org/lookup/github.com/rknightion/tailscale2otel/v3@v3.0.0:
             500 Internal Server Error
```

## Why

`.goreleaser.yaml` sets `gomod.proxy: true`, so GoReleaser does not build the checked-out tree — it
re-downloads the module from `proxy.golang.org` and verifies it against `sum.golang.org`. That is a
deliberate supply-chain property (the released binaries are built from exactly what the proxy serves)
and should be kept.

The tag was created at `09:08:11`; the job hit the sumdb at ~`09:09`. The checksum database had not
ingested the new tag yet and returned a 500. Both endpoints returned 200 a few minutes later and a
plain re-run of the failed job went green with all 17 assets attached, unchanged.

This is **not** the stale-module-path failure of #174. `1739277` (`build!: move the module path to /v3
and guard the next major`) landed on `main` before the release PR merged, so `go.mod` already said
`/v3` when the tag was cut. The major-bump guard worked; this is an unrelated timing race.

## Scope

The race is structural, not major-specific: release-please creates the tag and the `binaries` job
starts within the same second of the same workflow run, so **every** release rolls the dice on whether
the sumdb has ingested the tag yet. It has evidently won that race until now.

A fixed `sleep` was considered and rejected: sumdb ingestion latency is variable, so a fixed delay is
either wasted wall-clock on the common path or still too short on the bad path. Poll for the actual
precondition instead and proceed the moment it is satisfied.

## Approach

Add `scripts/wait-for-module-proxy.sh`, run from the `binaries` job's existing `pre-cmd` (which the
shared reusable executes immediately before GoReleaser, in the checkout of the tag). It polls
`go mod download <module>@<tag>` — the exact operation that failed, including sumdb verification —
until it succeeds or a timeout expires, then hands off to GoReleaser.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `scripts/wait-for-module-proxy.sh` polls proxy+sumdb availability for the module@tag and exits 0 as soon as it resolves
- [ ] Exits non-zero with a clear diagnostic on timeout, rather than letting GoReleaser fail with the opaque `failed to proxy module` error
- [ ] Degrades to a warning + exit 0 when it cannot determine the tag, so the guard itself never blocks a release
- [ ] Wired into `pre-cmd` in `.github/workflows/release-please.yml`, before the notices generation
- [ ] Verified locally against a published version (fast success) and an unpublished one (clean timeout)
- [ ] `shellcheck`/actionlint clean; full local gate green

comments.body:
Follow-up hygiene landed in `9401181` (green: CI, zizmor, actionlint, CodeQL, Docker Security, Scorecard, Release).

**Repinned the shared binaries reusable to a real tag.** It was on a floating `@main` SHA
(`d1c590b`) because the checksums-locate fix (#176) existed only on main. `v1.5.0` is the first
shared release containing it, verified by compare rather than assumed: the old pin is an ancestor
of `v1.5.0` (`behind_by=0`) and `v1.4.3` sits 4 commits behind the pin. The only change to
`binaries.yml` across that range is two action bumps (checkout v7.0.0 → v7.0.1, setup-go v6.5.0 →
v7.0.0, the latter already in use in this repo). This was the last floating pin in `.github/workflows/`.

**Documented the permission grants** flagged by zizmor's `undocumented-permissions` audit. Comments
have to *trail* the grant to satisfy it. Two facts fell out and are now recorded in place:

- `contents: write` on the `edge` path and `packages: write` on the `binaries` job are both unused
  (the `gh release upload` steps in container-publish are gated on `release-tag != ''`, and
  goreleaser runs `--skip=docker`).
- Neither can be dropped: a reusable's job-level permissions cap against the caller's, so granting
  less than the reusable declares fails the call.

**Declined:** zizmor's `secrets-outside-env` on `RELEASE_PLEASE_TOKEN`. The `release-please` job has
no `if:` gate, so it runs on *every* push to main to maintain the release PR — an environment with
protection rules would put a manual approval in front of every push, which is exactly what this PAT
exists to avoid, and one without protection rules is naming ceremony. Reasoning is now a comment at
the token so it isn't re-litigated.

Both audits are auditor-persona only and were never gating — the repo reports zero findings under
the persona CI actually runs, before and after.

**Still unproven:** the `wait-for-module-proxy.sh` guard from this issue has not executed in CI. The
`binaries` job is gated on `release_created`, so it was skipped on both pushes; it first runs on the
next actual release.

body:
## Problem

`ts2o-device-key-expiring-critical` ("Device key expiring (<48h)", severity `critical`,
`domain: security`) fired in IRM for `<device-1>` (user `<email-2>`) — an untagged,
user-owned laptop.

The alert is factually correct: a Tailscale node key does **not** silently auto-renew, and
the device drops off the tailnet at expiry until someone completes an interactive re-auth.
But the tier is wrong for this class of device:

- An untagged, user-owned device warns its signed-in user in the Tailscale client (and
  Tailscale emails the user). Re-auth is self-service, routine, and recurs every key
  lifetime (default 180d). Not pageable.
- A **tagged** device is typically headless — nobody sees the prompt, so expiry is a real
  impending outage that needs a human dispatched to it.

Two facts make the tag split the right cut:

1. `internal/collector/devices/devices.go:601` only emits the
   `tailscale.device.key.expiry` gauge when `!KeyExpiryDisabled`, so devices with expiry
   disabled never produce a series at all.
2. Tailscale disables key expiry on tagged devices **by default**. So a tagged device that
   *does* have a live expiry series has had expiry explicitly re-enabled — the high-signal case.

Net effect today: everything this critical alert can ever fire on is, by construction, the
untagged human-owned class. It is a page whose remediation is "a human clicks a prompt on a
laptop they are sitting in front of."

## Change

- `ts2o-device-key-expiring-critical` → restrict to `{tailscale_tags!=""}` and retitle
  "Tagged device key expiring (<48h)". Stays `critical`/paging.
- `ts2o-device-keys-expiring-7d` (warning, non-paging) keeps covering **both** tagged and
  untagged, so untagged devices retain a signal — just not a page. 48h ⊂ 7d, so no coverage gap.
- `ts2o-auth-key-expiring-critical` is deliberately **unchanged**: auth/API keys have no
  human-in-the-loop, so critical is correct there.

`tailscale_tags` is set on the per-device gauge only when the device has tags
(`internal/collector/devices/devices.go:589`), so `tailscale_tags!=""` selects tagged and
`=""` selects untagged.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `gen/build_rules.py` updated (expr + title + descriptions on both rules)
- [ ] `tailscale2otel.grafana-rules.yaml` regenerated
- [ ] `deploy/alerts/README.md` security table + rationale note updated
- [ ] Both rules pushed to the live Grafana Cloud stack via the provisioning API
- [ ] Live critical rule no longer has firing instances for untagged devices

body:
`protoNames` (`internal/flowlog/processor.go:973`) has no entry for IP protocol **99**, so those flows
render as the bare string `99` on `network.transport`, in the `/flows` transport breakdown and on every
log record. It should be `tsmp`, and the view should say what a TSMP flow means, because it is the one
protocol in a Tailscale flow log that is a **diagnostic signal rather than traffic**.

## What proto 99 is

From upstream (`tailscale.com/types/ipproto`):

> `TSMP` is the Tailscale Message Protocol (our ICMP-ish thing), an IP protocol used only between
> Tailscale nodes (still encrypted by WireGuard) that communicates **why things failed**, etc.
>
> Proto number 99 is reserved for "any private encryption scheme". **We never accept these from the
> host OS stack nor send them to the host network stack.** It's only used between nodes.

Two consequences that matter for how we present it:

1. **A TSMP flow is a rejection notice, and its SOURCE is the node that did the rejecting.** It travels
   in the opposite direction to the traffic it is about. On a live tailnet, a node's blocked DNS
   queries to a resolver produced a matching stream of TSMP flows from the resolver back to it.
2. **It never touches the host stack**, so it is invisible to `tcpdump` on any interface, including the
   Tailscale one. This cost real time to establish on a live network: a 10-minute capture across all
   interfaces on the reporting node, a 75-second `tailscale debug capture`, a 60-second capture on the
   apparent source's LAN interface (1,978,983 packets, zero matches) and its `pf` state table all came
   back empty while the API reported the flow continuously. Anyone who sees a `99` row will go looking
   for those packets, and will not find them.

IANA's name for 99 is "any private encryption scheme", which is what a generic table would give you.
In a *Tailscale* flow log it is always TSMP, since the protocol is only ever used between nodes — so
naming it `tsmp` is both correct and the more useful of the two.

## Suggested change

- Add `99: "tsmp"` to `protoNames`.
- `docs/flow-view.md`: a short note that a `tsmp` flow is Tailscale's own "why it failed" message, that
  the source is the rejecting end, and that it will never appear in a packet capture. That turns an
  unreadable row into the fastest ACL-debugging signal on the page — it names the node that dropped
  something and the node whose traffic was dropped.
- Consider surfacing it in the policy section rather than only as a transport: a TSMP flow is
  independent corroboration of a `no_rule` verdict, arriving from the other end.

Also worth checking as part of this: TSMP carries no ports, so it is one of the portless protocols in
#248 — its flows currently mint a `0/99` row in the ports table. That fix covers the port half; this
issue covers the name.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `network.transport` reads `tsmp` for proto 99 on metrics, logs and the flow view
- [ ] A test pins the mapping alongside the existing `protoNames` cases
- [ ] `docs/flow-view.md` explains what a TSMP flow means, including the direction rule and that it is
      invisible to packet capture

encryption scheme", but in a Tailscale flow log the number can only ever be TSMP, since tailscaled
neither accepts these from the host stack nor sends them to it. Naming it is exact rather than a guess,
and it is the more useful of the two names by a wide margin.

`docs/flow-view.md` gets a subsection in the **policy** section rather than a line in a protocol table,
because that is where someone chasing a denial is already looking. It states the two things that make a
`tsmp` row worth reading — the source is the node that did the rejecting, so the flow points backwards
at the traffic it is about and corroborates a `not explained` verdict from the other side; and it will
never show up in a packet capture, with the numbers from the live investigation so the next person does
not repeat it.

## One thing worth recording

**The repo's own real-data fixture has carried a TSMP flow since it was captured** —
`{"proto":99,...,"txPkts":10,"txBytes":270}` in `processor_test.go`, which is 27 bytes per packet, the

- [x] A test pins the mapping alongside the existing `protoNames` cases —
