## Phase 5 — data-model gate (design frozen, not yet built)

Per the method note in the body, phase 5's data model gets gated before any build. This is that gate.
It is deliberately posted **before** the Go exists, so the design survives a context loss.

### Decisions taken

| question | answer |
| --- | --- |
| Evaluator scope | **Full**, including `group:` and `autogroup:`. |
| Framing of an unexplained flow | **Diagnostic, clearly caveated** — never the word "violation". |

### Feasibility was prototyped first, and it found two design-critical bugs

Before writing any Go I built a throwaway evaluator in Python and ran it over the **real current policy**
(freshly pulled, 19 grants, 0 legacy `acls`, gitignored at `.capture/fresh_acl.hujson`) against the
**real 3h flow capture** (59,147 policy-evaluable connections). The first run said **56.9% of traffic
matched no rule**, which is impossible — Tailscale would have dropped it. Two bugs, both of which would
have shipped as thousands of false findings:

1. **`ip: ["*"]` must match ICMP.** I had modelled a bare port list as tcp/udp and let `*` inherit that,
   so every ping looked unexplained. `*` is a wildcard over **protocol as well as port**; a *bare* port
   number (`53`) is the thing that implies tcp/udp only.
2. **Flow logs report BOTH directions of a connection; ACLs govern only the direction it was
   established in.** The return half of every permitted connection matched nothing. **37.4% of all
   connections are explained only by the reverse tuple.** The evaluator must try `(src→dst)` and, on a
   miss, `(dst→src)` before concluding anything.

After both fixes:

| verdict | connections | share |
| --- | --- | --- |
| permitted (forward) | 27,218 | 46.0% |
| permitted (reverse / return traffic) | 22,143 | 37.4% |
| **not explained by any rule** | **9,786** | **16.5%** |

### The residue is one relationship, not noise

```
by source identity:            by relationship:
  tag:aws     8398  85.8%        tag:aws    -> <lan-ip-1>   7858  80.3%   (tcp/udp 53)
  <lan-ip-1>  1388  14.2%        <lan-ip-1> -> tag:aws      1388  14.2%
                                 tag:aws    -> <lan-ip-2>      540   5.5%
```

**Every unexplained connection involves `tag:aws` talking to two LAN addresses**, overwhelmingly DNS to
`<lan-ip-1>`. The only grant with `tag:aws` as source is `tag:aws -> <tailnet-ip-3> tcp:443`. So this is
either a genuine gap in the policy or a subtlety the evaluator misses (subnet-router semantics are the
prime suspect) — **which is exactly why the verdict is worded "not explained by our reading of the
policy", never "violation".** That this collapses to one relationship rather than 9,786 scattered rows
is the evidence the feature is worth building.

### Frozen data model

New leaf package **`internal/aclpolicy`** — pure, no collector dependencies, so it is testable in
isolation and cannot drag the app layer into a cycle.

```go
// Compile parses a HuJSON policy document into an evaluable form.
func Compile(doc []byte, dir Directory) (*Policy, error)

// Directory carries identity facts the policy REFERENCES but does not CONTAIN.
// Sourced from the users collector; without it every autogroup:* over people is
// undetermined rather than silently false.
type Directory struct {
    Roles map[string]string // loginName -> owner|admin|member|...
}

type Endpoint struct {
    User string
    Tags []string
    Addr netip.Addr
}

type Conn struct {
    Src, Dst Endpoint
    Proto    string  // tcp | udp | icmp | ...
    DstPort  uint16
    HasPort  bool    // false for icmp and for records carrying no port
    IsExit   bool    // destination is the internet (autogroup:internet)
}

type Verdict uint8
const (
    Undetermined Verdict = iota // we cannot decide — NOT the same as "no rule"
    Permitted
    NoRule
)

type Result struct {
    Verdict  Verdict
    Rule     int    // index into Rules(); -1 when none matched
    Reversed bool   // matched as return traffic
    Reason   string // why undetermined
}

func (p *Policy) Evaluate(c Conn) Result
func (p *Policy) Rules() []Rule // for the "not exercised" report
```

**Three-valued matching is the core of the design.** A selector match is yes / no / **unknown**, and the
verdict is `NoRule` only when *every* rule definitively fails. If any rule is undecidable (an unresolved
`group:`, a `svc:`, an endpoint with no identity) the answer is `Undetermined`. Collapsing unknown into
"no" is what would turn this from a diagnostic into a liar.

### Where evaluation happens, and why

**At record time in `flowlog.Processor`, not at query time.** Query-time evaluation could only see the
2,000-entry recent ring; record-time evaluation covers the whole retention window and makes "rules not
exercised" meaningful over hours rather than over the last few thousand connections. The verdict and
matched rule index become dimensions on the store, and a small `rulesExercised` map (bounded by rule
count, which is tiny) answers the second half of the phase.

Constraint this imposes: evaluation must be cheap and allocation-free on the emit path. The policy is
compiled once per ACL change (the collector already tracks the ETag) and swapped atomically.

### Known limits, to be stated on the page

- **`group:` support is implementable but UNVERIFIABLE here** — `groups` is `{}` on this tailnet, so
  there is no live case to test against. It ships with unit tests over synthetic policies and is marked
  as such.
- **`svc:` (VIP services) resolves to `Undetermined`** unless the services collector can supply the
  mapping. One grant uses it today.
- **`autogroup:admin` vs the Owner role** is a modelling choice, not a fact we can read: it is treated
  as `{owner, admin}` and documented.
- **Only `action: accept` rules are evaluated.** Tailscale has no deny rules in `acls`; `ssh` and
  `nodeAttrs` are out of scope.
- **`physicalTraffic` is not evaluated** — it is the underlay (WireGuard endpoints), not policy-governed.
- **Exit traffic carries no destination**, so it is evaluated only against `autogroup:internet`.

### Build order

1. `internal/aclpolicy` — parse + compile + evaluate, TDD, validated against the real policy.
2. Shared policy holder + user directory, updated by the acl/users collectors, swapped atomically.
3. `flowlog.Processor` evaluates per connection; verdict + rule index onto `flowstore.Observation`.
4. Store: verdict breakdown, unexplained-pair aggregate, per-rule exercise counts.
5. Page: a Policy section — unexplained relationships and unexercised rules, caveated inline.

## Phase 5 step 2 — the policy is live at runtime (`5587695`)

`aclpolicy.Store` coordinates the two inputs a compiled policy needs, and both collectors now feed it.
Nothing reads the policy yet, so runtime behaviour is still unchanged.

| input | source | why it is needed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| raw HuJSON document | acl collector | the rules themselves |
| login → role directory | users collector | without it every `autogroup:owner` / `autogroup:admin` is **undecidable**, not false |

Behaviours worth knowing:

- **Either order works.** The two collectors run on independent schedules; the store recompiles
  whenever either input changes, so whichever lands first, the policy ends up the same.
- **Identical inputs are a no-op.** A collector re-reporting an unchanged ACL does not churn the
  policy that readers are holding.
- **A malformed document keeps the previous policy.** A stale-but-valid answer beats no answer and
  beats a half-parsed one. The error is retained on the store for the status page.
- **Both collectors swallow the sink error on purpose.** The evaluator is a side consumer; a policy
  problem must not turn into an acl- or users-collector failure.
- **Reads are lock-free** (atomic pointer), because the flow emit path will read this per connection
  and must never block a collector.
- **One store per tailnet**, built only when the flow view is enabled.

`/flows` now shows what the tailnet's own ACL says about the traffic it is displaying. The four

| step | commit | what landed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | `a0a986e` | `internal/aclpolicy` — compile + three-valued evaluate |
| 2 | `5587695` | `aclpolicy.Store`, fed by the acl and users collectors |

### Cost on the emit path, measured

Reconciliation runs per connection on the same path that emits the OTLP metrics, so this was
measured rather than asserted:

| | ns/op | allocs/op |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Process` without a policy | 4,948 | 57 |
| `Process` with a policy | 5,234 | 57 |
| `Evaluate` alone — permitted | 40 | **0** |
| `Evaluate` alone — reversed | 179 | **0** |
| `Evaluate` alone — worst case (every rule, both directions) | 308 | **0** |

**+286 ns per connection and zero added allocations.** `TestEvaluate_DoesNotAllocate` holds it there.
Endpoint tag slices are the ones the record decoded, not copies, and the two node-block lookups the
observation already performed are reused rather than repeated.

### Three things step 3 had to get right

- **Both ports are supplied**, not just the destination. A record carrying only the destination port
  reverses into one carrying none, which makes every port-specific rule *undecidable* against return
  traffic — 37% of connections. The first version of the alloc test caught this by returning
  `undetermined` where `permitted` was expected.
- **`physicalTraffic` is skipped.** It is the WireGuard underlay, not a tailnet connection a policy
  describes; reconciling it would report every peer-to-peer path as unexplained.
- **An unevaluated connection carries an EMPTY verdict, never `undetermined`.** Undetermined means a
  policy was applied and could not decide, which is a real reportable state. "No policy collected
  yet" is not, and conflating them reports a tailnet with no ACL as one the evaluator is confused by.

### Evaluation reads unredacted identity — deliberately

`pii_filter` governs what the process **discloses**. A verdict discloses nothing about an endpoint, so
evaluation runs on the identity the record carried, before the filter. Deriving it from redacted input
would quietly turn a privacy setting into wrong security findings. What the page may **say about** an
unexplained relationship still comes from the filtered fields — an endpoint the operator chose not to
expose is named `unidentified`.

### The framing, which is the feature

Both decisions from the gate comment are enforced by tests, not by review:

- **The word "violation" appears nowhere**, and `TestRender_PolicySectionIsNeverAccusatory` fails the
  build if it or `breach`/`unauthorized`/`leak` ever does. The section says *"this is a diagnostic,
  not an audit"* and *"Tailscale itself carried all of this traffic"* in the page, not just here.
- **The unexercised list states its window prominently** and says *"idle is not dead"* in words.
- **`undecidable` is explained where an operator reads it** — *"Never a finding."*
- **An uncollected policy and a clean one are different empty states** with different text.

### Two bugs the real-data check caught

The page's own JavaScript was extracted and driven under a DOM stub against **real
`/api/flows.json` output** — the method that found the zero-time bug in phase 3. It found two more,
neither of which any Go test would have caught:

1. **An unexplained relationship named its endpoint `external`** — the sentinel the processor
   collapses an unresolvable address to — instead of the LAN address that made the finding
   actionable. This is precisely the shape of this tailnet's real residue (`tag:aws → <lan-ip-1>`),
   so it would have hidden the one thing worth acting on. Relationships now prefer the address to a
   sentinel and keep the sentinel only when nothing better is known.
2. **ICMP rendered as `icmp/0`.** Tailscale writes `:0` for the destination of a portless protocol —
   **all 3,427 ICMP entries** in the live capture — and `0` is not a port anyone could write a rule
   for. The relationship now carries no port.

The dump hook that produces a realistic payload is kept as `TestDumpFlowsJSON` (skipped unless
`FLOWSJSON_DUMP` is set) so the next change to this page can be checked the same way:

```sh
FLOWSJSON_DUMP=/tmp/flows.json go test ./internal/app -run TestDumpFlowsJSON
FLOWHTML_DUMP=/tmp/page.html  go test ./internal/app/flowhtml -run TestRender_Injects
# then run the page's last <script> block under a DOM stub with that JSON as the fetch response
```

Rendered output over that payload, for the record:

```
legend      24 permitted (29%)  12 return traffic (14%)  36 not explained (43%)  12 undecidable (14%)
unexplained tag:servers -> <lan-ip-2>     tcp/8080   59.6 KiB  12
            tag:servers -> <lan-ip-1>   udp/53     58.6 KiB  12
            tag:servers -> rob@…        icmp        1.5 KiB  12
unexercised 3 of 6 over 60 min
```

### API

`result` carries what the policy said — `verdicts`, `unexplained` (`{src, dst, transport, port,
counts}`), `rules` (`{rule, counts}`, complete and unranked so it can be subtracted). `policy`
carries what the policy is — `available`, an optional compile `error`, and `rules` as `{index, kind,
source}`. `recent` entries carry their own `verdict`/`reversed`/`rule`. `docs/flow-view.md` has a
`## Reading the policy section` covering the four verdicts, the known evaluator limits, and jq
one-liners for both halves.

### Verification

Full gate green on all three commits (`go build` · `go vet` · `go test -race` · `golangci-lint` 0
issues · `docs/metrics.md` in sync). Mutation-tested rather than assumed: dropping the source port,
evaluating the underlay, never marking exit traffic, dropping endpoint identity, treating
`undetermined` as unexplained, counting a rule index alongside a non-permitted verdict, unsplitting
return traffic, and ignoring tags when naming an endpoint each fail the suite. One mutation initially
survived (counting a rule index regardless of verdict); the rules test was strengthened until it
caught it. Also checked against the running binary: `/flows` 200, unknown tailnet 404, correct policy
block with no ACL collected, no external references and no `ZgotmplZ`.

### Remaining

Phase 6 (path quality) only. Unchanged and still deliberate: the SQLite backend behind
`flows.store.path` is not built, and #238 (object-store ingestion) is out of scope here.

Cross-reference: the phase 3 decision that the flow store applies `pii_filter` to what reaches `/flows` has been **reversed** — see #241. The page is admin-only and admins have implicit trust over their own tailnet, so identity will be shown in full. Phase 5's reconciliation already read unredacted identity for the same underlying reason; #241 makes the display consistent with it.

Nothing in phases 1–5 needs rework beyond what #241 lists.

## Phase 6 pre-flight — the design risk is gone, verified against the live capture

Phase 6's premise was that DERP-relayed vs direct paths could be recovered from `physicalTraffic`
correlated with the node-metrics collector. That correlation turns out to be **unnecessary**: the
classification is readable from the flow record alone.

### `127.3.3.40` is the DERP marker, and the port is the region ID

Measured over the live 3h capture (`.capture/fresh_network.json`, 44,825 `physicalTraffic` entries):

```
physical entries      44,825
via 127.3.3.40         5,219  (11.6%)
ports on 127.3.3.40    8:4894   27:161   28:89   4:72   13:3
bytes per region       8:705,920  28:477,048  27:32,240  4:6,912  13:580
```

Those "ports" are small integers in the DERP region-ID range. Every other physical destination carries
a genuine ephemeral port (59879, 56385, 54100, …). Region 8 dominating on a UK tailnet is consistent
with it being London. `127.3.3.40` is Tailscale's well-known loopback marker for a relayed path.

**So `physicalTraffic` already distinguishes relayed from direct, and names the region, per
connection.** This matters because the DERP map endpoint is one of the surfaces the API does not
expose (see the coverage work — it 404s), which was the obvious way this phase could have died.

### Per-node relay share falls straight out

```
nxrsyR7CNTRL         derp=2671  direct=17607   13% relayed
nzAYgE2DV521CNTRL    derp=17    direct=4418     0% relayed
nkAFvgeDYp11CNTRL    derp=246   direct=3039     7% relayed
nTpiBiib6411CNTRL    derp=0     direct=1824     0% relayed
nmHjDxkZRh11CNTRL    derp=38    direct=1520     2% relayed
nRvYzzzoBh11CNTRL    derp=111   direct=1052    10% relayed
```

A per-peer "how much of this conversation is being relayed" figure is exactly the thing an operator
cannot get anywhere else, and it is one classification away.

### What this changes about the phase

- **No DERP map needed**, and no dependency on the node-metrics collector for the *classification*.
- Node metrics remain useful for **enrichment, not identification**: `tailscale.node.derp.home_region`
  gives each node's home region ID (same numbering), and the curated `path` label already uses
  `direct_ipv4|direct_ipv6|derp|peer_relay_*` (`internal/semconv/attrs.go`). Region **ID → name** has
  no API source, so either ship a small static map or display the ID — decide and state it, do not
  invent names.
- **`proto` is 0 on all 44,825 physical entries**, so nothing here is protocol-classified. Already
  known from phase 1; restated because a path classifier must not depend on it.
- Phase 5's rule that **physical traffic is not policy-reconciled stands** — the underlay is not
  policy-governed. Path quality is a separate dimension on the same records, not a reason to revisit
  that.

### Still to decide when the phase is built

1. Where the classification lives — a `Path` field on `flowstore.Observation` (consistent with
   `Verdict`) versus a derived value at query time. The former matches how every other dimension
   works and covers the whole retention window rather than the recent ring.
2. Whether relay share is also emitted as a **metric**, or stays in the flow view only. The view is
   the phase's stated deliverable; a metric is a separate, larger decision about the OTLP surface.
3. Region ID → name: static map or raw ID.

Nothing here is blocking. Recorded now so the next session starts from the measurement rather than
re-deriving it.

## Phase 6 complete — the flow view is done

`6037e1c` the path section on `/flows` plus the API fields and docs; `08d1724` the classifier and the
store aggregates. That closes the last phase, and with it this tracker.

### The pre-flight measurement held

The [pre-flight comment](https://github.com/rknightion/tailscale2otel/issues/237#issuecomment-5070324779)
predicted the classification was readable from `physicalTraffic` alone. Building it confirmed one
further thing the comment had not established: **`src` on a physical entry is the PEER's overlay
address and `dst` is the underlay endpoint that peer was reached at**. Both describe the same peer —
its tailnet identity and how it was actually reached — which is what makes a per-peer table possible
at all. Verified over the live capture: 44,825 physical entries, **0 unresolved** peer addresses.

```
direct_ipv4  33,108        peer          total bytes    relayed
direct_ipv6   6,498        truenas-scale 7,606,736,944    0.0%
derp          5,219        <host-1>        4,254,639,848    0.0%
                           <device-3>            13,051,188    0.4%
regions  8:4894 27:161 28:89 4:72 13:3
```

### The three open questions, answered

| question | answer | why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Path` field on `Observation` vs query-time derivation | **Field.** | Matches `Verdict`, and covers the whole retention window rather than only the bounded recent ring. |
| Relay share as a metric too | **No — view only.** | The stated deliverable is the view. An OTLP surface for this is a separate, larger cardinality decision, and nothing here forecloses it. |
| Region ID → name | **Raw ID, and say why.** | The API does not serve the DERP map. A built-in name table would go stale silently and mislabel a region an operator was about to act on. `TestRender_DoesNotInventDERPRegionNames` fails the build if a region name ever appears in the page. |

### Connections, not bytes — and the page says so

The single most misreadable thing here: **11.6% of underlay connections were relayed but only 0.4% of
the bytes.** DERP carries handshakes and keepalives while bulk transfer finds a direct path, so the
two figures support opposite conclusions. The section heading states its unit, every per-peer column
header names its own, and `TestRender_PathSectionSaysWhatItCounts` holds it there. An earlier draft
had two columns both headed "Relayed"; the DOM check caught it.

### What it refuses to claim

- **Peer-relay paths are not distinguished from direct ones.** A flow record reports the endpoint a
  peer was reached at, and a peer relay is indistinguishable from a direct endpoint in that field.
- **A physical entry with no endpoint gets no path**, rather than being folded into direct. "We cannot
  tell" must not read as good news in the column an operator acts on.
- **`proto` is never consulted** — it is 0 on all 44,825 physical entries.
- **Physical traffic is still not policy-reconciled.** Path quality is a second dimension on the same
  records, not a reason to revisit that.

### Framing, tested rather than reviewed

The section says **"Relaying is not a failure"** in the page — a relayed peer is connected and
encrypted end to end, just going the long way — and a test fails the build if that sentence goes. The
two empty states stay distinct: *no underlay traffic at all* reads differently from *underlay traffic
where every peer was direct*, and the second reads as the good news it is.

### Verification

Full gate green on both commits. Mutation-tested: classifying overlay traffic, classifying an absent
endpoint, dropping the region, calling IPv6 direct IPv4, recording a path for traffic that has none,
attributing a region to a direct path, naming the peer by its tags, ranking by total volume instead of
relayed, and removing the per-peer cap each fail a named test. One survived initially — the region
guard — and the test now records a contradictory direct observation carrying a region until it does
not.

The page's own JavaScript was again driven under a DOM stub against real `/api/flows.json` output
(`TestDumpFlowsJSON` now emits all three path shapes). It found the duplicated column header and a
region chip rendering "region 8 12". Also checked against the running binary: `/flows` 200, unknown
tailnet 404, all seven path elements present, 0 external references, 0 `ZgotmplZ`.

### Closing this tracker

All six phases are in. Two things remain deliberately undone and are **not** defects:

- The **SQLite backend** behind `flows.store.path` is not built. The in-memory ring is the default and
  the config key is reserved.
- **Object-store ingestion** is #238, and always was out of scope here.

One decision taken during this programme was later reversed: the phase 3 rule that the flow store
applies `pii_filter` is gone as of `b0616a9` (#241) — `/flows` shows identity in full, since the
filter governs exported telemetry rather than what an authenticated administrator may look at locally.

body:
## Problem

`exitTraffic` entries never carry a destination address. We process them as if they do, so every exit flow emits a fabricated `dst_node` and an empty `destination.address`.

## Evidence

Live 3h capture, 18,702 records (2026-07-24 06:18–09:18Z). Missing `src` or `dst`, by traffic type:

| traffic type | entries | missing src or dst |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `virtualTraffic` | 20,233 | 0 |
| `subnetTraffic` | 38,914 | 0 |
| `physicalTraffic` | 44,825 | 0 |
| **`exitTraffic`** | **504** | **504 (100%)** |

Breaking down the 504 exit entries specifically:

- `dst` present on **0 / 504**
- `src` present on 270 / 504 (53%), and only **3 distinct values** — the exit node's own tailnet addresses, always with port `:0`
- remainder is byte/packet counters only

Representative entries:

```json
{"src": "<tailnet-ip-4>:0", "txPkts": 5, "txBytes": 320}
{"txPkts": 2, "txBytes": 128}
```

## Consequence in current code

`processConn` splits `cc.Dst` → `dstAddr = ""` → `resolve("", "")` → `DeviceCache.ResolveName("")` → `parseAddr` fails → returns `"unknown"` (`internal/enrich/devicecache.go:131-135`).

So for real exit traffic:

- `tailscale.network.io{traffic_type="exit"}` carries `dst_node="unknown"` on 100% of series — a label that looks like a cache miss but is structurally impossible to populate
- the rollup accumulator records `dstNode="unknown"` and `observeUnique(srcNode, "unknown", "")` pollutes the unique-peer gauge
- per-connection flow logs emit `destination.address=""`, `destination.port=""`, `tailscale.dst.node="unknown"`
- `network.transport` is `"unknown"` too (exit entries have no `proto` — see the null-proto count below)

`tailscale.exit_node.io` / `.packets` are **unaffected and correct**: they attribute by reporting node, which is the only meaningful dimension available.

## Why our tests did not catch it

`internal/flowlog/exitnode_test.go:49` builds a synthetic exit entry with both endpoints populated:

```go
ExitTraffic: []flowlog.ConnectionCounts{
	{Src: "<tailnet-ip-1>:1234", Dst: "1.1.1.1:443", Proto: 6, ...},
}
```

No real exit entry has ever looked like this. `CLAUDE.md` already warns: "Synthetic fixtures miss these — validate record-type changes against real captures in `.capture/`." This is that failure, realised.

## Fix

Treat "no destination" as a first-class shape rather than a resolution miss:

- Omit `dst_node` / `destination.address` / `destination.port` entirely when `dst` is absent, rather than emitting `"unknown"` and `""`. An absent attribute is honest; a fabricated one is not.
- Do not feed absent destinations into the rollup unique-peer gauge.
- Keep `tailscale.exit_node.io` / `.packets` as the intended way to measure exit traffic, and say so in `docs/metrics.md` prose.
- Consider the same treatment wherever `proto` is absent: 45,329 of 104,476 total connection entries (43%) have no `proto`, which is all of `physicalTraffic` plus `exitTraffic`. `transportName(0)` → `"unknown"` is defensible here since it is a genuine unknown rather than a structurally absent field — but it should be a deliberate documented choice, not an accident.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Absent `dst` omits destination attributes on both metrics and logs instead of emitting `unknown`/empty
- [ ] Rollup unique-peer gauge ignores absent destinations
- [ ] `exitnode_test.go` fixtures replaced with the **real** observed shapes: `{src, txPkts, txBytes}` and `{txPkts, txBytes}` only
- [ ] Regression test asserting no `dst_node="unknown"` series is produced from realistic exit traffic
- [ ] `docs/metrics.md` prose states exit traffic has no destination and points at `tailscale.exit_node.*`
- [ ] Full gate green

body:
## Problem

The network flow log API response embeds full node identity for both ends of every record, and we decode none of it. `internal/flowlog/record.go` defines only:

```go
type FlowLog struct {
	Logged, Start, End time.Time
	NodeID             string
	VirtualTraffic, SubnetTraffic, ExitTraffic, PhysicalTraffic []ConnectionCounts
}
```

The wire format also carries `srcNode` and `dstNodes`.

## Evidence

Live 3h capture, 18,702 records (2026-07-24 06:18–09:18Z):

| field | present on |
| --- | --- |
| `srcNode` | **18,702 / 18,702 (100%)** |
| `dstNodes` | 18,533 / 18,702 (99.1%) |

Shapes observed:

```json
"srcNode": {
  "nodeId": "...CNTRL",
  "name": "<host-1>.<tailnet>.ts.net",
  "addresses": ["100.x.y.z", "fd7a:115c:a1e0:..."],
  "tags": ["tag:servers", "tag:sshrecorder"],
  "user": "..."
}
"dstNodes": [
  { "nodeId": "...", "name": "...", "addresses": [...], "os": "linux",  "tags": [...] },
  { "nodeId": "...", "name": "...", "addresses": [...], "os": "macOS",  "user": "rob@..." }
]
```

Union of keys across the capture: `srcNode` → `nodeId, name, addresses, tags, user`; `dstNodes[]` → `nodeId, name, addresses, os, tags, user`. Fields are individually optional (`os` and `user` are absent on some nodes) — decode each defensively.

## Why it matters

**1. Flow enrichment currently has a hard dependency on the `devices` collector.** `CLAUDE.md` documents the failure mode: "flow/audit IP→name resolution silently degrades to `unknown`/`external` if `devices` is disabled." With `srcNode`/`dstNodes` decoded, a flow record self-enriches — name resolution keeps working when `devices` is disabled, rate-limited, or has not completed its first poll. The same applies to the streaming receiver, which today depends on a cache populated by an unrelated collector.

**2. We are discarding per-flow identity we cannot reconstruct any other way.** `user`, `tags` and `os` per flow end unlock grouping that device-level joins cannot express cleanly: traffic by user, tag-to-tag matrices, egress by OS. This is the data behind the identity views in the visualiser tracker.

## Design

- Add `SrcNode *NodeRef` and `DstNodes []NodeRef` to `flowlog.FlowLog`; `NodeRef{NodeID, Name, Addresses, Tags, User, OS}`. All fields optional.
- New method on the processor to fold a record's node refs into `enrich.DeviceCache` before processing its connections, so resolution within the same record benefits immediately. Must not clobber richer `devices`-collector entries — devices data wins on conflict; node refs fill gaps only.
- Cardinality: `user` and `tags` are **unbounded from our perspective** and must NOT go onto metrics by default. Gate behind `cardinality.flow.*` toggles, default off, exactly as `source_port`/`destination_port` are handled today. Flow **logs** may carry them unconditionally (logs already carry full detail by design).
- `tags` is a list — join deterministically (sorted, comma-separated) or emit only the first; decide during implementation and document it.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `NodeRef` decoded from both `srcNode` and `dstNodes`, all fields optional, absent fields do not error
- [ ] Fuzz corpus (`internal/flowlog/fuzz_test.go`) extended to cover the new fields, including null/absent/wrong-type
- [ ] Device cache seeded from node refs; `devices`-collector entries take precedence
- [ ] Test: name resolution succeeds with an **empty** device cache when node refs are present
- [ ] `tailscale.src.user` / `tailscale.dst.user` / tags / `os` on flow logs
- [ ] Same as opt-in metric dimensions behind `cardinality.flow.*`, default off, documented in `config.example.yaml` + `docs/configuration.md`
- [ ] Verified against the live capture shape, not synthetic fixtures only
- [ ] `docs/metrics.md`, `docs/env-vars.md`, Helm schema/README regenerated (`scripts/regen-generated.sh`)
- [ ] Full gate green

body:
## Problem

`flowlog.logTimestamp` (`internal/flowlog/processor.go:494`) timestamps every emitted flow log record with the record's `logged` field, falling back to `end`:

```go
func logTimestamp(flow FlowLog) time.Time {
	if !flow.Logged.IsZero() {
		return flow.Logged
	}
	return flow.End
}
```

`logged` is when the control plane **captured** the record, not when the traffic occurred. The record already carries the true occurrence window as `start`/`end`. Using `logged` places every flow log later on the time axis than the traffic it describes.

## Evidence

Measured against a live 3h capture of `GET /tailnet/{tailnet}/logging/network` (18,702 records, 2026-07-24 06:18–09:18Z):

| measure | min | mean | max |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `logged - start` (s) | 5 | **7.5** | **852** |
| `end - start` (window length, s) | 5 | 5.1 | 812 |

So the typical record is misplaced by ~7.5s and the worst by 14 minutes. The skew is not constant, so it cannot be corrected downstream by a fixed offset.

Impact: flow logs in Loki/Grafana do not line up with the metrics derived from the same records, and any log-to-metric or log-to-trace correlation over a short window silently mismatches.

## Fix

OTEL already models this distinction — use it rather than picking one field:

- `Timestamp` = `start` (when the traffic happened), falling back to `end`, then `logged`.
- `ObservedTimestamp` = `logged` (when we/the control plane saw it).

`telemetry.Event` currently has a single `Timestamp`; this needs an `ObservedTimestamp` field plumbed through the emitter to the OTEL log record.

Keep the window explicit on the record too, so a reader can see the bucket a flow belongs to rather than inferring it: add `tailscale.flow.window.start` and `tailscale.flow.window.end` (or a duration attribute) to the per-connection and per-record log attributes.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `logTimestamp` prefers `start`, then `end`, then `logged`
- [ ] `telemetry.Event` carries `ObservedTimestamp`, set from `logged`, and the OTEL log record sets both
- [ ] Flow window start/end exposed as log attributes
- [ ] Table-driven test covers: all three fields present; `start` absent; only `logged` present; all absent (zero value)
- [ ] Test asserts against `telemetrytest.Recorder` emitted records, not internals
- [ ] `docs/metrics.md` / env-vars regenerated if any catalog entry changes
- [ ] Full gate green: `go build ./... && go vet ./... && go test -race ./...` + `golangci-lint run`

## Notes

Breaking-ish for anyone alerting on flow-log arrival time, but the current behaviour is a defect, not a contract. Call it out in the changelog.

body:
## Context

The docs site (`m7kni.io/tailscale2otel/`) was outranking the GitHub repo, and the repo's discovery
surfaces were largely unconfigured. Research pass done first; findings below overturned several
common assumptions and drove the changes.

## Key research findings (verified, not folklore)

1. **GitHub repo search does NOT index the README.** Only `name`, `description`, `topics`
   ([docs](https://docs.github.com/en/search-github/searching-on-github/searching-for-repositories)).
   Verified: a phrase unique to our README returns `total_count: 0` without an explicit `in:readme`
   qualifier. README keyword work therefore affects Google only.
2. **The About description IS the page `<title>`** — GitHub renders
   `GitHub - rknightion/tailscale2otel: <description> · GitHub`, and reuses it for the meta
   description and all `og:`/`twitter:` tags. Highest-value single field in the repo.
3. **README external links and the About→Website link are both `rel="nofollow"`.** GitHub passes
   zero PageRank to the docs site. Backlinks docs→GitHub are worth doing for referral traffic and
   conversion, but they do not move either site's ranking.
4. **Competitive position.** `tailscale prometheus exporter` has 12 competing repos and is owned by
   `adinhodovic/tailscale-exporter` (112★, "exporter" in the repo *name*). But `tailscale
   opentelemetry` (2 repos), `tailscale otlp` (2), `tailscale flow logs` (3) are terms we already
   rank #1 for on GitHub, and the external SERP for them is **empty**.
5. **Strategy:** do not rename the repo (breaks Go module path, image tags, docs URLs). Own the
   OTel/flow-logs framing where the field is empty; keep "Prometheus" and "exporter" in the
   description to remain the second-best answer to the bigger query.

## Changes

### Repo metadata (applied via API)
- [x] Description rewritten, front-loading `Tailscale exporter` + OpenTelemetry/Prometheus, with
      Headscale included for the search index
- [x] About→Website set to `https://m7kni.io/tailscale2otel/` (was empty)
- [x] Topics retuned to 20/20: dropped low-value compounds (`otel-grafana`, `prometheus-grafana`,
      `tailscale-network`), added `headscale`, `observability`, `flow-logs`, `audit-logs`,
      `netflow`, `grafana-cloud`, `golang`, `wireguard`, `self-hosted`

### README
- [x] H1 now carries keywords instead of the bare brand token
- [x] Docs site linked prominently (it was linked from nowhere)
- [x] Quick start uses `ghcr.io/rknightion/tailscale2otel` — previously told users to `docker build`
      despite a published multi-arch image
- [x] Helm/Kubernetes quick start added (chart was never mentioned)
- [x] Differentiators moved above the fold with concrete counts (186 metrics, 15 collectors, 18 API
      endpoints, 89 alert rules)
- [x] Collector table corrected — `oauth_apps` was missing
- [x] Previously-invisible features documented: PII redaction (13 categories), workload-identity
      auth, `*_file` secrets, node-metrics auto-discovery, IANA service-name attribution
- [x] Badges: release, CI, container, Helm, Go Reference, licence (was Scorecard only)
- [x] Maintainer-only API-drift runbook collapsed into `<details>`

### Docs site
- [x] Homepage `<title>` was the bare word `tailscale2otel`; now keyword-bearing via front matter
- [x] `site_description` and `extra.keywords` expanded in `zensical.toml`
- [x] `docs/index.md` rewritten so it no longer duplicates the README near-verbatim (the two pages
      were self-competing; differentiation is the correct fix, not a cross-domain canonical)
- [x] GitHub backlinks added to the 6 pages that had none — all 16 pages now link back

### Helm chart
- [x] **Bug:** `appVersion` was `"0.1.0"` while the app is at v2.0.2 — corrected
- [x] `artifacthub.io/*` annotations, icon, expanded keywords, docs homepage → chart 0.9.1
- [x] Chart README regenerated (`scripts/regen-generated.sh helm`)

## Verification

`go build` · `go vet` · `go test -race ./...` (43 pkgs, exit 0) · `golangci-lint run` (0 issues) ·

body:
Follow-up from #228, noted during implementation and deliberately left unfixed there (it was outside that issue's scope and weakens no control).

## Problem

`internal/stream` sets `handlerProcessDeadline = 30 * time.Second` (wired via `http.TimeoutHandler` in `Handler()`), and `Run` configures the `http.Server` with `WriteTimeout: 30 * time.Second`. The two are equal, but they start at different moments:

- `WriteTimeout` starts when the request headers begin arriving.
- `TimeoutHandler`'s timer starts when `ServeHTTP` is entered.

So on a real listener `WriteTimeout` always expires first and closes the connection before `TimeoutHandler` can write its 503 body. The deadline's client-visible response is therefore effectively unreachable in production; it only works under `httptest`, which is where the tests exercise it.

## Impact

Low, and explicitly **not** a security regression. The deadline was only ever defence in depth — `http.TimeoutHandler` cannot preempt a CPU-bound goroutine anyway, and the real controls for #228/#229 are the unwrap depth cap and the per-request record cap, both of which are unaffected. The consequence is purely diagnostic: a sender that trips the deadline sees a dropped connection instead of a clear `503`, which is harder to debug.

## Suggested direction

Make the deadline strictly shorter than the write window — either lower `handlerProcessDeadline` (e.g. 25s) or raise the receiver's `WriteTimeout`, so the 503 has room to be written. Whichever is chosen, add a comment at both sites stating that the ordering is load-bearing, since the two values look independently reasonable and a future tidy-up could easily re-align them.

A test would need to drive a real listener (not `httptest`'s handler-level wiring) to observe the difference.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A request that exceeds the processing deadline receives a `503` over a real TCP listener, not a closed connection
- [ ] The relationship between `handlerProcessDeadline` and `WriteTimeout` is documented at both sites
- [ ] The unwrap-depth and record caps are unchanged

_Surfaced while implementing #228 (992d7f6)._

comments.body:
Fixed in f8dab4b (pushed to `main`).

## The gap was wider than this issue stated

My own suggested direction — "lower `handlerProcessDeadline` (e.g. 25s)" — **would not have worked**, and it is worth recording why.

`ServeHTTP` is entered up to `ReadHeaderTimeout` (10s) *after* the connection's write deadline starts, not immediately after. So the deadline can fire as late as `ReadHeaderTimeout + deadline` on the connection's clock:

| pairing | deadline can fire at | write window closes at | 503 reaches client? |
|---|---|---|---|
| 30s / 30s (before) | 40s | 30s | no |
| 25s / 30s (as suggested here) | 35s | 30s | **still no** |
| 30s / 50s (shipped) | 40s | 50s | yes |

## Fix

`WriteTimeout` is now **derived**, not a second hand-written constant:

```go
func writeTimeoutFor(d time.Duration) time.Duration {
    return readHeaderTimeout + d + writeGrace  // 10s + 30s + 10s = 50s
}
```

That was the point of this issue's own warning that "the two values look independently reasonable and a future tidy-up could easily re-align them" — so the relationship is structural rather than a comment asking people to be careful. The listener's timeout set also moved out of `Run` into an `httpServer()` constructor, so it exists in exactly one place and a test can assert it directly instead of restating the values.

## Tests, both verified against the pre-fix behaviour

Rather than assume the tests would catch a regression, I restored the old `writeTimeoutFor` (returning `d`) and re-ran them. Both fail, the second with precisely the production symptom this issue describes:

```
WriteTimeout = 30s, but the deadline can fire as late as ReadHeaderTimeout+deadline = 40s;
the connection would be closed before the 503 could be written
--- FAIL: TestServerTimeouts_WriteWindowOutlastsProcessDeadline

the deadline's 503 never reached the client (connection closed first):
Post "http://127.0.0.1:61849/services/collector/event": EOF
--- FAIL: TestProcessDeadline_503ReachesARealClient
```

Acceptance criteria:

- [x] A request exceeding the processing deadline receives a 503 over a real TCP listener, not a closed connection — `TestProcessDeadline_503ReachesARealClient` binds an actual `net.Listen("tcp", "127.0.0.1:0")`, since (as this issue predicted) `httptest`'s handler-level wiring has no `http.Server` write deadline and so cannot observe the bug
- [x] The relationship is documented at both sites (`writeTimeoutFor`'s doc comment, and the derivation point in `httpServer`)
- [x] The unwrap-depth and record caps are unchanged — those remain the real bounds on the work; this only makes the defence-in-depth layer's response reachable

One implementation note: `processDeadline` became a `Server` field (defaulting to `handlerProcessDeadline`) purely so the real-listener test can run in ~150 ms instead of waiting out the 30s budget. `Handler()` and `httpServer()` both guard a zero value so a literally-constructed `Server` cannot end up with a 0 deadline, which `TimeoutHandler` would treat as "expire immediately" and 503 every request.

title: Streaming receiver: the 30s processing deadline's 503 cannot reach a real client (WriteTimeout fires first)

body:
## Problem

The streaming (HEC) receiver caps the decompressed request body at 64 MiB but places no limit on the *number* of records parsed from it. A body of concatenated tiny objects is expanded into an unbounded slice of `json.RawMessage` plus a parallel `[]extractedRecord`, multiplying a 64 MiB input into multiple GB of transient allocation (~50×) and OOM-killing the process.

Distinct from #209: this is a *single*-body, per-request amplification. #209 explicitly assumes "the per-request decompression limit prevents one oversized body" — this finding refutes that assumption (the amplification is in record-object count, not byte count), so the two are complementary rather than duplicates.

## Evidence

- `internal/stream/stream.go:680` — `func extractRecords(raw []byte) (...)` parses the body into records with no per-record/count limit.
- `internal/stream/stream.go:714` and `:730` — `values = append(values, v)` / `append(values, json.RawMessage(line))` grow an unbounded slice; a parallel `[]extractedRecord` is built alongside.
- `readAllLimited` caps decompressed bytes (64 MiB) but not the record count, so a body of concatenated 2-byte objects (`{}{}…`) yields ~33M `RawMessage` values plus ~33M `extractedRecord` values.
- No in-flight/concurrency limiter on the handler.

## Failure scenario / impact

With the streaming receiver enabled (and `streaming.token` unset, which the example config permits with a warning), an attacker POSTs a ~64 MiB body of concatenated `{}` objects. `extractRecords` copies each into its own `json.RawMessage` and builds a parallel `[]extractedRecord`, allocating several GB before any record is classified. On a small deployment (memory limit below ~3–4 GB) the process is OOM-killed, denying flow/audit ingestion; repeating or parallelizing the request sustains the denial.

## Suggested direction

- Bound the number of records parsed per request (reject or truncate once a max-record count is exceeded, mirroring the existing `MaxBodyBytes` cap).
- And/or stream-process records instead of buffering all of `values`/`out` at once.
- Consider limiting concurrent in-flight requests on the receiver (this overlaps the aggregate control in #209; the per-request record cap is the part unique to this finding).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Requests exceeding a maximum per-request record count are rejected or truncated with a clear bounded-resource response
- [ ] A 64 MiB body of tiny concatenated objects no longer produces multi-GB transient allocation
- [ ] The existing decompressed body-size cap remains in place
- [ ] Tests cover a body at/above the record-count limit and a normal multi-record body
- [ ] Normal streaming ingestion is unchanged

_Found during a Claude Security high-effort repository scan (three-lens panel: 3/3 confirmed; derived from reading, no code executed), 2026-07-22, against main at 627c8b0a1c852424fa0e7fc75de441c3d058c29d._

comments.body:
Fixed in 992d7f6 (pushed to `main`).

`extractRecords` now stops at **500,000 records** per request and the handler answers **413** + `rejected{reason=too_many_records}`. The existing decompressed-body cap is untouched — the two bound different things (bytes vs. object count), which is exactly the gap this issue identified.

One deviation from the suggested direction, and it matters. The obvious implementation — check `len(out)` after unwrapping — is **not sufficient**: a single `{"logs":[...]}` wrapper can carry far more records than there are top-level values, so the unbounded allocation would already have happened by the time the check ran. The budget is instead threaded *into* the unwrap recursion (`unwrapState.remaining`, decremented per record produced), so the output is bounded during construction. The cap is enforced on all three paths: the `json.Decoder` stream, the NDJSON line scan, and the recursive envelope walk. Exactly-at-cap is accepted; cap+1 rejects.

Acceptance criteria:

- [x] Requests exceeding the per-request record count are rejected with a bounded-resource response (413 + a dedicated reason)
- [x] A 64 MiB body of tiny concatenated objects no longer produces multi-GB transient allocation
- [x] The existing decompressed body-size cap remains in place
- [x] Tests cover at/above the limit and a normal multi-record body — `TestRecordCap_{ConcatenatedObjectsRejected,NDJSONLinesRejected,LogsWrapperRejected,NormalBatchUnaffected}`
- [x] Normal streaming ingestion unchanged

The concurrency half you flagged as overlapping with #209 landed in the same commit; see that issue.

title: Bound per-request record count in the streaming receiver: single-body memory amplification enables OOM DoS

body:
## Problem

The streaming (HEC) receiver's envelope unwrapper re-`json.Unmarshal`s the full remaining request body at every nesting level. `encoding/json.Unmarshal` re-validates its entire input on each call, so a deeply-nested envelope forces O(depth × bodySize) scanning — a single small, highly-compressible request pins a CPU core for tens of seconds to minutes.

Distinct from #209: that issue is about *aggregate concurrency* (many valid in-limit bodies summing past the memory budget). This is a *single*-request CPU blowup via nested re-parse, with a different fix.

## Evidence

- `internal/stream/stream.go:780` — `func unwrap(v json.RawMessage, ...)` recurses into each nested HEC `event`/`logs` wrapper.
- `internal/stream/stream.go:800` — `json.Unmarshal(trimmed, &env)` is called on the full remaining bytes at each level (also at `:787`), re-scanning the whole slice every time.
- `readAllLimited` bounds the decompressed body to the default `maxBody` (64 MiB) but does nothing about re-scanning that body once per nesting level.
- No `http.TimeoutHandler` wraps the receiver; the `http.Server` `WriteTimeout` does not interrupt a CPU-bound handler goroutine.

## Failure scenario / impact

An attacker POSTs a gzip/zstd-compressed body (`Content-Encoding` selects decompression) that expands to ~64 MiB shaped as `{"event":{"event":…{"event":<large-flat-record>}…}}`, nested a few thousand levels deep — below `encoding/json`'s 10000-depth limit, so it decodes rather than being rejected. `unwrap` then re-scans ~64 MiB once per level: hundreds of GiB of total scanning for one request. Because the nested wrappers and the repeated leaf compress extremely well, the wire request is only kilobytes. A handful of concurrent requests saturates every core and makes the process — and its telemetry export — unresponsive.

## Suggested direction

- Cap unwrap recursion depth to a small constant (3–4, matching the documented envelope shapes).
- Stop re-`Unmarshal`ling the full remaining bytes at each level — decode the wrapper once with `json.Decoder` / index into the `RawMessage` rather than `json.Unmarshal`, which re-validates the whole slice.
- Wrap the handler in `http.TimeoutHandler` (or enforce a per-request processing deadline) so a CPU-bound request cannot run unbounded.
- Consider requiring `streaming.token` by default for the receiver.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Envelope unwrapping is bounded to a small recursion depth and rejects deeper nesting cleanly
- [ ] Wrapper decoding no longer re-scans the full body at each level (no O(depth × bodySize) behavior)
- [ ] A per-request processing deadline bounds handler CPU time
- [ ] Tests cover a deeply-nested envelope (rejected/bounded) and a normal envelope (unchanged)
- [ ] Normal single-record and documented multi-record envelopes still decode correctly

_Found during a Claude Security high-effort repository scan (three-lens panel: 2/3 confirmed; derived from reading, no code executed), 2026-07-22, against main at 627c8b0a1c852424fa0e7fc75de441c3d058c29d._

comments.body:
Fixed in 992d7f6 (pushed to `main`) — but **one claim in this issue's suggested direction did not survive measurement**, and the correction matters for anyone reading this later.

## The fix: the depth cap, measured

`unwrap` now takes a depth and stops past **4 levels**. Control experiment, run before and after on the same ~1 MiB, 4000-level nested envelope:

| configuration | wall clock for one request |
|---|---|
| `maxUnwrapDepth = 100000` + `json.Unmarshal` (i.e. the old code) | **21.1 s** |
| `maxUnwrapDepth = 4` | **0.03 s** |

So the premise of the report is confirmed: one small, highly-compressible request could pin a core for tens of seconds. ~700× reduction.

Over-deep nesting is treated as a **drop, not corruption** — it increments the existing `#67` unwrap-drop counter and the batch still succeeds. An unrecognised shape is a forward-compatibility question, not evidence the sender's batch is broken, so it must not trip the `#201` atomic-batch rejection.

## Correction: the `json.Decoder` change is *not* a performance win

The suggested direction says to stop re-`Unmarshal`ing the full remaining bytes at each level and use `json.Decoder` instead. That was implemented — and then benchmarked, because it should not be asserted without evidence. On one 1 MiB envelope level:

- `json.Unmarshal`: **9.82 ms/op**
- `json.Decoder`: **11.25 ms/op** (~15% *slower*, it copies through an internal buffer)

Both do the same two scans, and every value the walk sees is already exactly one JSON value, so there is no sub-slice win available. The decoder form was kept (the cost is negligible once depth is capped at 4 levels) but its doc comment now states plainly that it is not the performance fix. **The depth cap is the entire fix** — please do not repeat the "quadratic re-parse eliminated" framing from the title/body, it is not what happened.

## Processing deadline: defence in depth only

`http.TimeoutHandler` is wired into `Handler()` at 30 s, but it **cannot preempt a CPU-bound goroutine** — it bounds the *response*, not the work. The code comment says exactly that rather than overselling it. Noting a related limitation for a possible follow-up: `handlerProcessDeadline` (30 s) equals the server's `WriteTimeout` (30 s), and `WriteTimeout` starts earlier, so on a real listener the connection will generally close before the 503 body is written. It weakens no control, since the caps are what bound the work.

## Also done

"Consider requiring `streaming.token` by default" was approved as scope and landed in the same commit: an empty token on a non-loopback bind now refuses every request with 403 + `rejected{reason=auth_required}` and logs an ERROR at startup. Loopback stays open.

Acceptance criteria:

- [x] Envelope unwrapping bounded to a small recursion depth, deeper nesting rejected cleanly (as a skip)
- [x] Wrapper decoding no longer re-scans the full body at each level — **done, but see the correction above: this was not the source of the win**
- [x] A per-request processing deadline bounds handler CPU time — **partially; see the caveat above**
- [x] Tests cover a deeply-nested envelope (bounded) and a normal envelope (unchanged)
- [x] Documented single- and multi-record envelopes still decode correctly

A 30 s fuzz run over the rewritten parse chain (`FuzzExtractRecords`, 1,109,030 execs) passed with no new corpus entries.

title: Bound envelope unwrapping in the streaming receiver: quadratic JSON re-parse enables single-request CPU DoS

body:
## Problem

The admin HTTP server fails open: when `admin.auth.token` is empty, `requireAdminAuth` returns the wrapped handler unauthenticated. The shipped defaults enable the admin server on the wildcard bind `:9091` with `landing_page=true` and no token, so every admin endpoint is reachable with no credential by any client that can reach the port.

This affects the **default** configuration — unlike the two streaming-receiver DoS findings, no opt-in is required.

## Evidence

- `internal/app/admin.go:70-74` — `requireAdminAuth` returns `next` unwrapped when the configured token is empty (fail-open):
  ```go
  func (a *App) requireAdminAuth(next http.HandlerFunc) http.HandlerFunc {
      token := ...
      if token == "" {
          return next   // line 73
      }
  ```
- `internal/app/admin.go:114-118` — every endpoint is registered through `requireAdminAuth`, so all of them (`/`, `/api/status.json`, `/api/cardinality.json`, `/api/config.json`, `/api/rdns/purge`) are unauthenticated when no token is set.
- Defaults enable the admin server on `:9091` (wildcard) with the landing page on and no token.
- `Warnings()` flags the wildcard-bind + no-token + landing-page combination only as an advisory; `Validate()` does not reject it. Contrast `profiling.pprof.enabled`, which `Validate()` hard-errors unless `admin.auth.token` is set.

## Failure scenario / impact

An operator deploys the container with `-p 9091:9091` (or runs the binary on a host with a routable interface) on defaults, assuming the admin page is internal-only. An attacker who can reach `:9091` — another device on the same LAN/tailnet, or anyone if the port is exposed — issues `GET /api/status.json` and receives, with no credential:

- every observed device's name, hostname, OS version, user, IP addresses, and tags — across **all** tailnets in multi-tailnet/MSP mode;
- the OTLP endpoint URL, the TLS-insecure flag, the enabled collectors, the auth method, and OTLP header key names.

This is unauthenticated disclosure of the full device inventory of one or more tailnets plus the exporter's configuration shape.

## Suggested direction

Do not fail open. Preferred: promote the current `Warnings()` advisory to a `Validate()` error for the wildcard-bind + no-token + landing-page combination, mirroring the existing pprof rule. Alternatively (or additionally) default `admin.listen` to loopback/tailnet rather than the wildcard `:9091`. The root fix is at the auth wrapper / config validation, not at individual call sites.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A wildcard-bound admin server serving the landing page with no `admin.auth.token` is rejected by `Validate()` (or the default bind is loopback and the wildcard case requires a token)
- [ ] `requireAdminAuth` no longer silently returns an unauthenticated handler for a network-reachable, wildcard-bound configuration
- [ ] Loopback-bound / explicitly-tokened configurations are unaffected
- [ ] Tests cover: default config rejected/denied, tokened config allowed, loopback config allowed
- [ ] Docs state the auth requirement for a non-loopback admin bind

_Found during a Claude Security high-effort repository scan (three-lens panel: 3/3 confirmed; derived from reading, no code executed), 2026-07-22, against main at 627c8b0a1c852424fa0e7fc75de441c3d058c29d._

comments.body:
Fixed in effb816 (pushed to `main`).

`requireAdminAuth` no longer returns the handler unwrapped when `admin.auth.token` is empty. An empty token is honoured only on a **loopback** `admin.listen`; on any other bind the landing page and every JSON API are refused with **HTTP 403** and counted as `rejected{reason=auth_required}`.

**403, not 401 + `WWW-Authenticate`** — the condition is operator misconfiguration, not a missing credential, and a challenge would make browsers prompt for a password that does not exist. The existing 401 path is unchanged for the case where a token *is* configured and the caller presents a wrong/absent one.

**Deliberately not a `Validate()` hard error.** Mirroring the pprof rule (the issue's preferred direction) was considered and rejected: it would crash-loop every existing deployment running on the shipped defaults. Refusing at the handler closes the disclosure while keeping the process up and the probes answering. Defaulting `admin.listen` to loopback was also rejected — it would silently break `docker run -p 9091:9091` and Kubernetes probes.

A **tailnet address counts as network-reachable**, not loopback. Every peer on the tailnet can reach it, which is the threat model in the report. The new leaf package `internal/listenaddr` makes that classification and fails closed on anything it cannot prove is loopback (empty, wildcard, unparseable, or a non-`localhost` hostname — hostnames are not resolved, since a DNS answer is not a security boundary).

Acceptance criteria:

- [x] A wildcard-bound admin server serving the landing page with no token is rejected — at the handler (403), not at `Validate()`, for the reason above
- [x] `requireAdminAuth` no longer silently returns an unauthenticated handler for a network-reachable bind
- [x] Loopback-bound / explicitly-tokened configurations are unaffected
- [x] Tests cover default config rejected, tokened config allowed, loopback config allowed, and the `reason=auth_required` metric
- [x] Docs state the auth requirement (`docs/configuration.md`, plus `SECURITY.md`/`docs/security.md`/`README.md` corrected in a33c6b7 — they still claimed the page failed open)

Behaviour matrix now:

| bind | token | endpoint | result |
|---|---|---|---|
| `:9091` (default) | none | `/`, `/api/*` | **403** `auth_required` |
| `:9091` (default) | none | `/healthz`, `/readyz` | 200 |
| `127.0.0.1:9091` | none | any | 200 |
| any | set | correct Bearer/Basic | 200 |
| any | set | wrong/absent | 401 + challenge |

title: Admin status page and JSON APIs served unauthenticated by default on a wildcard bind

body:
## Why

The admin status page already has a **"Runtime trend (~10 min)"** block (goroutines / heap in use / GC rate) and an active-series chart, driven by `internal/app/sampler.go` and rendered via `registerChart`/`drawChart` in `internal/app/statushtml/page.html.tmpl`. Two things it cannot answer:

- **Is the pipeline actually shipping anything right now?** There is no emit-side throughput signal at all. A collector fleet that is polling happily but emitting nothing looks identical to a healthy one.
- **Is the fleet degrading?** Per-collector state is on the Collectors tab, but there is no roll-up trend — a slow creep from 0 to 3 failing collectors, or a mean run duration doubling, is invisible until someone reads the table row by row.

This is one of three matching ports (graph2otel and opnsense-exporter are getting the same charts) so an operator moving between the exporters reads the same window and the same shapes.

## Scope

Add a `sub-h` section **"Throughput & fleet trend (~10 min)"** immediately after the existing runtime block on the Overview tab, using the same sampler cadence, ring capacity and chart mechanism:

- `chEmit` — two series: metric data points/sec and log records/sec, measured with `atomic.Uint64` counters at the innermost `*otelEmitter` and differenced over elapsed wall time
- `chFailing` — collectors whose last run failed
- `chDuration` — mean collector run duration (ms)

Plus four stat cards (metric rate, log rate, active/failing, mean duration), refreshed from the JSON poll.

**Out of scope:** rate-limit / throttle-headroom trends. That surface is graph2otel-specific (it has per-workload client-side token buckets); there is no analogue here.

## Design constraints

- Emit counters must be free on the hot path: atomics only, no lock, no allocation. `Histogram` delegates to `HistogramCtx`, so only `HistogramCtx` counts — counting both would double every histogram.
- Emit counting is **distinct from `ExportStats`**: emit counts what collectors produced, export counts what the OTLP exporters shipped. Under cumulative temporality those are different numbers by design, and conflating them would be a wrong chart, not a rounding difference.
- **Headscale shares the process emitter with its runtime.** Aggregating per-runtime emitters must deduplicate by pointer identity or throughput reads double — the same trap as #54.
- A rate is only defined *between* samples, so the throughput headline is the newest sampled rate, never a cumulative total divided by uptime.
- Nothing here is emitted as OTLP — introspection only, no new metric descriptors, so `docs/metrics.md` is untouched.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `atomic.Uint64` emit counters on `*otelEmitter` + an `EmitStats()` accessor and a `Provider` passthrough
- [ ] Sampler gains rings for metric rate, log rate, failing count and mean run duration
- [ ] `statusdata.Status` gains `throughput` and `fleet` blocks
- [ ] Section markup + 3 `registerChart` calls + stat-card refresh in the page template
- [ ] Tests: per-instrument counter coverage, histogram-counted-once, rate differencing, fleet aggregation, JSON field presence, HTML render assertions
- [ ] Full gate green (build, vet, `test -race`, golangci-lint, govulncheck)

comments.body:
Landed in `a1c1fe9`. Full gate green: build, vet, `go test -race ./...`, golangci-lint (0 issues), govulncheck (no vulnerabilities). `docs/metrics.md` and `docs/env-vars.md` unchanged and in sync — no new metric descriptors, no new config keys.

**What shipped**

| chart id | series | source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `chEmit` | metric points/sec + log records/sec | `atomic.Uint64` counters on `*otelEmitter`, differenced over elapsed wall time |
| `chFailing` | collectors failing | `collector.StatusTracker.Snapshot()` across every tailnet runtime |
| `chDuration` | mean run duration (ms) | same |

Plus four stat cards, refreshed from the JSON poll.

**Design points worth keeping**

- **Emit counting is distinct from `ExportStats`.** Emit counts what the collectors produced; export counts what the OTLP exporters shipped. Under cumulative temporality a pipeline re-exports idle series, so the two answer different questions — conflating them would be a wrong chart, not a rounding difference.
- **Per-runtime emitters are deduplicated by pointer identity.** Headscale *shares* the process emitter with its runtime, so summing per-runtime would double the reported throughput — the same trap that produced #54 for `export.*`.
- `Histogram` delegates to `HistogramCtx`, so only `HistogramCtx` counts. Counting both would double every histogram.
- **Counters are unconditional**, unlike `ExportStats` (which is zero when self-obs is off, because the counting exporters are not installed). Two atomic adds cost nothing, so the throughput chart works with `self_observability` disabled — matching the sampler's existing "introspection runs regardless" stance.
- **Fleet headline numbers are live; only the series are sampled.** `fleet.active/failing/mean_duration_ms` are read from the status tracker at snapshot time (fresher than a ≤10s-old ring). Throughput is the opposite by necessity: a rate is only defined *between* samples, so its headline is the newest ring value, never a cumulative total divided by uptime.
- New series fields carry no `omitempty`, so the JSON contract stays stable for the chart JS; a nil ring serialises as `null`, which the `||[]` guards already handle.
- `runtimeHistory.sample` / `runSampler` gained `samplerTick` and `samplerSources` structs rather than growing to 6 and 8 positional params of near-identical types. Mechanical migration of the existing call sites, no behaviour change.

**Test gap, deliberate:** `collector.StatusTracker.record` is unexported, so package `app` cannot synthesise collector runs. The fleet reduction is covered by a table-driven test on `fleetAggregate` (including the never-run and multi-runtime cases), and a separate test proves the live path is wired to the tracker rather than the ring. `record` was not exported just to test this.

**Not done, deliberately:** nothing is emitted as OTLP (introspection only, no new metric descriptors), and no throttle-headroom surface — that is graph2otel-specific.

Sibling ports: graph2otel `rknightion/graph2otel#227`, opnsense-exporter `rknightion/opnsense-exporter#347`.

title: admin: emitted-throughput and collector-fleet trend charts on the status page

body:
Part of the fleet-wide operator-console alignment tracked in **rknightion/opnsense-exporter#337**. The three exporters (opnsense-exporter, graph2otel, tailscale2otel) are converging their operator consoles, and **tailscale2otel's console is the chosen reference implementation** — its tabbed single-page layout + theme/style is what the other two adopt.

## Role

This repo is the reference; most alignment work lands in the other two. This issue tracks the **minor diffs to reconcile here** so the three end up identical in behaviour.

## Work

- [ ] **Configurable refresh interval.** The 10s poll is currently hardcoded (`internal/app/statushtml/page.html.tmpl`, `setInterval(refresh, 10000)`). Add a config knob for it, **default 5s** (fleet standard, matching opnsense-exporter's `--web.ui-refresh-interval`). Keep the 1s freshness ticker independent.
- [ ] Reconcile any further small divergences surfaced while porting the layout to the other two repos (column set, health-state wording, badge classes, sparkline sizing) — update here if the fleet standard differs from current t2o.

## Acceptance

- [ ] Refresh interval is configurable, default 5s.
- [ ] No behavioural drift between this console and the aligned opnsense-exporter / graph2otel consoles.
- [ ] Full gate green.

comments.body:
Done in `9b13a84`.

Added `admin.status_refresh_interval` (YAML `Duration`, env `TS2OTEL_ADMIN__STATUS_REFRESH_INTERVAL`), default **5s** — the fleet standard matching opnsense-exporter's `--web.ui-refresh-interval`. Wired through `AdminConfig` → `Default()` → `buildStatus` → `statusdata.Status.RefreshMs` → the page's `window.__refreshMs`; `startPolling` now uses it instead of the hardcoded `setInterval(refresh, 10000)`. The 1s freshness ticker (`tickFreshness`) stays independent per the acceptance note.

Docs: documented the key in `docs/configuration.md` + `config.example.yaml` and regenerated `docs/env-vars.md`. Gate green: `go test ./...` (incl. config completeness/env-ref doc checks), `go test -race ./...`, golangci-lint 0 issues.

This is the reference-lock for the fleet console-alignment epic (rknightion/opnsense-exporter#337); opnsense + graph2otel adopt the 5s default next.

body:
## Problem

The documented PII filter protects metrics and logs, but it is not applied to span attributes. The Tailscale API transport records `url.full`, so endpoint paths carrying tailnet or device identifiers are exported to the configured OTLP trace backend even when endpoint-path filtering is disabled.

## Evidence

- `internal/tsapi/transport.go:280-307` records `url.full` on API spans.
- `internal/telemetry/provider.go:309-335` creates the trace provider with resource, batch, sampler and constant-attribute options, but no PII filtering span processor.
- The existing PII-filter tests cover metrics and logs; focused tracing tests confirm API spans are emitted when tracing is enabled.

## Failure scenario / impact

An operator sets `pii_filter.endpoint_paths=false` expecting endpoint-path identifiers to stay out of self-observability. The same identifiers remain in `url.full` on exported spans, exposing them to the trace backend and anyone with access to those traces.

## Suggested direction

Apply the configured PII filter to span attributes before export. The narrow option is to remove or sanitize `url.full` when endpoint-path filtering is disabled; the broader option is a category-aware span processor shared with the existing redaction policy.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `pii_filter.endpoint_paths=false` removes or sanitizes endpoint-path identifiers from trace attributes
- [ ] `url.full` and related HTTP/URL span attributes are covered
- [ ] Allowed PII categories keep their current trace detail
- [ ] Regression tests assert emitted span attributes for both filtering states
- [ ] Documentation states whether trace attributes are included in the PII-filter contract

_Found during the Codex Security repository scan, 2026-07-18. Verified against main at 5991d21195ace8cb0a554728e208f8c02778d882._

comments.body:
Fixed in 0550813 (pushed to `main`).

Took the **broader** of the two options in the suggested direction — a category-aware filter sharing the existing redaction policy, not a narrow `url.full` patch. That turned out to be necessary rather than merely nicer:

## The narrow fix would not have closed this

Removing `url.full` leaves the same URL reaching the trace backend by two further routes on the same span:

1. **Span status description** — `sanitizeTransportError` (`internal/tsapi/transport.go`) builds `"<op> <URL>: <inner>"`, so on any request error the full URL lands in the status.
2. **`exception.message`** — `RecordError` puts the same string in a span-event attribute.

All three are now filtered: attributes are dropped by category, and redacted *values* are additionally scrubbed out of the status description and event/link attributes using the same `RedactBody` mechanism as `#197`.

## Implementation note: it could not be a SpanProcessor

Worth recording, since the obvious approach does not work in the pinned SDK (v1.44.0). `OnEnd` receives an immutable `snapshot`, not the `*recordingSpan` — the assertion back to `ReadWriteSpan` fails (`sdk/trace/span.go:610-613`) — and the trace API has no attribute *removal* in any case, only add/overwrite. `OnStart`, where the existing `constAttrSpanProcessor` works, runs before instrumented code calls `SetAttributes`, so it would see nothing. `ExportSpans` is the only point where an attribute can actually disappear, so the filter is a `SpanExporter` wrapper that embeds `ReadOnlySpan` (method promotion satisfies the unexported method) and overrides `Attributes()`/`Events()`/`Links()`/`Status()`. Verified through the real `stdouttrace` exporter, not just an in-memory one.

When no category is disabled the wrapper is not constructed at all, so the default configuration is byte-identical and allocation-free.

Acceptance criteria:

- [x] `pii_filter.endpoint_paths=false` removes endpoint-path identifiers from trace attributes
- [x] `url.full` and related HTTP/URL span attributes covered (plus status description and error events)
- [x] Allowed PII categories keep their current trace detail
- [x] Regression tests assert emitted span attributes for both filtering states, and prove the contract is general (`hostnames=false` drops `host.name` from spans)
- [x] Documentation states that trace attributes are in the PII-filter contract (`docs/configuration.md`)

**Two residual gaps, documented rather than papered over:** span *names* are safe by construction, not by policy — `endpointLabel` already strips the tailnet segment and elides variable ID segments before the name is built, so a future span name that interpolates an identifier would not be caught. And resource attributes continue to go through the separate pre-existing resource gate. Both are stated in `docs/configuration.md`.

Also added `TestSpanAttributeKeysAreClassified` as a guard for this surface: the existing catalog-driven completeness test is structurally unable to see span keys, since spans are not in the catalog.

title: Apply the PII filter to Tailscale API trace attributes

## Problem

The Headscale client bounds non-200 diagnostic bodies to 512 bytes, but decodes successful JSON responses directly from the network stream with no byte or record limit.

## Evidence

- `internal/hsapi/client.go:45-52` sends the authenticated request and closes the body.
- `internal/hsapi/client.go:53-55` limits only non-200 bodies with `io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 512)`.
- `internal/hsapi/client.go:57` calls `json.NewDecoder(resp.Body).Decode(out)` for a 200 response without a limiting reader.

## Failure scenario / impact

A malicious or compromised configured Headscale endpoint can send an oversized valid JSON response. The exporter decodes it before normal collection continues, which can exhaust process memory and stop telemetry collection.

## Suggested direction

Wrap successful response bodies in an explicit byte-limiting reader and return a typed oversized-response error before JSON decoding. Use endpoint-specific limits where response sizes differ materially.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Successful Headscale JSON responses have an explicit byte limit before decoding
- [ ] Oversized 200 responses fail cleanly without unbounded allocation
- [ ] Existing 512-byte non-200 diagnostic handling remains intact
- [ ] Tests cover normal and oversized successful responses
- [ ] Collection skips the affected cycle cleanly and resumes on the next valid response

_Found during the Codex Security repository scan, 2026-07-18. Verified against main at 5991d21195ace8cb0a554728e208f8c02778d882._

comments.body:
Fixed in 054ee09 (pushed to `main`), alongside the sibling finding (#210/#211 share one fix shape).

`internal/hsapi`'s `getJSON` now decodes successful responses through an explicit byte limit of **32 MiB**, returning an exported `ErrResponseTooLarge` sentinel when exceeded. The existing 512-byte non-success diagnostic body handling is unchanged.

**The subtle part, and why a naive fix would be wrong.** Decoding from a reader that truncates mid-document fails with `io.ErrUnexpectedEOF` — which is indistinguishable from ordinary malformed JSON. Relying on that error to signal an oversized body would silently conflate "the Headscale endpoint sent too much" with "the Headscale endpoint sent garbage", and an operator debugging the second would chase the wrong cause. The implementation instead reads through `limit+1` bytes and tests whether the allowance was fully consumed, which is positive proof the body exceeded the cap regardless of what the decoder returned. A test asserts the two cases produce genuinely different errors (`errors.Is` vs. `*json.SyntaxError`).

Deliberately **not** factored into a shared helper package: `internal/tsapi` and `internal/hsapi` are unrelated packages, and a shared utility package for eight lines would couple them for no benefit. The duplication is intentional.

Acceptance criteria:

- [x] Successful JSON responses have an explicit byte limit before decoding
- [x] Oversized successful responses fail cleanly with a typed error and no unbounded allocation
- [x] Existing 512-byte error-body handling intact
- [x] Tests cover normal and oversized successful responses (plus the malformed-under-cap case, and an end-to-end `httptest` run at the real production constant)
- [x] Callers surface the bounded failure without exporting partial data — the collection cycle fails and resumes on the next valid response

title: Bound successful Headscale API JSON responses before decoding
