body:
## Problem
Three dashboard/alert consumers treat the cumulative `tailscale_devices_key_expiry_days_bucket` histogram counters as if they were current, point-in-time device counts. They are lifetime observation totals (observed once per device per scrape at the default 60s interval) that only ever grow — so any derived "current count" latches and never resolves after a key is rotated. A correct, gauge-based alert for the same underlying concern (`ts2o-device-key-expiring-critical`) already ships enabled by default, so the alerting gap itself is narrow — but the two flagship dashboard panels that use the cumulative buckets show garbage numbers to every viewer.

## Evidence
- `internal/collector/devices/devices.go:667-670` — histogram observed once per device per `Collect` (default interval 60s per `devices.go:174`); bucket bounds `{0,7,30,90,180,365}` (`devices.go:183`).
- `internal/telemetry/provider.go:492-493` — cumulative temporality (Mimir OTLP requires it), pinned by `provider_internal_test.go:126-143`.
- **Alert** `ts2o-device-keys-expiring-7d` (`build_rules.py:410-418` / `grafana-rules.yaml:2369`, **paused by default**): `sum(..._bucket{le="7"}) - sum(..._bucket{le="0"}) > 0 for 1h`.
- **Dashboard stat** "Keys already expired" (`deploy/grafana/gen/build.py:722-726`): `sum(last_over_time(tailscale_devices_key_expiry_days_bucket{le="0"}[10m]))`, described as "Devices whose node key has already expired" — enabled/default-visible.
- **Dashboard barchart** "Devices by days-to-expiry bucket" (`build.py:731-736`): raw `sum by (le)(..._bucket)`, also cumulative-in-`le` (le=30 includes le=7), so not a per-bucket device distribution even as a snapshot.
- A correct pattern already exists in-repo: `ts2o-device-key-expiring-critical` (`grafana-rules.yaml:1801`) and recording rule `ts2o-rec-keys-expiring-7d` (`build_rules.py:640-642`) both use the per-device gauge `tailscale_device_key_expiry_seconds - time()`.

## Failure scenario / impact
Default deployment: one device key expires and is re-authed an hour later. The "Keys already expired" stat reads 60+ and keeps climbing, red, forever (it never decreases outside a process restart) — a garbage number shown by default on the flagship dashboard. Separately, an operator who explicitly enables the paused `ts2o-device-keys-expiring-7d` alert gets a warning that never clears until the exporter restarts.

## Suggested direction
Use the per-device gauge, mirroring the already-correct recording rule: `count(max by (host_id)(tailscale_device_key_expiry_seconds) - time() < 7*86400 ...)` for the 7d-expiring case, and `count(... - time() <= 0)` for expired. For a bucketed distribution panel, use `increase()` of the buckets over one scrape interval, or a histogram panel type over `rate()` — as the existing (correct) median panel at `build.py:727-729` already does.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] "Keys already expired" stat uses the per-device gauge (or `increase()`-over-interval), not the raw cumulative `le="0"` bucket sum
- [ ] "Devices by days-to-expiry bucket" barchart uses a non-cumulative representation (increase-over-interval or histogram/rate panel type)
- [ ] The (paused, opt-in) `ts2o-device-keys-expiring-7d` alert is fixed or removed in favor of the existing correct `ts2o-rec-keys-expiring-7d`-based path, so it clears after key rotation if kept
- [ ] Regenerated dashboard/alert artifacts pass the byte-identical drift gate

_Found by automated v1 bug bash, 2026-07-03. Verified adversarially by opus._

comments.body: Closed by `08d0b87`. The 7d-expiry alert, the "keys already expired" stat, and the days-to-expiry barchart no longer treat cumulative-temporality histogram buckets as current counts (they only grow / are cumulative-in-le); all rebuilt from the point-in-time per-device `tailscale_device_key_expiry_seconds` gauge, so they clear after re-auth. The median-quantile panel (a legitimate `histogram_quantile(rate(_bucket))` use) is unchanged. _(Opus subagent; gated on main.)_

body:
## Problem
`tailscale2otel.enrich.cache_age` is only recorded synchronously, immediately after a successful device-cache refresh — the one instant its value is guaranteed to be ~0. There is no observable/async gauge callback that recomputes age at export time. As a result, the unpaused `ts2o-enrich-cache-stale` alert (threshold >3600s) and the corresponding dashboard panels can never actually detect staleness.

## Evidence
- `internal/collector/devices/devices.go:418-420` — the sole emit site: `c.cache.Replace(toMetas(devs)); e.Gauge(docCacheAge..., c.cache.Age().Seconds(), nil)`, executed right after `Replace`.
- `internal/enrich/devicecache.go:60-72,139-144` — `Replace` sets `updated=now`, so `Age()` at that point is ~0.
- Alert `ts2o-enrich-cache-stale` (`build_rules.py:246-252`, rendered `grafana-rules.yaml:719`, unpaused starter set) fires on `max(tailscale2otel_enrich_cache_age_seconds) > 3600`.
- The exporter-health dashboard "Enrich Cache Age" stat and the flagship diagnostics panel read the same gauge.
- `internal/telemetry` emitter confirms this is a synchronous `Float64Gauge` (last-value) with no `ObservableGauge`/`RegisterCallback` for cache age anywhere in the codebase.

## Failure scenario / impact
The devices collector starts failing (e.g. API 500s) while flowlogs keeps running. Flow/audit IP→name enrichment silently degrades to `unknown`/`external` — exactly the condition this starter alert claims to catch — but `enrich_cache_age_seconds` stays pinned at ~0 (the last-value gauge keeps re-exporting the stale near-zero reading), so the alert never fires and the dashboard stat shows a healthy 0s age. Note: this is a false-confidence monitoring gap on a self-observability alert/panel pair — it does not affect actual telemetry correctness or cause data loss.

## Suggested direction
Emit cache age from an asynchronous/observable gauge callback (computed at each export: `now - cache.updated`) instead of synchronously inside the devices `Collect`, or emit it from a periodic app-level reporter (e.g. alongside the checkpoint reporter). This makes the age actually grow while stale, matching what the alert and docs assume.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] `tailscale2otel.enrich.cache_age` is computed at export time (`now - cache.updated`), not only immediately post-refresh
- [ ] `ts2o-enrich-cache-stale` can actually fire when the devices collector stops refreshing successfully
- [ ] Test drives a stale device cache (collector failing/disabled) and asserts the emitted cache-age value grows accordingly

_Found by automated v1 bug bash, 2026-07-03. Verified adversarially by opus._

comments.body: Closed by `e3ef49e`. `tailscale2otel.enrich.cache_age` is now emitted by a periodic app-level reporter (`runEnrichCacheAgeReporter`) that computes `now - cache.updated` per runtime at the export interval, instead of synchronously in the devices collector right after refresh (when it was always ~0 and a last-value gauge could never grow). Gated on `collectors.devices.enabled`. So `ts2o-enrich-cache-stale` (>3600s) and the dashboard stat can now actually detect a devices collector that stopped refreshing. A `testing/synctest` test drives a stale cache and asserts cache_age grows past the threshold; the devices sync emit was removed (descriptor exported + still declared in the devices catalog).

body:
## Problem
Seven distinct PromQL expressions in the shipped Grafana-managed alert rules and the flagship dashboard have broken semantics — mostly introduced by label-shape refactors that the generators weren't fully updated for, plus a couple of pre-existing aggregation bugs. Each sub-item below is independent and should be fixed separately in the generator, then regenerated.

- **R0 — `ts2o-tailnet-api-errors` group_left join is stale.** After commit `6cfbb52`, `tailscale_tailnet` is a direct per-series data-point label, not something carried only by `target_info`. The rule still does `group_left(tailscale_tailnet) target_info`, which — since `target_info` no longer carries the label — overwrites/erases the real per-series label instead of copying it.
- **R1 — `ts2o-series-budget-high` + "Series headroom" stat divide by an unaggregated `tailscale2otel_series_limit`.** `on() group_left()` requires the RHS to resolve to exactly one series; whenever more than one exporter series exists (redeploy overlap, or two exporter instances into one stack), the RHS has ≥2 series and evaluation errors.
- **R2 — `ts2o-receiver-rejections` regex-`__name__` `rate()` collides labelsets.** `rate()` drops `__name__`; `tailscale_stream_rejected_total{reason=...}` and `tailscale_webhook_rejected_total{reason=...}` share the same `reason` label space, so once both receivers reject with the same reason, the resulting series are byte-identical and the query aborts.
- **R3 — rDNS lookup hit-rate panel always reads 100%.** Binary division with no `on()`/`ignoring()` matches on ALL labels including `result`; the `{result="hit"}` numerator can only pair with the `{result="hit"}` denominator (never the `{result="miss"}` series), so the panel computes `hit/clamp_min(hit,1)` — never the real hit fraction.
- **R5 — DERP relay-fraction alert/recording-rule/panels use inner-join vector addition.** `rate(A)+rate(B)` is a one-to-one match on all shared labels; a node emitting only inbound-or-outbound `path="derp"` series (asymmetric relay traffic) is silently dropped from both numerator and denominator before `sum()` runs.
- **R6 — "Devices per tailnet" bargauge sums the 0/1 online gauge.** `sum by (tailscale_tailnet) (last_over_time(tailscale_device_online_ratio[10m]))` counts only online devices (offline devices contribute 0), yet the panel is titled/described as a device count.
- **R7 — `ts2o-posture-match-low` computes `0/clamp_min(0,1)=0` for a never-synced/failing integration.** When `possible=0` (integration failing or no matchable devices), `clamp_min` turns the denominator into 1 and the expression evaluates to `0 < 0.8` — firing a misleading "match rate low" alert instead of signalling the actual sync failure.

## Evidence
- **R0**: `build_rules.py:599-608` / `grafana-rules.yaml:4144`; `deploy/grafana/gen/build.py:78-84` documents the label-shape change; the dashboard's equivalent panel already uses the direct matcher `{... tailscale_tailnet!=""}`.
- **R1**: `build_rules.py:188-195` / `grafana-rules.yaml:152`; same shape at `build.py:573` ("Series headroom" stat). The generator's own header (`build_rules.py:23-25`) documents wrapping gauge reads in `max by` for exactly this reason, but the RHS here is left raw.
- **R2**: `build_rules.py:516-522` / `grafana-rules.yaml:3345`; `internal/stream/stream.go:130-132` and `internal/webhook/webhook.go:309` both use `reason="too_large"`.
- **R3**: `deploy/grafana/gen/build.py:1731` ("rDNS lookup hit-rate" panel, unit `percentunit`).
- **R5**: `build_rules.py:541-551` (`ts2o-high-derp-relay-usage`, unpaused, `grafana-rules.yaml:3562`); recording rule `ts2o-rec-derp-byte-fraction` (`build_rules.py:625-631`); `build.py:1464-1483`.
- **R6**: `deploy/grafana/gen/build.py:548-552`, titled "Devices per tailnet", desc "Device count per tailnet (online devices visible to the exporter)". The adjacent overview stats already use `count()`/`count(==1)` correctly.
- **R7**: `build_rules.py:530-537` / `grafana-rules.yaml:3487`; vendor spec `spec/tailscale-api.json` `PostureIntegration.status` example shows failing integrations reporting `matchedCount=0` AND `possibleMatchedCount=0`.

## Failure scenario / impact
- **R0**: An MSP runs three tailnets; one tailnet's OAuth client is revoked. The alert fires with an empty (or errored) tailnet label, so on-call cannot tell which tailnet's credentials to fix — the rule's whole stated purpose.
- **R1**: Running two exporter instances into one Grafana Cloud stack (a documented MSP pattern) permanently breaks this alert (`execErrState=OK` masks it as silent OK) and the overview stat.
- **R2**: Both receivers enabled, an oversized-body client hits each at least once in 10m — from then on the rule silently evaluates to error→OK and never fires despite ongoing rejections.
- **R3**: rDNS cache thrashing at a 5% hit rate shows a healthy 100% on the dashboard, hiding the misconfiguration the panel exists to expose.
- **R5**: Receive-only nodes relaying heavily via DERP inbound (with no outbound `derp` series) vanish from the fraction; the >50% starter alert stays quiet despite most fleet bytes being relayed.
- **R6**: An MSP compares tailnets at 8am when laptops are asleep — a 200-device tailnet shows 45, sending the operator chasing a phantom ingestion problem.
- **R7**: A tailnet configures a posture integration (e.g. Kolide) with a bad token: `possible=matched=0` forever. The operator gets a permanent "match rate low" warning pointing at ACL posture-gate investigation instead of the integration's actual auth failure.

## Suggested direction
- **R0**: Replace with the same direct-label form the dashboard already uses: `sum by (tailscale_tailnet) (rate(tailscale2otel_api_requests_total{http_response_status_code=~"4..|5..", tailscale_tailnet!=""}[10m]))`.
- **R1**: Divide by `max(tailscale2otel_series_limit)` in both the rule generator and `build.py:573`.
- **R2**: Sum the two metrics with `or vector(0)` guards so an absent side doesn't break the sum: `(sum(rate(tailscale_stream_rejected_total[10m])) or vector(0)) + (sum(rate(tailscale_webhook_rejected_total[10m])) or vector(0))`.
- **R3**: Aggregate away the `result` label before dividing: `sum(rate(...{result="hit"}[$__rate_interval])) / clamp_min(sum(rate(...[$__rate_interval])), 1)`.
- **R5**: Sum each direction independently before dividing, with `or vector(0)` guards if one direction can be wholly absent. Apply to the alert, the recording rule, and both dashboard panels.
- **R6**: Use `count by (tailscale_tailnet) (max by (tailscale_tailnet, host_id) (last_over_time(tailscale_device_online_ratio[10m])))` for a true device count, or retitle the panel "Online devices per tailnet".
- **R7**: Guard the denominator, e.g. only evaluate when `tailscale_posture_integration_possible_matched_ratio > 0`, and let a real error/staleness signal (see the related posture-staleness issue) own the sync-failure case.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] R0: `ts2o-tailnet-api-errors` uses the direct `tailscale_tailnet` label match, no stale `group_left(target_info)` join
- [ ] R1: `ts2o-series-budget-high` and the "Series headroom" stat divide by an aggregated (single-series) `tailscale2otel_series_limit`
- [ ] R2: `ts2o-receiver-rejections` sums stream+webhook rejections without a label-collision failure mode
- [ ] R3: rDNS lookup hit-rate panel correctly aggregates away `result` before dividing, and reads a real (non-100%) hit fraction under a mixed hit/miss workload
- [ ] R5: DERP relay-fraction alert, recording rule, and panels sum each direction independently (no inner-join drop of asymmetric nodes)
- [ ] R6: "Devices per tailnet" reflects true device count (or is retitled to "Online devices per tailnet")
- [ ] R7: `ts2o-posture-match-low` does not fire for a never-synced/zero-possible-matches integration
- [ ] All seven expressions are corrected in the Python generator (`build_rules.py`/`build.py`), regenerated (byte-identical drift gate passes), and semantically verified against representative data; panel titles/descriptions match what they actually compute

body:
## Problem
`log_level` is documented and framed as a validated enum, but is never actually validated. `docs/configuration.md:119` documents it as "One of debug, info, warn, error", and the page's Conventions section (`:92-94`) states "invalid enum values and inconsistent combinations are rejected at startup by `Config.Validate()`". Every other documented enum key in the file (`otlp.protocol`, `tailscale.auth.method`, `checkpoint.store`, `collectors.*.source`, `flowlogs.log_mode`, `cardinality.flow.metrics_mode`, `streaming.decompress`, `tracing.sampler`, `node_metrics.discovery.*`, etc.) is actually enforced via a `oneOf(...)` check in `Validate()`. `log_level` is the one enum-shaped key with no corresponding check.

## Evidence
- `docs/configuration.md:119` — documents `log_level` as a validated enum.
- `docs/configuration.md:92-94` — "invalid enum values ... are rejected at startup by `Config.Validate()`".
- `internal/config/validate.go` — no reference to `LogLevel`/`log_level` anywhere.
- `cmd/tailscale2otel/main.go:55-66` — `parseLevel` silently maps any unrecognized string to `slog.LevelInfo`, with no error and no WARN advisory.

## Failure scenario / impact
An operator sets `TS2OTEL_LOG_LEVEL=warning` (a natural but wrong spelling — the valid value is `warn`), expecting either a startup error (per the docs' stated `Validate()` guarantee) or at least a config-file WARN. Instead the exporter starts silently at INFO level, and the mistake is only discovered later when unexpectedly verbose (or unexpectedly quiet) logs are noticed.

## Suggested direction
Either add a `oneOf(c.LogLevel, "debug","info","warn","error")` check to `Validate()` (or a `Warnings()` advisory) to match the documented guarantee, or soften the `docs/configuration.md` wording for this key to say it fails open to `info` on an unrecognized value.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] `log_level` is validated against its documented enum (`debug`/`info`/`warn`/`error`) at `Validate()`, matching the page's stated Convention — or the docs are corrected to describe the actual fail-open behavior
- [ ] Test covers an invalid `log_level` value producing the expected error (or documented fail-open behavior)

_Found by automated v1 bug bash, 2026-07-03. Verified adversarially by sonnet._

comments.body: Closed by 4781a88. `Validate()` now rejects a `log_level` outside `debug/info/warn/error`, matching the documented enum guarantee (previously it silently failed open to info in `parseLevel`). Test covers the classic `warning` misspelling.

body:
## Problem
Checkpoint keys silently change on single↔multi-tailnet transitions and on tailnet renames. The checkpoint namespace is applied (`collector.WithCheckpointNamespace(rt.name)`) only when the deployment is in multi mode (`len(resolved) > 1`), so growing from a single `tailscale:` block to a `tailnets:` list changes a collector's key from e.g. `flowlogs` to `<name>/flowlogs` (and shrinking back reverses it); renaming a `tailnets[].name` has the same effect. Nothing migrates or prunes the old key.

## Evidence
- `internal/app/tailnetruntime.go:78-80` — namespace applied only `if d.multi`.
- `internal/app/app.go:115` — `d.multi = len(resolved) > 1`.
- `internal/collector/scheduler.go:87-91` — checkpoint key = `namespace + "/" + name`.
- `internal/app/status.go:146-151` — mirrors the same namespacing logic.
- `internal/collector/checkpoint.go` — only has `Get`/`Set`; no migration or pruning of stale keys.

## Failure scenario / impact
An operator grows from the single `tailscale:` block to a `tailnets:` list (the natural MSP migration path). On the next start, every window collector (flowlogs, auditlogs) fails to find its stored high-water mark under the new namespaced key, treats it as a cold start (re-polling the `initial_lookback` window, default 5m each), and the poll-window dedup set is empty after restart — the overlap window is re-emitted to the backend as duplicate flow/audit records. The superseded un-namespaced key stays in `checkpoints.json` indefinitely.

## Suggested direction
On startup, migrate a legacy un-namespaced key to the namespaced form when the namespaced one is absent (and the reverse for a multi→single transition), or at minimum log a WARN naming the affected collectors. Consider pruning store keys that match no registered collector/namespace.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A legacy un-namespaced checkpoint key is migrated to the namespaced form when present and the namespaced key is absent (and vice versa on multi→single transitions)
- [ ] Or: a WARN is logged at startup naming affected collectors when a namespace-shape change is detected
- [ ] Stale checkpoint keys that match no registered collector/namespace are pruned (or at least logged)
- [ ] Test covers a single→multi (and multi→single) transition preserving the checkpoint cursor

_Found by automated v1 bug bash, 2026-07-03. Verified adversarially by opus._

comments.body: Closed by 38dfcaa. `migrateCheckpointKeys` runs at startup and reconciles stored keys with the current namespacing shape: a window collector whose current key is absent adopts a single matching legacy key (same collector basename) — preserving the high-water mark on single↔multi transitions and tailnet renames — deletes the old key, and cold-starts (with a WARN) when the mapping is ambiguous. Stray keys matching no collector are logged. Added `Keys()`/`Delete()` to `CheckpointStore`. Tests cover multi→single (cursor preserved), single→multi (first tailnet adopts, rest cold-start), and the ambiguous case.

body:
## Problem
`tailnets[]` entries do not receive the documented `tailscale.http` defaults. `Default()` only populates the single top-level `tailscale:` block's HTTP retry settings (`MaxAttempts: 4`, `BaseDelay: 500ms`, `MaxDelay: 10s`); `ResolvedTailnets` copies each `TailnetConfig` verbatim with no default-filling. An entry that omits an `http:` block decodes to a zero-valued `TailscaleHTTPConfig`, and `tsapi`'s auth layer clamps a zero `MaxAttempts` to `1` — silently disabling retries (including 429 `Retry-After` handling) for every multi-tailnet client that follows the example config's minimal snippet.

## Evidence
- `internal/config/defaults.go:26-33` — retry defaults seeded only under `Tailscale.HTTP`.
- `internal/config/config.go:211-227` — `ResolvedTailnets` copies `TailnetConfig` verbatim, no default filling.
- `internal/tsapi/auth.go:27` — `max(opts.MaxAttempts, 1)`: a zero `MaxAttempts` becomes 1 attempt (no retry).
- `config.example.yaml:75-83` — the `tailnets:` snippet shows entries with no `http:` block.
- `docs/configuration.md:186` — documents the `max_attempts` default as `4`.
- Relatedly: `TS2OTEL_TAILSCALE__HTTP__*` env overrides map to the (unused) `tailscale` block and are silently ignored in multi mode, with no unknown-env warning.

## Failure scenario / impact
An MSP configures three tailnets by copying the example snippet (name + auth only). Multi-tailnet triples API request volume; Tailscale starts returning 429/transient 5xx. With max attempts clamped to 1, every such response fails the collector tick outright instead of being retried — producing scrape-failure noise and data gaps that single-tailnet deployments never see.

## Suggested direction
In `ResolvedTailnets` (or a Load-time normalize pass), fill zero-valued per-entry HTTP fields from `Default().Tailscale.HTTP` (or from the top-level `tailscale.http` block so operators can set fleet-wide policy once). Alternatively, align `tsapi`'s `MaxAttempts` fallback with the documented default of 4.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Per-entry zero-valued HTTP fields (at minimum `max_attempts`) are backfilled from `Default().Tailscale.HTTP` (or an equivalent documented fallback of 4)
- [ ] The env-override path for `tailnets[]` HTTP settings is documented, or an unknown-env WARN is added
- [ ] Test covers a `tailnets[]` entry with no `http:` block getting real retry defaults

_Found by automated v1 bug bash, 2026-07-03. Verified adversarially by opus._

comments.body: Closed by 4781a88. `ResolvedTailnets` now backfills each `tailnets[]` entry's HTTP fields with precedence *entry > `tailscale.http` > `Default().Tailscale.HTTP`*, so an entry omitting `http:` gets real retry defaults (no more zero `max_attempts` clamped to 1) and `tailscale.http` / `TS2OTEL_TAILSCALE__HTTP__*` acts as fleet-wide policy. Tests cover both the default-backfill and fleet-policy-with-override paths; documented in `docs/configuration.md`.

body:
## Problem
With `prometheus.enabled: true`, setting `pii_filter.tailnet_name: false` makes `/metrics` return HTTP 500 on every scrape. The `tailscale.tailnet` distinguisher is a data-point attribute gated by the `tailnet_name` PII category. `service.instance.id` only lives on `target_info`, never on the series themselves. With the category disabled:
- In **multi-tailnet** mode, the per-tailnet Prometheus registries produce byte-identical series across tailnets.
- In **single-tailnet** mode, the process and tailnet registries both emit the self-obs `tailscale2otel.export.datapoints` / `series.active` metrics, which also collide.

`prometheus.Gatherers.Gather` reports these collisions as duplicate-metric errors, and the default `promhttp` `HandlerOpts` (`ErrorHandling` unset ⇒ `HTTPErrorOnError`) turns any `Gather` error into a hard HTTP 500 — permanently, not just as a one-off blip.

## Evidence
- `internal/telemetry/provider.go:425-431` — `constLabelAttrs` omits `tailscale.tailnet` when `pii.CatTailnetName` is false.
- `internal/telemetry/providerset.go:72-85` — `PromGatherers` merges one registry per provider.
- `internal/app/metrics.go:20` — `promhttp.HandlerFor(g, promhttp.HandlerOpts{})`, default `ErrorHandling=HTTPErrorOnError`.
- Empirically reproduced in a throwaway worktree: multi-tailnet repro returns `status=500` with body `collected metric "tailscale_devices_count_ratio" ... was collected before with the same name and label values`; single-tailnet repro (process + tailnet providers both emitting `tailscale2otel.export.datapoints`, per `app.go:411`/`420`) also returns 500.
- `docs/configuration.md:569` claims "series stay distinct via `service.instance.id`"; `docs/configuration.md:624` claims the tailnet constant label prevents `/metrics` collisions — both contradicted by the repro.

## Failure scenario / impact
An operator enables `prometheus.enabled: true` and, following `docs/configuration.md:569`'s assurance, sets `pii_filter.tailnet_name=false` for a privacy posture. From the next scrape onward, `GET /metrics` returns 500 with a duplicate-metric error; Prometheus marks the target down and all pull-path telemetry is lost until the PII toggle is reverted.

## Suggested direction
Either make `Validate()`/`Warnings()` reject-or-warn on `prometheus.enabled` + `pii_filter.tailnet_name=false`, or keep series distinct on the pull path when the label is dropped (e.g. inject a per-provider constant label on the Prometheus registerer, or set `promhttp.HandlerOpts{ErrorHandling: ContinueOnError}` so first-occurrence-wins instead of 500). Fix the docs claims at `configuration.md:569`/`624` either way.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] `/metrics` scrapes return 200 with `pii_filter.tailnet_name=false` in both single-tailnet and multi-tailnet mode
- [ ] Either `Validate()`/`Warnings()` flags the unsafe combination, or the registry/handler is made collision-safe (e.g. per-provider constant label or `ContinueOnError`)
- [ ] `docs/configuration.md:569` and `:624` corrected to match actual behavior
- [ ] Regression test covers the duplicate-series scrape in both single- and multi-tailnet mode

_Found by automated v1 bug bash, 2026-07-03. Verified adversarially by opus._

comments.body: Closed by 16246da. `buildMetricsServer` now uses `promhttp.ContinueOnError` so a duplicate-series Gather collision (from dropping `tailscale.tailnet` when `pii_filter.tailnet_name=false`) serves 200 (first-wins) instead of a permanent 500. Regression test in `metrics_test.go` asserts 200 in single- and multi-tailnet mode; a throwaway check confirmed the *default* handler 500s on the identical series. Added a `Warnings()` advisory for the multi-tailnet series-collapse, and corrected the contradicted claims at `docs/configuration.md` (`pii_filter.tailnet_name` + the multi-tailnet Prometheus note).

body:
## Problem

`toMetas` in the devices collector (`internal/collector/devices/devices.go:1030-1054`) builds
`enrich.DeviceMeta` from `NodeID`, `Name`, `Hostname`, `OS`, `OSVersion`, `User`, `Addrs`, and
`External` only — it never copies `Tags`, even though `DeviceMeta` already declares a `Tags` field
(`internal/enrich/devicecache.go:13-23`). As a result, `rt.cache.Snapshot()[i].Tags` is always empty,
and the admin status page's device-tags column (`internal/app/status.go:403`) reads from that same
cache — so it renders blank for every device, regardless of what tags are actually configured on the
tailnet.

This was surfaced as a side finding during adversarial verification of finding [73] (devices/
node-metrics inventory reuse): the verifier traced `enrich.DeviceCache`'s schema to check whether it
could support node-metrics discovery, and found this pre-existing gap unrelated to that finding's own
scope.

## Evidence

- `internal/collector/devices/devices.go:1030-1054` (`toMetas`) — populates `DeviceMeta` from
  `NodeID, Name, Hostname, OS, OSVersion, User, Addrs, External` only; `Tags` is omitted.
- `internal/enrich/devicecache.go:13-23` — `DeviceMeta` already declares a `Tags` field.
- `internal/app/status.go:403` — the status page's device-tags column reads
  `rt.cache.Snapshot()[i].Tags`, which is always empty as a result.

## Failure scenario / impact

An operator opens the admin status page to check which tags are applied to devices (e.g. to
diagnose an ACL/posture issue tied to tag membership) and sees an empty tags column for every
device, even though tags are correctly configured and used elsewhere (e.g. in the devices collector's
own tag-based metrics). The status page silently under-reports available device metadata.

## Suggested direction

Have `toMetas` copy the device's `Tags` into `enrich.DeviceMeta.Tags` alongside the other fields it
already populates.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `toMetas` copies `Tags` into `DeviceMeta`
- [ ] the admin status page's device-tags column shows real tag data
- [ ] a test asserts `DeviceMeta.Tags` is populated from a device with tags configured

_Found during adversarial verification (opus) in the automated v1 bug bash, 2026-07-03._

comments.body: Closed by `6035361`. `toMetas` now copies device `Tags` into `enrich.DeviceMeta.Tags`; the status page already reads it (`runtimeDeviceRows`), so the per-device tags column is no longer blank — no status.go change needed. Test asserts the cache entry carries the source tags. _(Sonnet subagent; gated on main.)_

body:
## Problem

`.goreleaser.yaml` still defines a dead docker pipeline pointed at a divergent Dockerfile, and
`deploy/CLAUDE.md` plus the `.goreleaser.yaml` header describe an architecture that no longer exists:

- `.goreleaser.yaml:63-92` defines `dockers_v2`/`docker_signs` pointed at
  `dockerfile: deploy/Dockerfile.goreleaser` (line 65). Its header (lines 6-8) claims "Real releases
  run in `.github/workflows/release.yml` ... produce ... a multi-arch GHCR image (with image SBOM
  and SLSA provenance) + keyless cosign signatures" via GoReleaser — but that workflow file doesn't
  even exist (the real one is `release-please.yml`, triggered on push to `main`, not a `v*` tag).
- Every real invocation path disables this: `release-please.yml:104`'s `binaries` job passes
  `goreleaser-args: "release --clean --skip=docker"`, and `ci.yml`'s snapshot job hits
  `dockers_v2`'s `disable: "{{ .IsSnapshot }}"`. So `dockers_v2`/`docker_signs` are unreachable on
  every real CI path — the actual multi-arch image is built by `publish.yml`'s `image` job via the
  shared `container-publish.yml` reusable, using plain `deploy/Dockerfile` (not `.goreleaser`).
- `deploy/Dockerfile.goreleaser` has already silently drifted from `deploy/Dockerfile`: it lacks the
  pre-seeded `/var/lib/tailscale2otel` checkpoint directory (unlike `deploy/Dockerfile:18-20,44`) and
  its `CMD` auto-loads `config.example.yaml`, unlike the real image's `CMD []`.
- `deploy/CLAUDE.md:9,83-92,93` still describes the old (pre-628ad87) architecture: calling
  `Dockerfile.goreleaser` "the variant GoReleaser uses for the published multi-arch image", GoReleaser
  as building+signing the image, and referencing `main-publish.yml`, which was deleted in commit
  `628ad87` and replaced by the `edge` job in `release-please.yml:74-86`.

Finding [27] confirmed `Dockerfile.goreleaser`'s divergence (specifically: no `/var/lib` pre-seed for
the checkpoint directory), but its "this breaks the actual published image" premise was refuted by
the orchestrator: the published image is built from `deploy/Dockerfile` via `publish.yml` →
`container-publish.yml` (`release-please.yml:104` passes `--skip=docker`, so `dockers_v2` never
runs). [27] folds into this issue as evidence for deleting/retiring the dead pair, not as a
production defect in its own right.

At HEAD, this is dead code + stale docs, not a live defect: no CI job exercises `dockers_v2`, no
build breaks, no user is affected. The headline "double-publish race" scenario (GoReleaser and the
container-publish reusable both pushing to the same GHCR tags) is contingent on a hypothetical future
edit that removes `--skip=docker` from `release-please.yml:104` — it does not exist today. Deleting
the dead pair removes both the divergence and that hypothetical future hazard.

## Evidence

- `.goreleaser.yaml:6-8,63-92,107-114` — stale header + dead `dockers_v2`/`docker_signs` config.
- `release-please.yml:104` — `--skip=docker` on the real release path.
- `ci.yml` — `dockers_v2`'s `disable: "{{ .IsSnapshot }}"` on the snapshot path.
- `publish.yml:28-39` + shared `container-publish.yml` — the actual image build, using
  `deploy/Dockerfile` (line 38).
- `deploy/Dockerfile.goreleaser` vs `deploy/Dockerfile:18-20,44,56` — missing checkpoint dir
  pre-seed; wrong default `CMD`.
- `deploy/CLAUDE.md:9,83-92,93` — stale description; `main-publish.yml` confirmed deleted in
  `628ad87`, replaced by the `edge` job (`release-please.yml:74-86`).

## Failure scenario / impact

If `--skip=docker` were ever dropped from the `binaries` job (e.g. during a future refactor or a
copy-paste from another repo's workflow), GoReleaser's `dockers_v2` would build and push to the exact
same `ghcr.io/rknightion/tailscale2otel` tags the container-publish reusable already pushed in the
same run, racing/clobbering image manifests and cosign signatures — the same failure class the
628ad87 restructure's own commit message notes already happened once for SBOM assets. Separately,
anyone reading `deploy/CLAUDE.md` today gets a wrong mental model of the publish pipeline.

## Suggested direction

Delete the now-dead `dockers_v2`/`docker_signs` sections and `deploy/Dockerfile.goreleaser` (or
clearly mark them unused-by-CI with a check that would catch reactivation); update `deploy/CLAUDE.md`
to describe the current pipeline (container-publish reusable owns the image; GoReleaser is
binaries-only; `main-publish.yml` no longer exists, replaced by the `edge` job in
`release-please.yml`); fix the stale `.goreleaser.yaml` header.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] dead `dockers_v2`/`docker_signs` GoReleaser config and `deploy/Dockerfile.goreleaser` are
      removed (or explicitly guarded against reactivation)
- [ ] `deploy/CLAUDE.md` describes the current container-publish pipeline accurately, with no
      reference to the deleted `main-publish.yml`
- [ ] `.goreleaser.yaml`'s header no longer references a nonexistent `release.yml` workflow

_Found by automated v1 bug bash, 2026-07-03. Verified adversarially by opus/sonnet. Dockerfile.goreleaser divergence confirmed by finding [27]; its 'published image' premise was refuted by the orchestrator (release-please passes --skip=docker; the shipped image uses deploy/Dockerfile)._

comments.body: Closed by `413b314`. Retired the dead GoReleaser docker pipeline: removed `dockers_v2`/`docker_signs` from `.goreleaser.yaml`, deleted `deploy/Dockerfile.goreleaser`, and corrected the stale `deploy/CLAUDE.md` + `ci.yml` references (the real image build is `release-please.yml`'s publish/edge jobs). `goreleaser check` + a snapshot build pass; grep confirms no remaining references. _(Sonnet subagent.)_

body:
## Problem

`.github/actions/report-drift/action.yml:60-65` instructs the Claude enrichment step: "If the fix is
mechanical ... optionally open a DRAFT pull request." Both callers that enable this step —
`.github/workflows/api-drift.yml:8-11` and `.github/workflows/live-contract.yml:15-18` — grant only
`contents: read, issues: write, pull-requests: write`; neither grants `contents: write`. Opening any
PR (even a draft one) requires pushing a new branch/commit, which needs `contents: write` on the
token; `pull-requests: write` only authorizes the final `POST /pulls` call, not branch/commit
creation. The action uses the default `GITHUB_TOKEN` (no GitHub App override), so any attempt to push
a fix branch will be rejected with a 403. `report-drift/README.md:32` itself documents
`pull-requests: write` as sufficient for the draft PR — the docs reinforce the mistaken belief rather
than sanctioning the gap as deliberate.

The draft-PR step is explicitly optional/best-effort ("optionally open a draft PR when the fix is
mechanical") — the action's two mandatory outputs (a deduped tracking issue, and a commented concrete
fix) both work fine under the granted permissions, and these are advisory-only scheduled lanes that
never gate PRs. When the PR push 403s, the run degrades gracefully to exactly the fallback already
described: the maintainer applies the fix by hand from the issue comment.

## Evidence

- `.github/actions/report-drift/action.yml:60-65` — draft-PR instruction to the enrichment step.
- `.github/workflows/api-drift.yml:8-11` and `.github/workflows/live-contract.yml:15-18` — both grant
  only `contents: read` (+ `issues: write`, `pull-requests: write`).
- `.github/workflows/clientlib-main.yml:18-20` — correctly excluded from this issue; it withholds
  the enrichment secret and grants only `issues: write`.
- `report-drift/README.md:32` — documents `pull-requests: write` as sufficient (the mistaken belief).

## Failure scenario / impact

A scheduled `api-drift` or `live-contract` run detects a mechanical, auto-fixable API drift; the
prompt asks Claude to open a draft PR with the fix, but the push fails with a 403 because the
workflow's permissions block never grants `contents: write`. The maintainer never gets the promised
draft PR and has to apply the fix by hand from the issue comment instead — which is also the built-in
fallback, so there's no product/runtime/security consequence, just an unreachable advertised
capability.

## Suggested direction

Either grant `contents: write` to the two enrichment lanes (scoped, since the prompt already
restricts edits to `internal/tsapi` and `spec/tailscale-api.json`), or drop the "open a draft PR"
instruction from the shared prompt/README to match the actual, read-only-on-contents capability.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] either `contents: write` is granted to `api-drift.yml` and `live-contract.yml`'s enrichment
      steps, or the draft-PR instruction is removed from `report-drift/action.yml` and
      `report-drift/README.md:32`
- [ ] the chosen behavior (draft PR works, or is documented as unsupported) is verified end-to-end

_Found by automated v1 bug bash, 2026-07-03. Verified adversarially by opus._

comments.body: Closed by `413b314`. Dropped the report-drift draft-PR path (least-privilege; the manual fallback is already documented) from the action + README, and removed the now-unused `pull-requests: write` permission from `api-drift.yml` and `live-contract.yml` (only `contents: read` + `issues: write` remain, matching the issue-only operations). _(Sonnet subagent.)_

## Problem

`internal/collector/postureintegrations/postureintegrations.go:86-89` emits `docLastSync` whenever
`!in.Status.LastSync.IsZero()`, with no check of any failure indicator, and its catalog description
(`catalog.go:47-54`) overclaims it as "Unix timestamp of the integration's last **successful** sync".
`internal/tsapi/posture.go:13-40` decodes only `ID`/`Provider`/`LastSync`/`MatchedCount`/
`PossibleMatchedCount`/`ProviderHostCount` from the wire `status` object — it has no field at all for
`status.error`. Tailscale's own OpenAPI spec (`spec/tailscale-api.json:6567-6608`) documents
`status.error` ("If the last synchronization failed, this shows the error message...") and its model
example shows a *failing* integration with `error` populated alongside a **fresh** `lastSync` and
`matchedCount`/`possibleMatchedCount`/`providerHostCount` all `0` — i.e. `lastSync` records the last
synchronization *attempt*, not the last successful one.

The matched/possible/provider-host-count gauges *do* already collapse to 0 and get exported on a
failing sync, so a symptom signal already exists in telemetry today — what's genuinely missing is
the human-readable error text and a dedicated success/health indicator, plus the wrong "successful"
wording in the catalog description.

## Evidence

- `internal/collector/postureintegrations/postureintegrations.go:86-89` — emits `docLastSync`
  gated only on non-zero, no failure check.
- `internal/collector/postureintegrations/catalog.go:47-54` — description says "last successful
  sync".
- `internal/tsapi/posture.go:13-40` — no `error` field decoded.
- `spec/tailscale-api.json:6567-6608` — vendor spec confirms `status.error` exists and `lastSync`
  updates on failed attempts too.
- Precedent already in the codebase: `internal/tsapi/logstream.go`'s `LastError` field →
  `internal/collector/logstream/logstream.go:138-150` emits a `docError` gauge plus an ERROR
  `LogEvent` with the error body — the same pattern posture integrations should follow.

## Failure scenario / impact

An MDM/EDR integration (e.g. Intune) gets a revoked client secret or an expired OAuth grant. Every
600s the provider keeps retrying and updating `lastSync` to "now" while
`matchedCount`/`possibleMatchedCount`/`providerHostCount` collapse to 0 (an already-exported symptom
signal). An operator alerting solely on `tailscale_posture_integration_last_sync_seconds` staleness
sees a perpetually fresh timestamp and concludes the integration is healthy, while the human-readable
root cause (the API-provided error string) is nowhere in the exported telemetry.

## Suggested direction

Decode `status.error` in `internal/tsapi/posture.go` and surface it (a health/error gauge, or an
ERROR-severity log event containing the error text) mirroring the existing `log_stream` `LastError`
handling; correct the `last_sync` description to stop calling it a "successful" sync.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `status.error` is decoded and surfaced (health gauge and/or ERROR log event containing the
      error text)
- [ ] the catalog description for `last_sync` describes it as the last synchronization *attempt*,
      not "successful"
- [ ] a test covers a failing-sync response and asserts the error is surfaced

_Found by automated v1 bug bash, 2026-07-03. Verified adversarially by opus._

comments.body:
**From the v1 bug-bash round-2 sweep:**

The shipped `ts2o-posture-integration-stale` alert (`deploy/alerts/gen/build_rules.py:478-486`, unpaused starter set) is structurally unable to fire for the same root cause already tracked in this issue: Tailscale updates `status.lastSync` on every sync *attempt*, including failures, so a persistently failing posture integration (bad credentials, revoked tenant) keeps `lastSync` fresh and `time() - lastSync` never exceeds the alert's 24h threshold. The gauge only goes stale if Tailscale stops attempting syncs entirely — it cannot detect a broken-but-retrying integration.

`internal/tsapi/posture.go:31-40` deliberately does not decode `status.error`, so the actual failure signal is dropped at decode time and nothing downstream can alert on it — unlike logstream, where `lastError` IS collected as `tailscale.logstream.error`.

Fix should also add a `tailscale.posture_integration.error` 0/1 gauge mirroring the existing `tailscale.logstream.error` pattern (surfaced as a gauge, not a label, since the raw error text can embed tenant-identifying strings — consistent with this package's "never emit provider identifiers" stance), and correct the "last successful sync" wording in `docs/metrics.md:333` and `internal/collector/postureintegrations/catalog.go:51` to "last sync attempt" (the vendor API's own wording is "last synchronization", not "last successful sync" — confirmed against `spec/tailscale-api.json:6567` and the FAILED-sync example at `spec/tailscale-api.json:3208-3216`/`6595-6609`, which shows a just-created integration's `lastSync` timestamp equal to its `error` timestamp on an integration that never once succeeded).

_cx=subtle → verified adversarially by opus._

Closed by `6035361`. `status.error` is now decoded (`tsapi/posture.go`) and surfaced as a 0/1 `tailscale.posture_integration.error` gauge (raw text never on a label); `last_sync` description corrected to "last synchronization ATTEMPT" (the API advances lastSync even on failure, so it can't detect a failing sync — the error gauge is the signal). A `ts2o-posture-integration-error` Grafana alert rule was added and the previously-unfireable staleness rule annotated. Test covers a failing-sync response → gauge=1 with no text leak. _(deploy alert by a Sonnet subagent; core tsapi/collector fix on main.)_

body:
## Problem

`internal/app/nodediscovery.go:87-109` (`disambiguateInstances`) builds its collision `counts` map
purely from the *current* `targets` slice returned by a single `Discover()` call. Whether a given
device's instance label gets the `@address` disambiguation suffix depends entirely on which other
devices happen to be present in that same discovery result — as devices with a colliding non-unique
`instance_source` value (e.g. `hostname: "localhost"`) go on/offline between discovery refreshes, a
device that no longer collides in one cycle reverts to its bare (unsuffixed) instance label, then
gets re-suffixed once its sibling reappears. Separately, `unionTargets`
(`internal/collector/nodemetrics/nodemetrics.go:496-512`) merges the discovered batch with
`c.static` and dedups *only* by `Target.URL` — disambiguation never runs against `c.static` at all,
so an operator-configured static target and a discovered device sharing the same instance value are
silently merged with no warning.

This only manifests under the non-default `instance_source: hostname` config (default is `"name"`,
documented unique, immune to this entirely) combined with duplicate hostnames and device flapping —
a misconfiguration the tool already emits a startup WARN discouraging.

## Evidence

- `internal/app/nodediscovery.go:87-109` (`disambiguateInstances`) — collision set is
  batch-relative, not per-device-stable; corroborated by the existing test
  `TestNodeDiscoverer_DisambiguatesCollidingInstances` (`nodediscovery_test.go:200-205`), which
  asserts assignment is relative to the current batch.
- `internal/collector/nodemetrics/nodemetrics.go:496-512` (`unionTargets`) — dedups strictly by URL,
  never checks `Instance` against `c.static`.
- `internal/config/defaults.go` / `config.go:548` comment — `instance_source: hostname` is
  documented as "NOT unique — collisions ... disambiguated by address + WARN"; default is `"name"`.

## Failure scenario / impact

With `instance_source: hostname` (or a custom static `instance:` colliding with a discovered
device's derived value) and a device flapping online/offline, a sibling's `tailscale.node` label
alternates between `localhost` and `localhost@100.x.y.z` across ticks. The per-series counter-delta
baseline (keyed by name+attrs, `nodemetrics.go:701` `seriesKey`) resets every time the label changes,
silently dropping that one scrape's delta at each transition. A static+discovered instance collision
merges two genuinely different nodes' series under one label with no warning. Impact is transient
telemetry churn (a one-scrape delta gap, label instability), not data corruption or loss, and is
confined to a discouraged non-default configuration.

## Suggested direction

Compute collisions over the full active set (`static ∪ discovered`) rather than the discovery batch
alone, and consider a stable disambiguation key (always suffix by address, or persist prior
assignments) so a device's instance label doesn't change based on which other devices are currently
present.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] instance-label disambiguation is computed over `static ∪ discovered`, not the discovery batch
      alone
- [ ] a device's `tailscale.node` label stays stable regardless of sibling devices' online/offline
      transitions
- [ ] a test covers a static target colliding with a discovered device's instance label

_Found by automated v1 bug bash, 2026-07-03. Verified adversarially by opus._

comments.body: Closed by `403dd98`. For the non-unique `instance_source: hostname`, every instance is now unconditionally address-suffixed (host@address) instead of only batch-colliding ones — so a device's `tailscale.node` label is a pure function of the device (stable across refreshes, distinct from static/bare instances) and no longer flaps as a colliding sibling goes on/offline (which reset the scraper's per-series delta baseline). name/address sources unchanged. Tests: label stable across sibling churn; all hostname instances suffixed; updated the source-mapping/collision tests to the stable behavior.

body:
## Problem

`internal/collector/auditlogs/auditlogs.go:123-129` (`eventKey`) computes the grouped boundary-dedup
key as *only* `eventGroupID + "|" + eventTime`, omitting action/target — even though the sibling,
more-careful `empty-groupID` branch on the same function (line 128) deliberately includes
`Action + Target.ID` "so distinct events sharing a timestamp are not collapsed", with its own guard
test. The cross-source processor-level dedup key (`internal/audit/processor.go:124-127`) is even
more precise, including `Action + Target.ID + Target.Property`, because "within one eventGroupID
each (action, target, property) is a distinct sub-change" (verified unique across a real 70-event
capture, `processor.go:110-112`). The collector's coarser key runs *first* and would silently drop a
distinct sub-change before it ever reaches the processor's finer key.

## Evidence

- `internal/collector/auditlogs/auditlogs.go:123-129` (`eventKey`) — grouped branch:
  `groupID + "|" + t` only.
- `internal/collector/auditlogs/auditlogs.go:128` — empty-groupID branch already includes
  `Action + Target.ID` with a dedicated test
  (`TestCollectWindow_DistinctEmptyGroupIDNotCollapsed`, `auditlogs_test.go:160-203`).
- `internal/audit/processor.go:110-112,124-127` — the finer, verified-unique key that the collector's
  coarse key can prevent from ever being reached.

## Failure scenario / impact

A multi-part admin operation (e.g. an ACL update changing three properties in one operation) produces
several audit events sharing one `eventGroupID`. If two or more of those sub-events are stamped with
an identical `eventTime` (plausible for a single transaction; not API-guaranteed either way — this is
an unverified precondition, not a proven real-world occurrence), the collector's coarse key admits
only the first and silently drops the rest before the processor's finer key would have preserved
them — two configuration-audit events lost with no error or drop metric. No test or real capture at
HEAD currently demonstrates this exact same-time-distinct-identity input actually occurring.

## Suggested direction

Align the collector's grouped `eventKey` with the processor's sub-change identity — append
`action|target.id|target.property` to the `groupID|time` key. This stays boundary-safe (a boundary
repeat has identical everything) while never collapsing distinct sub-changes. Verify against a real
`.capture` fixture whether same-group same-time events actually occur in practice.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] the grouped `eventKey` includes `action`/`target.id`/`target.property` alongside
      `groupID`/`time`
- [ ] the existing boundary-safety test (`TestCollectWindow_DistinctEmptyGroupIDNotCollapsed`-style
      coverage) is retained/extended for the grouped case
- [ ] verified against a real `.capture` fixture if available, to confirm same-group same-time
      sub-events actually occur

_Found by automated v1 bug bash, 2026-07-03. Verified adversarially by opus._

comments.body: Closed by `47f0eb1`. The bug was in `internal/collector/auditlogs/auditlogs.go`'s `eventKey` (not `internal/audit`, whose `DedupKey` was already correct). The grouped branch now keys on `eventGroupID|time|action|target.id|target.property` instead of just `eventGroupID|time`, so two distinct sub-changes sharing a group ID and identical event time no longer collapse. Boundary-safe (a true repeat has identical everything). Test `TestCollectWindow_DistinctGroupedEventsSameTimeNotCollapsed` covers it. (No `.capture` fixture present locally to also verify against.)

body:
## Problem

`internal/stream/stream.go:548-580` (`extractRecords`) decodes the concatenated-JSON HEC body with a
`json.Decoder` loop; on any mid-stream syntax error it discards every value already decoded
(`values = nil`) and falls back to a newline-split path (`:568-576`) that only works for NDJSON. But
the package doc (`stream.go:10-14`) pins the *real* Tailscale wire format as "one-or-more
concatenated Splunk-HEC objects with NO separators" (~73 records per POST observed). Reproduced
empirically: `json.Decoder` correctly decodes the valid prefix of a concatenated no-separator body
and only errors on reaching a syntactically-malformed object; the newline fallback salvages zero
records from such a body since `json.Valid` fails on the whole concatenated blob. So one malformed
record anywhere in a batch causes the *entire* batch to be rejected as `unparsable`, not just the
bad record.

## Evidence

- `internal/stream/stream.go:548-580` (`extractRecords`) — discards decoded prefix on decoder error
  (`values = nil`); newline fallback doesn't apply to the real no-separator format.
- `internal/stream/stream.go:10-14` — package doc pinning the real wire format (concatenated, no
  separators).
- `stream.go:303-310` — a rejected batch surfaces as `rejected{reason=unparsable}` (observable, not
  silent).

Note: `json.RawMessage` decoding validates JSON *syntax* only, not schema — a record with unexpected
fields is still valid JSON and would decode fine. The realistic trigger is genuinely
corrupted/truncated wire data (e.g. a torn transfer), not a schema/field-shape surprise.

## Failure scenario / impact

A genuinely truncated or corrupted body (e.g. a torn transfer) inside a ~73-record HEC POST causes
the entire batch to be rejected with a 400 and lost, rather than salvaging the records that decoded
cleanly before the corruption point. The loss is observable via the `rejected{reason=unparsable}`
counter, so it's not silent, but a retry of a genuinely truncated payload would likely succeed on
resend (well-behaved shippers don't typically retry-loop a 4xx indefinitely).

## Suggested direction

Keep the successfully decoded prefix when the decoder errors partway through (only fall back to
line-splitting when zero values were decoded), and count how many values were salvaged vs. dropped
so partial-batch loss is visible.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `extractRecords` preserves the valid decoded prefix instead of discarding it on a mid-stream
      decode error
- [ ] salvaged vs. dropped record counts are visible (metric or log)
- [ ] a test covers a concatenated batch with one malformed record and asserts the valid records
      are still processed

_Found by automated v1 bug bash, 2026-07-03. Verified adversarially by opus._

comments.body: Closed by `829c09a`. `extractRecords` now keeps the decoded prefix when a mid-stream JSON error occurs after ≥1 clean value (the newline-split fallback is reached only when nothing decoded), so one corrupt record no longer rejects an entire separator-less HEC batch; a WARN logs `salvaged_records`/`dropped_bytes`. Tests cover a concatenated batch with a trailing corrupt record and the salvage-vs-fallback priority. Reviewed trade-off: a mid-NDJSON corruption now salvages only the prefix (matching the issue title), which required updating one pre-existing test. _(Sonnet subagent; gated on main.)_

body:
## Problem

Two related robustness gaps in `internal/collector/flowlogs`:

- **Substring-based 403 classification**: `flowlogs.go:237-240` classifies a "feature disabled"
  condition via `strings.Contains(strings.ToLower(err.Error()), "403")` or `"forbidden"`, instead of
  type-checking the error. `internal/tsapi/errors.go:6-8` explicitly documents the intended pattern
  ("Callers can `errors.As` it to branch on the HTTP status code"), and the sibling `logstream`
  collector already does this correctly (`logstream.go:93-94`,
  `errors.As(err,&se) && se.Code>=400 && se.Code<500`). The scanned error text embeds the full
  request URL and up to 16KB of response body (`internal/tsapi/errors.go:17`), plus raw transport
  error strings, so any non-403 failure whose rendered text happens to contain "403" or "forbidden"
  (e.g. a transport error naming a proxy port like `<lan-ip-3>:8403`, or a 5xx body/HTML page
  mentioning "Forbidden") gets misclassified as feature-disabled. A match emits
  `feature.enabled=0` and *advances the checkpoint* (`flowlogs.go:143-150`), silently dropping the
  entire `[from,to]` window of flow logs with the collector reporting success.
- **Catch-up window timeout wedge**: `internal/tsapi/transport.go:58-62`'s `attemptTimeout` (default
  30s, `auth.go:14-16,30`) bounds each HTTP attempt including body read. After an outage longer than
  the poll interval, the next window is capped at `MaxWindow` (default 1h for flowlogs,
  `defaults.go:98`). Flow-log body size scales with tailnet size/activity (measured: 7 MB/hour on a
  26-device tailnet). If streaming+decoding a catch-up window's body takes longer than 30s, the
  attempt deadline fires mid-body; the retry re-fetches the *identical* full-size window (no
  shrink-on-timeout logic anywhere in `window.go`), so every attempt fails identically and
  `CollectWindow` returns a zero high-water mark — the checkpoint never advances and the next tick
  recomputes the same oversized window, a durable wedge until an operator manually raises
  `tailscale.http.timeout` or lowers `max_window`. This is one instance of the collector's
  documented at-least-once retry-on-failure design, not a distinct bug in the retry mechanism
  itself — but there's no shrink/scale mitigation for the specific timeout case, and no doc note
  that `max_window` and `http.timeout` need to be tuned together.

## Evidence

- `internal/collector/flowlogs/flowlogs.go:143-150,237-240` (`isForbidden`, checkpoint-advancing
  match)
- `internal/tsapi/errors.go:6-8,16-17` (intended `errors.As` pattern; error text embeds URL + body)
- `internal/collector/logstream/logstream.go:93-94` (correct precedent already in the codebase)
- `internal/tsapi/transport.go:58-62`, `internal/tsapi/auth.go:14-16,30` (30s `attemptTimeout`)
- `internal/config/defaults.go:98` (flowlogs `MaxWindow` default 1h)
- `internal/collector/window.go` (no shrink-on-timeout logic; identical window recomputed each tick)

## Failure scenario / impact

A deployment egresses through a proxy on port 8403 that goes down for an hour: every flowlogs tick
during the outage is classified as feature-off, the checkpoint keeps advancing, and an hour of flow
logs is permanently lost with no scrape error recorded. Separately, a 400-node tailnet's exporter
down for 2 hours: on restart, every flowlogs tick times out at 30s downloading the 1h catch-up
window, forever — flow data stops permanently while other collectors look healthy (though the
flowlogs collector itself does emit classified timeout scrape-error metrics and surfaces the failure
on the status page, so it's not fully silent to an operator watching self-obs).

## Suggested direction

Classify with `errors.As(&tsapi.StatusError{})` and `Code == 403` (keeping at most a narrow
fallback), and never advance the checkpoint on ambiguous errors. For the timeout wedge: shrink the
window on timeout-classified failures, or scale the attempt timeout for the logging endpoints (known
large bodies), or document that `max_window` and `http.timeout` must be tuned together.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `isForbidden` uses `errors.As` on `*tsapi.StatusError` with `Code == 403`, following the
      logstream precedent
- [ ] the checkpoint is never advanced on an ambiguous/misclassified error
- [ ] a timeout on a catch-up window no longer wedges permanently (window shrink, timeout scaling,
      or documented tuning coupling between `max_window` and `http.timeout`)
- [ ] tests cover both the classification fix and the timeout-wedge mitigation

_Found by automated v1 bug bash, 2026-07-03. Verified adversarially by opus._

comments.body: Closed by `3b4cbbb`. `isForbidden` now uses `errors.As(err, *tsapi.StatusError)` + `Code==403` (logstream precedent) instead of substring-matching the error text (which embeds the URL + up to 16KB of body), so a non-403 error containing "403"/"forbidden" (e.g. a `:8403` proxy port, a 5xx HTML body) is no longer misclassified as feature-off — it propagates and the checkpoint is NOT advanced. Timeout-wedge mitigated via the documented `max_window`↔`tailscale.http.timeout` tuning coupling (window-shrink judged out of scope). Tests: 403-StatusError→feature-off, plus three ambiguous-text traps→not-misclassified + checkpoint-not-advanced. _(Implemented by a Sonnet subagent; reviewed + gated on the main thread.)_

body:
## Problem
`otlp.tls.insecure` is documented as "skip TLS certificate verification (debugging only)," but the implementation actually disables TLS entirely — it maps to plaintext transport (`WithInsecure()` on every exporter: metrics, logs, grpc, traces). Because option order applies the endpoint URL first and then `WithInsecure()`, setting `insecure: true` overrides even an `https://` endpoint's scheme-derived security, so the exporter POSTs plaintext HTTP — transmitting the `Authorization: Basic <instanceID:token>` header (Grafana Cloud's Basic-auth credential) in cleartext on the wire. There is also no real certificate-skip-verify knob at all: `tlsConfig` never sets `InsecureSkipVerify`. Three docs currently disagree with each other: `config.example.yaml` and the generated `docs/env-vars.md` both have the wrong ("skip verification") wording, while `docs/configuration.md` has the correct ("disable transport security / plaintext") wording.

## Evidence
- `config.example.yaml:94`: `insecure: false  # skip TLS certificate verification (debugging only — do not use in production)` — wrong wording, propagated into `docs/env-vars.md:58` (generated from this comment).
- `docs/configuration.md:221`: "Disable transport security (plaintext)" — the correct wording.
- `internal/telemetry/provider.go:512-513` (metrics), `:557-558` (logs), `:528-533` (grpc), `trace.go:35-36` (traces) — all append `WithInsecure()`, which the underlying `otlpmetrichttp`/`oconf` library treats as "no TLS," not "skip cert verification."
- `internal/telemetry/provider.go:588-612` (`tlsConfig`) — never sets `InsecureSkipVerify`, confirming no real skip-verify option exists.
- `internal/app/options.go:26-29` — builds the `Authorization: Basic <instanceID:token>` header sent over whatever transport `insecure` selects.

## Failure scenario / impact
An operator with a self-signed OTLP gateway certificate reads `config.example.yaml`, sets `otlp.tls.insecure: true` expecting skip-verify (the documented meaning), and instead sends their Grafana Cloud Basic-auth token unencrypted across the network on every export cycle — while exports themselves still fail, since the far end expects TLS.

## Suggested direction
Fix the `config.example.yaml` comment (and regenerate `docs/env-vars.md`) to say "disable TLS / plaintext," matching `docs/configuration.md`. Add a real `insecure_skip_verify` option for the self-signed-cert use case, mirroring the node-metrics TLS config, and document the Basic-auth-in-cleartext hazard of the existing `insecure` flag explicitly.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] `config.example.yaml` and the regenerated `docs/env-vars.md` describe `otlp.tls.insecure` correctly (disables TLS/plaintext, not cert-verification skip), matching `docs/configuration.md`.
- [ ] A real `insecure_skip_verify`-style option exists for the self-signed-certificate use case (or its absence is explicitly documented as a deliberate gap).
- [ ] The Basic-auth-in-cleartext hazard of `insecure: true` is documented.

_Found by automated v1 bug bash, 2026-07-03. Verified adversarially by sonnet._

comments.body: Closed by `33942fe` (Phase 6 code/security). See the commit body for specifics.

Also: added the real skip-verify knob `otlp.tls.insecure_skip_verify` (keep TLS on, skip server-cert verification; default false, footgun-guarded, wired config→telemetry→tlsConfig, mirroring node_metrics targets), corrected `config.example.yaml`'s misleading `insecure`='skip verification' comment, and rewrote the configuration.md callout (in `edeec54`) now that the knob exists. Test asserts it builds a skip-verify tls.Config even with no CA files.

body:
## Problem

`internal/collector/scheduler.go:216-233` computes `failed := panicked || runErr != nil` with no
branch for shutdown cancellation, so on SIGTERM, any collector mid-tick that returns a
`context.Canceled`-wrapped error is treated identically to a real API failure: `scrape.success=0`
is emitted, `scrape.errors` is incremented, a `"collector failed"` WARN log fires
(`scheduler.go:250-252`), and the failure is recorded into the `StatusTracker` (`:243`).
`selfobs.go:123-131` (`scrapeErrorType`) classifies `context.Canceled` as a generic `"error"` — there
is no `Canceled` branch (only `DeadlineExceeded` is special-cased). Because the emitter uses sync
gauges/counters, the final telemetry shutdown flush (`app.go:505-507`) exports these values as the
last-ever sample for that collector.

## Evidence

- `internal/collector/scheduler.go:216-233` — `failed := panicked || runErr != nil`, no
  `context.Canceled` branch.
- `internal/collector/scheduler.go:250-252` — WARN log on every clean shutdown that catches a
  collector mid-tick.
- `internal/collector/selfobs.go:123-131` (`scrapeErrorType`) — no `Canceled` classification.

## Failure scenario / impact

Every deploy/restart of an instance with in-flight ticks can flip `scrape.success` to 0 as the
final exported value and increment `scrape.errors`, plus emit a WARN log on routine rollouts. In
practice this is bounded: the repo's own shipped alert rules
(`deploy/alerts/tailscale2otel.rules.yaml`) both use a 15-minute `for:` window
(`CollectorScrapeFailing`, `CollectorScrapeErrorRateHigh`), and a rollout completes in seconds — a
single terminal sample or one counter tick cannot sustain a 15-minute firing condition. Residual
real impact is a cosmetic transient dashboard blip, one counter increment, and one extra WARN log
per mid-tick shutdown; it could still spuriously trip a custom user alert with no `for:` guard.

## Suggested direction

Detect `errors.Is(err, context.Canceled)` (when the parent ctx is done) in `runTick` and skip
failure accounting/logging for it, or classify it distinctly and exclude it from `success=0`.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] a collector tick that fails purely due to shutdown-context cancellation is not counted as a
      scrape failure in metrics, status, or WARN logs
- [ ] a test exercises a collector mid-tick at shutdown and asserts no failure is recorded

body:
## Problem
Several ticker-driven reporters lack emission-asserting tests, leaving invariants as prose rather than executable checks:

- **The app-level final rollup flush on shutdown is untested.** `Run()` performs an "authoritative final flush" of each runtime's rollup accumulator after the schedulers stop and before telemetry shutdown, explicitly to avoid losing the last interval's accumulated counts. No existing test processes any flow records in rollup mode before cancelling `Run()`, so this path is never exercised or asserted.
- **`runRollupFlusher` and `runCardinalityReporter` are the only two ticker-driven reporters without synctest tick coverage.** Both wrap a `time.NewTicker` in the identical `select{ctx.Done()/t.C}` pattern as their sibling reporters (heartbeat, confighealth, sampler, runtimeobs, dedupobs, updatecheck) — all of which ARE tick-tested with `testing/synctest` — but no test ever advances the clock and asserts the ticker branch actually invokes `FlushRollup`/`reportCardinalityCycle`. This is a test-coverage gap, not a known-broken code path: the dispatched functions (`reportCardinalityCycle`, `FlushRollup`) each already have their own direct unit tests: only the thin ticker/select plumbing that dispatches to them is uncovered.

## Evidence
- `internal/app/app.go:496-502` — the final rollup flush (`rt.flowProc.FlushRollup(rt.emitter)`) after schedulers stop, before telemetry shutdown.
- `internal/app/app_test.go`'s `TestApp_RunGracefulShutdown` (line 649) never processes flow records in rollup mode before cancelling.
- `internal/app/rollupflusher.go:19-36` (`runRollupFlusher`) and `internal/app/cardinality.go:52-69` (`runCardinalityReporter`) — both a `time.NewTicker(interval)` + `select{ctx.Done()/t.C}` loop.
- `internal/app/rollupflusher_test.go`/`internal/app/cardinality_test.go` — both pre-cancel `ctx` before the ticker ever fires; neither imports `testing/synctest`.
- Sibling comparison (`rg -l synctest internal/app/*.go`): `confighealth_test.go`, `heartbeat_test.go`, `runtimeobs_test.go`, `dedupobs_test.go`, `sampler_test.go`, `updatecheck_test.go` all drive their ticker loops with `synctest.Test` + `time.Sleep` + `synctest.Wait()`.
- `reportCardinalityCycle` already has direct unit coverage (`TestReportCycleEmitsByGroup`), and `FlushRollup` has extensive direct coverage in `internal/flowlog` (10+ call sites across `processor_rollup_test.go`/`catalog_test.go`) — the gap is specifically the ticker/select dispatch, not the dispatched logic.

## Failure scenario / impact
A code change that reorders the final flush after `a.shutdown(shutdownCtx)` (which tears down the OTLP exporters), drops the loop over `a.runtimes`, or breaks either reporter's select loop specifically, would silently drop up to one full export interval's worth of rollup counters on every graceful restart, or stop periodic cardinality/rollup reporting entirely after the first tick — and nothing in the test suite would fail. This is a real but self-revealing failure mode (dashboards going flat) rather than silent corruption.

## Suggested direction
Extend `TestApp_RunGracefulShutdown` (or add a focused test) to configure rollup mode, feed the flow processor a record before cancelling the run context, and assert the rollup counters appear in the recorder after `Run()` returns. Add a `synctest.Test` case per function (`runRollupFlusher`, `runCardinalityReporter`) that starts the goroutine with an injected processor/tracker, advances the fake clock by one interval, and asserts the expected emission fired — mirroring `TestRunConfigHealthReporter_EmitsImmediatelyThenOnTick`.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A test (extending `TestApp_RunGracefulShutdown` or a new focused test) asserts rollup counters are flushed to the recorder on shutdown in rollup mode.
- [ ] `synctest`-based tick-driven tests exist for `runRollupFlusher` and `runCardinalityReporter`, mirroring the sibling reporters' pattern.

_Found by automated v1 bug bash, 2026-07-03. Verified adversarially by sonnet._

Added `TestApp_RunFlushesRollupOnShutdown` (feeds the rollup accumulator, runs+cancels `App.Run`, asserts the `*.rollup` counters appear only via the authoritative final flush — the 60s ticker can't fire in the window) and `testing/synctest` tick tests for `runRollupFlusher` and `runCardinalityReporter` (nothing before the first tick; the expected emission after one interval), mirroring the sibling reporters' pattern.

body:
## Problem

`internal/telemetry/emitter.go:268-302` (`buildAttrs`) appends the const attrs
(`tailscale.tailnet`/`tailscale2otel.provider`) *after* `resolveLabelCollisions` runs, on the
reasoning (stated in a comment at `emitter.go:268-271`) that "no collector emits
`tailscale.tailnet`/`tailscale2otel.provider` as a data-point attr ... so a plain append is safe".
That reasoning is flawed: it checks the exact dotted OTEL key, but the collision that actually
matters is on the *normalized* Prometheus label name. `internal/collector/nodemetrics/nodemetrics.go`
forwards arbitrary scraped/target labels and only strips `tailscale_node`
(`mergeAttrs`, lines 730-746) — it does not strip `tailscale_tailnet`/`tailscale2otel_provider`. The
repo's own `reservedPromotedLabels` comment (`provider.go:449-456`) documents that a duplicate
normalized label "gets the whole sample rejected as `otlp_parse_error`", and
`reservedPromotedLabels` (`provider.go:457-472`) only lists `job`/`instance`/`service_*` — not these
two const-attr names.

## Evidence

- `internal/telemetry/emitter.go:268-302` (`buildAttrs`) — const attrs appended unconditionally
  after the collision guard: `return append(kvs, e.constAttrs...)`.
- `internal/telemetry/provider.go:449-472` (`reservedPromotedLabels`) — doesn't include
  `tailscale_tailnet`/`tailscale2otel_provider`.
- `internal/collector/nodemetrics/nodemetrics.go:730-746` (`mergeAttrs`) — strips only
  `attrInstancePromLabel` (`tailscale_node`).
- No test covers this collision (`prometheus_test.go:53-84` only checks the const attr appears
  exactly once on the happy path).

## Failure scenario / impact

A node_metrics target (static `labels:` in config, or a custom endpoint reached via discovery)
exposes a series with a label literally named `tailscale_tailnet` or `tailscale2otel_provider`.
Every forwarded sample of that series is rejected by the backend as `otlp_parse_error`; the operator
sees only `export.failures` ticking with no indication which label caused it — the exact failure
class the collision guard was built to prevent. This is reachable only via an operator explicitly
naming a target label after the tool's own reserved namespace (no natural tailscaled scrape triggers
it), so the practical blast radius is small, but the guard should still close the gap.

## Suggested direction

Extend the collision guard to also treat the const attrs' normalized names as reserved
(drop-and-log the data-point copy), or strip those two normalized spellings in nodemetrics
`mergeAttrs` the same way `tailscale_node` already is.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] a passthrough label named `tailscale_tailnet` or `tailscale2otel_provider` is dropped-and-logged
      by the collision guard, not left to cause a sample-rejecting duplicate
- [ ] a test covers a node_metrics target label colliding with a const attr's normalized name

_Found by automated v1 bug bash, 2026-07-03. Verified adversarially by opus._

comments.body: Closed by 16246da. `newOtelEmitter` now adds the normalized names of the const attrs actually present (`tailscale_tailnet`, `tailscale2otel_provider`) to the reserved set, so a data-point/passthrough attr colliding with one is dropped-and-logged by `resolveLabelCollisions` (like `job`/`instance`/`service_*`) rather than appended as a duplicate. Test drives a node_metrics-style passthrough label named `tailscale_tailnet`/`tailscale2otel_provider` through a real Prometheus scrape and asserts exactly one of each label, with the const value winning.

body:
## Problem
The Helm chart's default `GOGC=200` ships without the `GOMEMLIMIT` backstop that docker-compose applies for the identical memory limit. Doubling `GOGC` from the Go default of 100 lets live heap grow further before a GC cycle triggers — that's fine as long as there's a `GOMEMLIMIT` soft ceiling backing it up, but Go has no automatic cgroup-memory-limit awareness, so without an explicit `GOMEMLIMIT` the runtime has no backstop at all and relies entirely on the periodic GOGC-triggered GC to stay under the container's memory limit.

## Evidence
- `deploy/helm/tailscale2otel/values.yaml:69-73` — `goRuntime.gogc: "200"`, `goRuntime.memLimit: ""` (empty by default).
- `deploy/helm/tailscale2otel/templates/deployment.yaml:44-54` — renders `GOGC` unconditionally but `GOMEMLIMIT` only when `goRuntime.memLimit` is non-empty.
- `deploy/docker-compose.yaml:46-50` — the same 256Mi `mem_limit`, but sets both `GOGC: 200` **and** `GOMEMLIMIT: 230MiB`, with the comment "GOMEMLIMIT below sits ~10% under this so the Go GC backs off before the cgroup OOM-kills the process."
- Verified via `helm template` with default values: the rendered container env contains only `GOGC: "200"`, no `GOMEMLIMIT`.

## Failure scenario / impact
A Helm-deployed pod under real load (flowlog streaming enabled, or a large multi-hundred-device tailnet — both explicitly called out in `values.yaml` comments as needing raised limits) sees a heap growth burst; with `GOGC=200` and no soft memory ceiling, the process can grow past the 256Mi cgroup limit before Go's GC re-triggers, and the kubelet OOM-kills the container — precisely the failure mode the docker-compose default was designed to avoid, but the Helm chart (the primary production deployment surface) doesn't get the same protection.

## Suggested direction
Default `goRuntime.memLimit` in `values.yaml` to a value ~10% under the default `resources.limits.memory` (e.g. `"230MiB"` for the current 256Mi default), mirroring docker-compose — or better, compute it from `.Values.resources.limits.memory` directly in the template.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The Helm chart's default `GOMEMLIMIT` sits ~10% under the default `resources.limits.memory` (statically or computed from the memory limit).
- [ ] `helm-docs` and `values.schema.json` are regenerated to reflect the new default.

_Found by automated v1 bug bash, 2026-07-03. Verified adversarially by sonnet._

comments.body: Closed by `413b314`. The Helm chart now defaults `GOMEMLIMIT` via a `tailscale2otel.gomemlimit` template computing ~90% of `resources.limits.memory` (default 256Mi→230MiB, matching docker-compose; Gi normalized to MiB — a truncation bug was caught/fixed); an explicit `goRuntime.memLimit` still wins, and it's omitted when no memory limit is set. helm-docs README + values.schema.json regenerated (fail-on-diff gate); helm lint/template + configcheck verified. _(Sonnet subagent; gated on main.)_
